en: The Combined Edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra,
compiled by the Sui dynasty śramaṇa Shi Baogui from the translations of the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the great city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Tathāgata was dwelling within the immeasurable and profoundly deep nature of phenomena—the sphere of action of all Buddhas—which transcends the pure conduct of all bodhisattvas.
"This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the king of all sūtras; whoever hears it shall be able to contemplate its unsurpassed, subtle, and profound meaning.
Such a scripture is constantly protected and sustained by the World-Honored Buddhas of the four directions:
Akṣobhya in the east, Ratnaketu in the south, Amitāyus in the west..."
The Northern Sublime Sound said:
"I shall now explain the dharmas of repentance and so forth; the merit thereby produced is unsurpassed, capable of destroying all sufferings and exhausting unwholesome karma:
'All-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) serves as the root; immeasurable merits..."
By this adornment, all sufferings are extinguished and immeasurable bliss is bestowed.
Those with impaired faculties, diminished lifespans, poverty and hardship, those abandoned by the devas,
those embroiled in strife with kin and friends, and those oppressed by royal law— [all these are relieved].
Each shall experience mutual strife and contention; wealth and possessions shall be depleted; there shall be sorrow, anxiety, and terror;
malevolent stars and calamitous portents; various demonic arts and sorcery; and strange transformations shall occur in succession.
Seeing evil dreams while lying down, one shall be plagued by grief and distress during the day. One should, therefore, bathe with purity.
Listen to this sutra with a mind that is utterly sincere and pure; clad in clean and fresh garments, listen single-mindedly to this scripture, the sphere of profound practice.
The majestic power of this sutra can completely eliminate all such evils and cause them to be stilled and extinguished.
The Four World-Protecting Kings, together with their retinues and immeasurable hosts of yakṣas,
will all come to protect those who uphold this scripture.
The Great Eloquence Deity, the Nairañjanā River Deity, the Kūṣmāṇḍī Mother Deity, the Earth Deity Sthāvarā,
the Great Brahmā Honored Deity, the Gods of the Thirty-three Heavens,
the Great Divine Dragon Kings, the Kiṃnara Kings, and the Garuḍa Kings.
The Asura King, together with his retinue,
will all go there to protect this person, never leaving them by day or night.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess profound secrets and subtle spheres of practice;
even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they are extremely difficult to encounter.
Whether one explains it to others, rejoices in it with the heart, or makes offerings to it—
such a person shall, for immeasurable kalpas, always be revered by the devas and the eight classes of beings.
Practicing in this way, those who give rise to merit obtain inconceivable and immeasurable accumulations of blessings;
they are also protected and sustained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the deeply practicing Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Wearing clean garments and offering exquisite incense, one should provide offerings with a compassionate heart,
never departing from them.
With body and mind pure and free from defilement, one shall rejoice with gladness, deeply delighting in this scripture.
If you are able to hear this, know that you have gained a true boon: a human body, a human realm, and a right livelihood.
If you hear this confession and hold it in your heart, this is a supreme root of goodness praised by all Buddhas.

2. Chapter on Life Span (1) The Golden Light Sūtra, Chapter Two: On the Life Span. At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Śraddhālakṣaṇa, who had already made offerings to immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of buddhas in the past and had planted various roots of goodness.
The Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa reflected thus:
"By what cause and by what condition is the lifespan of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni so short, being only eighty years?
He further thought to himself:
“As the Buddha has taught, there are two causes and conditions by which one attains a long life. What are these two?
First, refraining from killing; second, giving food.”

Yet our World-Honored One, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas, has practiced the precept of non-killing, fulfilled the ten wholesome paths of action, and bestowed food and drink in measureless abundance; he even satisfied hungry beings with his own bones, marrow, blood, and flesh—how much more so with other food and drink?

As the Great Being thus mindfully recollects the Buddha and contemplates this meaning with a sincere heart, his chamber spontaneously becomes vast and magnificently adorned; its floor is composed of celestial lapis lazuli and various kinds of precious jewels interspersed and inlaid, just like the pure land where the Tathāgata dwells.
There was a wondrous fragrance—surpassing all celestial perfumes—whose clouds of smoke hung suspended and filled his chamber.
On each of the four sides of the chamber, there spontaneously appeared four exquisite, high seats made of the four precious substances, with cushions made entirely of celestial garments.
Upon each of these exquisite seats there is a Buddha; the flowers they enjoy are composed of various jewels. Upon each lotus flower are four Tathāgatas:
in the east is named Akṣobhya, in the south is named Ratnaketu, in the west is Amitāyus, and in the north is Svarasvati.

These four Tathāgatas spontaneously sat upon lion thrones, emitting a great radiance that illuminated Rājagṛha, this trichiliocosm, and even the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; they rained down celestial flowers and performed celestial music.

At that time, all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, experienced celestial bliss; those with impaired faculties immediately attained their full restoration.
To state the essentials: all the benefits existing in the world and all unprecedented events appeared in their entirety.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, seeing these Buddhas and these rare occurrences, leaped for joy with great exultation. With palms joined in reverence toward the World-Honored Ones, he called the Buddha to mind with utmost sincerity and reflected thus:
"The Tathāgata Śākyamuni possesses immeasurable merit; I have harbored doubts only regarding his lifespan."
"How is it that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is thus only eighty years?
At that time, the four Buddhas, with their perfect and universal knowledge, addressed the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa:
"Good son!..."
You should not now conceive the thought that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is short. Why is this?
O son of good family!

Among the gods, worldlings, hosts of Māras, hosts of Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, and non-humans, we do not see anyone capable of calculating or determining the limit of the Tathāgata’s lifespan, except for the Tathāgata himself.

At that time, as the four Tathāgatas were about to proclaim the lifespan attained by Śākyamuni Buddha, the devas of the desire and form realms, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, all came together and assembled in the chamber of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
At that time, the four Buddhas, in the midst of the great assembly, briefly explained the lifespan attained by Śākyamuni Tathāgata through verses and similes, reciting these stanzas:
"The waters of all the oceans May have their drops counted, But none can calculate The lifespan of the World-Honored Śākyamuni."
The weight of all the Sumeru mountains may be known; There is no one who can measure the lifespan of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni.
The number of dust motes in the entire great earth may be known; There is no one who can calculate the lifespan of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni.
Even the boundaries of space may be reached; There is no one who can reckon it.
The lifespan of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni is incalculable kalpas—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions; such is the Buddha’s life, immeasurable and boundless.
For these reasons, two conditions are taught: not harming the lives of sentient beings, and giving food immeasurably.
Therefore, O Great Being!
His lifespan is incalculable, immeasurable and boundless, without any limit.
Therefore, you should now not harbor doubts regarding the Buddha’s immeasurable life span. (The five lines from "Therefore, you now" onwards are absent in the Danben [Cinnabar Edition]).

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, hearing these four Buddhas proclaim that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is immeasurable, believed and understood it with a profound mind, leaping for joy.
When this "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" was being spoken, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the four Tathāgatas suddenly disappeared. (Supplemented by Xuánjuéduō’s translation.
Then, after the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa had heard from those Buddhas the teaching regarding the lifespan of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, he addressed those Buddhas, saying:
“O World-Honored Ones!”
"How is it that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni manifests such a short lifespan?
When they had spoken thus, those World-Honored Ones addressed the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, saying:

"Indeed, during the age of the five corruptions, when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni appeared in the world with a lifespan of one hundred years, he manifested such a short lifespan in order to benefit ordinary beings and non-Buddhist ascetics such as the Nirgranthas and Parivrājakas—beings of inferior faith and understanding who possess few roots of goodness and are immersed in the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a nourisher (pudgala), wrong views, and the grasping at 'I' and 'mine. It was for their sake that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni manifested such a short lifespan to bring sentient beings to maturity."

“Good son! However, that Tathāgata Śākyamuni has manifested such a short lifespan so that those sentient beings, upon knowing that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, will give rise to thoughts of suffering, thoughts of rarity, thoughts of the unprecedented, and thoughts of sorrow, and will thus swiftly receive such sūtras as these, uphold and recite them, and refrain from slandering them.”
Therefore, the Tathāgata manifests such a short lifespan.

If those sentient beings were to see that the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa, they would not conceive of him as something rare, nor would they feel sorrow or wonder at such an unprecedented occurrence; consequently, they would not accept the various sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, nor would they uphold, read, or recite them.
Why is this? It is because of the view of permanence.
"O son of good family!

For example, suppose there is a man whose parents possess great wealth as the fruit of their merit; yet, once that man's sons have come to know of this accumulation of riches, they do not conceive of it as something marvelous or unprecedented.
Why is this? It is because it yields manifold karmic retributions. Good son!

It is so, it is so. If those sentient beings were to know that the Tathāgata does not enter parinirvāṇa, they would not give rise to the thought of rarity, the thought of something unprecedented, or the thought of something difficult to obtain.
Why is this? It is because of the view of eternalism. "Good son!

For example, suppose there is a man whose parents are poor and possess little karmic fruitfulness; they might go to the house of a king or a royal minister, where he sees various kinds of treasures filling the storehouses and granaries.

In that place, he will attain rare conduct, conceive the thought of what has never been before, and give rise to the thought of its being difficult to obtain; furthermore, for the sake of that accumulation of wealth, he will exert himself and arouse the mind of diligence, desiring to acquire that accumulation of wealth.
Why is this? It is because the retribution is slight. Good son!

It is so, it is so. When those sentient beings see that the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa, they will experience what is rare and unprecedented, and they will conceive the thought of suffering:
"Only after immeasurable time do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world."
Just as the udumbara flower appears in the world only after immeasurable time has passed;
even so, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world only after immeasurable time has passed.
Those sentient beings will attain a rare practice and experience what has never before occurred; they shall be filled with exultation.
Having seen the Tathāgata, they will place their faith and turn toward him; and when they hear the Tathāgata’s true words, they will accept such sūtras and will not oppose or dispute them.
"Good son!
For this reason, the Tathāgata will not remain long in the world, but shall soon enter parinirvāṇa.
Good son!"
"In this way, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity.
At that time, those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, vanished and were no longer seen.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and immeasurable koṭis, nayutas, and hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the presence of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Standing to one side, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa addressed the Buddha regarding all the matters previously described.

Finally, those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, proceeded to Vulture Peak to the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was; having arrived, they each sat upon their seats according to their respective directions.
At that time, each of those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, addressed their respective attendant bodhisattvas, saying:
"O son of good family!
Go to the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is; having arrived, inquire after his welfare on our behalf."
"Are you free from illness? Are you light in body and rising easily? Is your vigor and strength at ease?
They further said: "Excellent!
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni now wishes to proclaim the Dharma-source of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*; we shall rejoice in it."

At that time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas went to where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was; having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and having paid their respects, they withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stood to one side, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The four World-Honored Buddhas of the four directions inquire after your health:”
"World-Honored One!
Are you free from illness and light in your rising? Is your physical strength at ease and your conduct peaceful?
He further spoke these words:
“Excellent,
World-Honored One!

We pray that you will expound the Dharma-fundamental of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and even to eliminate famine and other such calamities.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, praised the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Sons of good family!"
"You have indeed been able to exhort the Tathāgata for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I shall not leave this mountain, But shall constantly preach this treasure of a sutra."
For the sake of maturing sentient beings, I manifest parinirvāṇa;
ordinary people, clinging to views, do not believe what I have taught.
To mature them, I manifest parinirvāṇa.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the great assembly—of the Kauṇḍinya clan, named Ājñāta—who sat among the multitude with a mind of concentrated composure. Surrounded by and together with a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of brahmins, they were all reverently making offerings to the Tathāgata. Hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would enter parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty, they wept and wailed in grief. Together with the multitude of hundreds of thousands of brahmins, they rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!”

If the Buddha-Tathāgata, out of compassion and for the benefit of all sentient beings, with great kindness and great pity, desires that they all attain supreme peace and happiness; if he acts as the true father and mother of sentient beings, the most supreme, the peerless, and the unequaled; if he acts as the refuge and protection for the world, bringing joy and coolness to all beings like the pure full moon emitting great radiance, or like the sun shining upon Mount Udayana; and if the Buddha-Bhagavān regards all sentient beings as he does Rāhula—may the Buddha bestow a single grace upon me.
At that time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not answer.

Within this assembly was the prince of the Licchavi king, named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (Joyful Vision of All Beings), who was present among the great multitude, possessed of perfect eloquence, and skilled in questioning and answering.
At that time, the prince, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, addressed the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, saying: "Great Brahmin!
What grace or merit do you seek from the World-Honored One?"
"I can bestow upon you the boon of your heart's desire.
The brahmin said, "Excellent!"
"O Prince!
We wish to reverently make offerings to the body of the World-Honored One; for this reason, we desire to obtain even as much as a mustard seed of the Tathāgata’s relics. Why is this so?"
As I have heard:
if good men and good women reverently make offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata, they will surely obtain inexhaustible wealth, honor, and peace and happiness as the lords of the six heavens.
At that time, the prince immediately replied:
"Great Brahmin! Listen with a single-minded focus."

If you wish to seek immeasurable merit and the rewards of the six heavens, this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the king of all sūtras—inconceivable and difficult to comprehend—yields inexhaustible blessings and retributions, which cannot be known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"This sutra upholds such merits; its boundless rewards are inconceivable, and I have now briefly explained them for you.
The brahmin said, "Excellent!"
"O Prince!
This subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Golden Light possesses boundless merit; it is difficult to understand and difficult to awaken to, even to the extent that it is inconceivable."
The Brahmins and others of our borderlands speak thus:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family obtains even as much of the Buddha’s relics as a mustard seed and places them within a small stupa, worshipping, honoring, and making offerings to them for a brief moment, their merit will be boundless; at the end of that person's life, they will become a lord of the six heavens of desire, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss that is inexhaustible."
Why do you now not aspire to honor the relics and seek this reward?
It is thus, Prince, for these reasons that I now seek one favor from the Buddha.
At that time, the prince replied to the brāhmaṇa in verse:
"Even if the *kubjaka* flower could grow in the midst of a swift-flowing river,
the bodily relics of the World-Honored One could never exist."
Even if a crow were red in color, or a kokila bird were white in form,
the true body of the World-Honored One could not become śarīra relics;
even if a Jambu tree were able to produce tāla fruit, [it would remain impossible].
Just as the *khajjūra* tree and others can produce the fruit of the *āmra*,
yet the body of the Tathāgata does not perish and cannot produce relics;
even if one could make garments from tortoise hair and the like, [the Buddha’s remains would likewise be impossible].
The Buddha’s body is not illusory, yet in the end there are no śarīras;
even if the legs of a mosquito could be used to build a city tower,
the Tathāgata’s tranquil body has no such matter of śarīras.
Even if leeches were to grow white teeth within their mouths,
The Tathāgata’s body of liberation would never possess the nature of bondage.
One might as well use rabbit horns to build a ladder And ascend from the earth to the heavens.
With wrong reflection regarding the *śarīra*, there is no possibility of merit;
Like a rat climbing a ladder made of rabbit horns to devour the moon and destroy the asuras—
To rely on the *śarīra* to exhaust delusions and attain liberation is impossible.
Like a fly intoxicated by wine, unable to build its nest;
one who lacks right practice toward the Buddha cannot reach the Three Vehicles.
Like a donkey that merely eats its fill, it ultimately possesses no skill or ability.
To delight others through song and dance—
this is impossible for ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles, whether in terms of speech or practice, for themselves or for others.
Even if a crow and an owl were to perch together upon the same tree at the same time, [such a thing could not occur].
United in mutual affection;
the Tathāgata’s true essence and the śarīra’s illusory body—both being present simultaneously is impossible.
Like a leaf from Vārāṇasī, it cannot shield one from wind and rain.
To harbor false conceptions toward the Buddha, one will never escape the cycle of birth and death.
Just as a great ocean-going ship, fully laden with all manner of treasures,
could never be held up by the strength of a newly born woman— it is simply impossible.
The Dharma-body is boundless; the afflictions of the impure stages cannot encompass the Tathāgata—this meaning is likewise so.
It is like various birds and sparrows, which cannot carry away Mount Gandhamādana.
The afflictions rely upon the dharmakāya, yet they do not disturb it.
Such is the body of the Tathāgata—profound and difficult to fathom;
if one does not contemplate it according to the Dharma, one's aspirations will not be fulfilled.
When the brahmin had heard this teaching, he immediately spoke a verse in response to the prince, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You are truly a son of the Buddha!"
O Greatly Auspicious One, you who are skilled in expedient means, remain unshakable in principle and have already received the authentic prediction.
O Prince, listen to me as I now explain in sequence:
the refuge for crossing over the world, the inconceivable virtues of the Buddha;
The realm of the Tathāgata cannot be known by anyone.
All Buddhas do not share it with others;
all Buddhas are from the beginning quiescent.
All Buddhas are identical in their practice;
all Buddhas abide eternally throughout the future;
all Buddhas are of one and the same essence.
Such meanings as these are the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the true body of the Tathāgata, and are not something created. Why is this so?
All Buddhas are unborn; like adamant, they are indestructible. With no obstruction between inner and outer, they manifest physical forms to transform sentient beings according to their needs.
The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, has no physical form; such a body as this is not of flesh and blood.
How, then, can there be śarīras?
To transform sentient beings, they manifest through skillful means.
All Perfectly Awakened Ones take the True Dharma as their body; the purity of the Dharma-realm is what is called the Tathāgata.
"Prince, you should know that the Buddha’s body is thus, as the Tathāgata has taught.
Having heard and understood this, I have requested the Tathāgata to extensively expound and analyze the meaning of reality;
therefore, I seek the śarīra to open the gate of skillful means."

At that time, thirty-two thousand devaputras in the assembly, having heard this teaching on the Tathāgata’s exceedingly profound lifespan, all conceived a firm resolve for unexcelled bodhi. Elated and leaping with joy, they spoke these verses in praise with one voice:
"All Tathāgatas do not enter parinirvāṇa;
The bodies of all Buddhas are indestructible."
It is solely for the sake of maturing all sentient beings that, through skillful means and supreme wisdom, they manifest nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata of the past limit is inconceivable;
the Tathāgata of the future limit is eternally indestructible.
"The Tathāgata of the intermediate period is adorned with various ornaments; for the sake of benefiting others, he pervades the dharma-realm of all sentient beings.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa had heard from the various Tathāgatas and the two Great Beings this explanation of the meaning of Śākyamuni’s lifespan, his wishes were fulfilled. His mind was free from doubt, and he leaped for joy with great delight; happiness filled his body and mind, pervading both internally and externally.
At that time, there were again immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of sentient beings who, upon hearing this teaching, all resolved their minds toward the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the four Tathāgatas suddenly vanished, and within this great assembly, only Śākyamuni remained.

Chapter Three: The Distinction of the Three Bodies (1) The Golden Light Sūtra, Chapter Three: The Distinction of the Three Bodies Translated by Paramārtha, Tripiṭaka Master of the Liang Dynasty At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja rose from his seat amidst the great assembly. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Having offered exquisite flowers of gold and jewels, as well as precious banners and canopies, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the correct cultivation of the Dharma in accordance with all Tathāgatas?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall analyze and explain it for you. "Good son!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should know that all Tathāgatas possess three kinds of bodies."
What are the three?

First, the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body); second, the saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment body); and third, the dharmakāya (dharma body). These three bodies encompass anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment).
“How does a bodhisattva discern the transformation body?
Son of good family!

In the past, while on the stage of practice, the Tathāgata cultivated various dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings. When these cultivated practices reached fulfillment through the power of cultivation, he attained mastery.”

By the power of mastery, in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, their conduct, and the manifold distinctions of their realms, and without waiting for the proper time or missing it, he manifests various bodies corresponding to place, time, conduct, and the teaching of the Dharma; this is called the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
“Good son! These Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach the ultimate truth so that bodhisattvas may attain thorough penetration;

they do so so that one may penetrate the single flavor of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, so that sentient beings who harbor views of a self may experience both fear and joy, and so as to serve as the foundation for the boundless Buddha-dharmas. Thus, the Tathāgata is in accord with suchness.”

By the power of the wisdom and vows of suchness, this body manifests as fully endowed with the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and the circular halo behind the neck and back; this is called the response body (nirmāṇakāya).
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva discern the dharmakāya?

It is because one wishes to eliminate all hindrances such as the various afflictions, and because one wishes to fulfill all wholesome dharmas; there is only suchness and the wisdom of suchness—this is called the dharmakāya.”
"The first two kinds of bodies exist as provisional designations, whereas this third body is called truly existent, for it serves as the basis for the former two. Why is this so?"
Apart from the suchness of dharmas (*dharmatathatā*) and non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), there is no other distinct dharma for all Buddhas. Why is this?

Because all Buddhas are fully endowed with wisdom, because all afflictions have been ultimately extinguished, and because they have attained the pure stage of Buddhahood; therefore, the suchness of dharmas and the wisdom of suchness encompass all Buddha-dharmas.
"Furthermore, noble son!
All Buddhas bring benefit to themselves and others to ultimate perfection.

That which benefits oneself is the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*); that which benefits others is the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*). Because they attain mastery over these various and boundless functions within the sphere of benefiting self and others, the Buddha-dharmas are thus distinguished as being immeasurable and boundless in their variety."
“Good son! For example, based on conceptualization and discursive thought, one speaks of various afflictions, speaks of various karmas, and speaks of various retributions;
likewise, based on suchness (tathatā) and the wisdom of suchness, one speaks of various Buddha-dharmas, speaks of various Pratyekabuddha-dharmas, and speaks of various Śrāvaka-dharmas.”
By relying on the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*), all Buddha-dharmas attain sovereign accomplishment; this is the first inconceivable [quality].
For example, it is difficult to conceive how one might paint ornaments upon empty space;
likewise, it is difficult to conceive how the Buddha-dharmas are gathered and accomplished within the suchness of phenomena and the wisdom of suchness.
“Good son! How does one attain mastery over the two kinds of non-discrimination—namely, the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*)? Good son!”
For example, although the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa, because he possesses mastery over his vows and because various activities remain unfinished, he continues to act;
in this same way, the suchness of phenomena (dharmatathatā) and the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna) attain mastery over their activities.

"Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the concentration of non-thought and, relying on the power of his prior vows, arises from that meditative absorption to engage in activity, these two dharmas are without discrimination, because he has attained mastery over all things."

“Good son! For example, the sun and moon have no discrimination; likewise, water and mirrors have no discrimination; and light also has no discrimination. It is through the conjunction of these three factors that a reflection can appear.”

In this way, both the suchness of phenomena (dharmatathatā) and the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna) are without discrimination; yet, through the sovereignty of vows, when sentient beings have a resonance with them, the two bodies—the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and the transformation-body (sambhogakāya)—are produced in conjunction like the reflections of the sun and moon.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like immeasurable and boundless water-mirrors; by depending upon light, various different forms of empty reflections appear. That which is 'empty' is precisely signless (animitta)."

“Good son! In this way, the assembly of disciples who have been transformed by the teachings are reflections of the Dharma-body. By the power of their vows, they manifest various appearances within the two bodies, yet within the ground of the Dharma-body, there are no distinct characteristics.”
“Good son! Based on these two bodies, all Buddhas speak of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder);
based on the *dharmakāya*, they speak of *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).”
Why is this? Because all other [conditioned] things have been completely exhausted.
Based on these three bodies, all Buddhas speak of non-abiding nirvana.
Why is this? Because of the two bodies, he does not abide in nirvāṇa;
apart from the dharma-body, there is no other Buddha.
For what reason do the two bodies not abide in nirvana?
Because the two bodies are merely provisional designations and lack substantial reality; they perish moment by moment and do not abide, appearing repeatedly because they are indeterminate.
The Dharma-body is not like this.
Therefore, the two bodies do not abide in nirvāṇa;
as for the dharma-body, it is non-dual, and thus it does not abide in parinirvāṇa.
It is based upon the three bodies that "non-abiding nirvāṇa" is taught.
“Good son! Because all ordinary beings are subject to the three marks, they possess bondage and hindrances; they remain far removed from the three bodies and do not attain the three bodies.”
What are these three? First, the characteristic of conceptualization through discursive thought; second, the characteristic of dependence on others; and third, the characteristic of perfection.
Because these characteristics cannot be understood, cannot be extinguished, and cannot be purified, one is therefore unable to attain the three bodies (trikāya).
These three characteristics can liberate, extinguish, and purify; therefore, all Buddhas are fully endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*). "Good son!
Because ordinary worldlings have not yet uprooted these three minds, they remain far removed from the three bodies and cannot attain them."
What are these three?
First, the mind that initiates activity; second, the mind that relies on the fundamental mind; and third, the fundamental mind.
Through reliance on the various paths of subduing, the mind that initiates activity is exhausted.
By means of the path of abandonment according to the Dharma, the fundamental mind is exhausted through reliance;
by means of the path of supreme extraction, the fundamental mind is exhausted.
Because the mind that gives rise to phenomena ceases, the manifestation body (nirmāṇakāya) is revealed.
Because the fundamental mind is extinguished, the response body (nirmāṇakāya) is manifested;
because the fundamental mind is extinguished, one attains the dharma body (dharmakāya).
Therefore, all Tathāgatas are fully endowed with the three bodies.

“Good son! All Buddhas share the same activity as all other Buddhas in their first body; they share the same intention as all other Buddhas in their second body; and they share the same essence as all other Buddhas in their third body.”
“Good son! This first Buddha-body manifests various marks because it accords with the diverse intentions of sentient beings; therefore, it is said to be ‘many.
This second Buddha-body manifests a single mark because its disciples have a single intention; therefore, it is said to be ‘one.’”
This is the third Buddha-body, which transcends all characteristics of every kind and is not a realm of grasped characteristics; therefore, it is called neither one nor two. "Good son!
This first body (the *svābhāvika-kāya*) is manifested by depending upon the *nirmāṇa-kāya*;
these various *nirmāṇa-kāyas* are manifested by depending upon the *dharmakāya*.
This *dharmakāya* is truly existent, as it has no further basis upon which to depend.
“Good son! Regarding these three bodies, they are said to be permanent for certain reasons, and they are said to be impermanent for certain reasons.

As for the Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body), because it constantly turns the wheel of Dharma, manifests in accordance with reality everywhere, and continues its skillful means without interruption, it is therefore said to be permanent.”
Because it is not the fundamental [nature], and because its complete functioning is not manifested, it is said to be impermanent.

As for the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya), because it has continued uninterruptedly through beginningless saṃsāra, and because it is able to sustain all the unique qualities of the Buddhas; and because as long as sentient beings are not exhausted, its function is likewise not exhausted, it is therefore said to be permanent.
Yet, because it is not the fundamental [nature], and because its complete functioning is not manifested, it is therefore said to be impermanent.
The Dharma-body is not a conditioned phenomenon; it is without differentiation or distinction because it is its own fundamental source, just like empty space.
Therefore, it is said to be eternal. "Good son!
Apart from non-conceptual wisdom, there is no superior wisdom;
apart from the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*), there is no superior realm.
This suchness of phenomena and the wisdom of suchness—these two kinds of suchness—are neither identical nor different.
Therefore, because the wisdom of the dharma-body is pure and its cessation is pure, these two are pure.
Consequently, the dharma-body is fully endowed with purity.
"Furthermore, good son, there are four kinds of bodies when distinguished:

there is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) that is not the response body (saṃbhogakāya); there is the response body that is not the transformation body; there is that which is both the transformation body and the response body; and there is that which is neither the transformation body nor the response body."
What is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) that is not the response body (saṃbhogakāya)?
When the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa, this kind of body—which exists by virtue of mastery over his vows—is the transformation body.
What is the response body (saṃbhogakāya) that is not the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya)?
It is the stage prior to the [ten] stages (bhūmi).
What is the transformation body that is also the response body?
The body of the Tathāgata abides in *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*.
What is neither a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) nor a response body (*saṃbhogakāya*)?
It is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata.
“Good son! This Dharma-body is manifested because of the non-existence of duality.
What is meant by the non-existence of duality?

Regarding this Dharma-body, both its characteristics and the locus of those characteristics are non-existent; they are neither existent nor non-existent, neither one nor two, neither numerical nor non-numerical, and neither luminous nor dark.

In this way, the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna) does not perceive characteristics or the locus of characteristics; it does not perceive that which is neither existent nor non-existent; it does not perceive that which is neither identical nor different; it does not perceive that which is neither numerical nor non-numerical; it does not perceive that which is neither light nor darkness.
Therefore, the purity of the objective realm and the purity of wisdom are indivisible and without interval.
Because it is the fundamental source of cessation and the path, the Tathāgata manifests within this Dharmakāya.

“Good son! Because the causes, conditions, objects, and locations of this body, as well as the fruit that depends upon its basis, are difficult to conceive, if explained according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), this body is itself the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgata-nature, and the Tathāgata-garbha.”

Based upon this body, the initial resolve is generated; within the mind of practice, the mind of non-retrogression on the stages is fully manifested; the mind of the stage of one birth remaining before Buddhahood, the diamond-like mind, and the Tathāgata-mind are all fully manifested; and the immeasurable, boundless, wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgatas is entirely revealed.

It is by relying on this inconceivable mahāsamādhi of the dharmakāya that [the other bodies] are manifested; it is by relying on this dharmakāya that all great wisdoms are made manifest. Therefore, the two bodies are manifested by relying upon samādhi and by relying upon wisdom.

"Thus, this Dharma-body is said to be eternal and real by virtue of its own essence; it is said to be blissful by virtue of the great samādhi; and it is said to be pure by virtue of great wisdom. Therefore, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, sovereign, blissful, and pure."

Based on the Great Samādhi, all meditative concentrations such as the Śūraṅgama, all foundations of mindfulness such as the Great Dharma-mindfulness, great loving-kindness and great compassion, all dhāraṇīs, all six supernormal powers, all masteries, and the impartial embrace of all dharmas—all such Buddha-dharmas thus manifest.

Relying on this great wisdom, the Buddha’s ten great powers, four fearlessnesses, four unimpeded analytical knowledges, one hundred and eighty unique qualities, and all rare and inconceivable dharmas are fully manifested.
For example, just as by relying on a wish-fulfilling jewel, immeasurable and boundless varieties of all kinds of jewels appear;
so too, by relying on the jewel of the great samādhi and the jewel of great wisdom, there emerge the immeasurable and boundless jewels of the various sublime dharmas of the Buddhas.

“Good son! Thus, the samādhi and wisdom of the dharmakāya transcend all marks; they do not cling to marks and are beyond conceptual discrimination. They are neither eternal nor annihilated; this is called the Middle Way.”

Although there is conceptual differentiation, it lacks the substance of differentiation; although there are three numbers, they lack three substances. There is neither increase nor decrease; they are like dreams and illusions, with neither that which is grasped nor that which grasps.

The essence of the Dharma is suchness; it is the locus of liberation, transcending the realm of the King of Death and surpassing the darkness of birth and death. It is that which all sentient beings are unable to cultivate, that which cannot be reached by any practice, and the dwelling place of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

“Good son! It is like a person who, desiring to obtain gold, searches everywhere until he sees gold ore. Having found it, he breaks the ore and selects the gold, placing it in a furnace. By refining and smelting it, he obtains pure gold, which he may then fashion at will into various rings, bracelets, and diverse ornaments. Although it serves many purposes, the nature of the gold remains unchanged.”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, seeking supreme liberation and practicing worldly virtues, should behold the Tathāgata and his assembly of disciples; having approached them, they should address the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is wholesome?
What is unwholesome?
What is right practice that leads to purity and liberation from impurity?
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and their assemblies of disciples think thus:
"This son of good family or daughter of good family desires to seek purity and desires to hear the true Dharma."
Having understood this, he then preached the True Dharma:

"When these sons and daughters of good family have heard the True Dharma, they maintain it with right mindfulness and resolve to practice it, thereby attaining the power of diligence to break through the obstacle of indolence."
Having overcome the obstacle of laziness, one eliminates all obstacles of sinful karma;
having overcome the obstacles of sinful karma, one overcomes the obstacle of lack of respect regarding the bodhisattva training;
and having overcome the obstacle of lack of respect, one overcomes the mind of agitation and regret.
Having destroyed the mind of regret, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Relying on the first stage, one uproots the obstacle to benefit; having uprooted the obstacle to benefit, one attains entry into the second stage.
Relying on the second stage, one destroys the obstacle of being oppressed by affliction and suffering; having destroyed this obstacle, one enters the third stage.
Relying on these three stages, one destroys the obstacle to the pliancy and purity of mind; having destroyed the obstacle to the pliancy and purity of mind, one enters the fourth stage.
Relying on this fourth stage, one destroys the obstacle to skillful means; having destroyed the obstacle to skillful means, one enters the fifth stage.

Relying on this fifth stage, one destroys the obstacle to the vision of the ultimate and the conventional; having destroyed the obstacle to the vision of the ultimate and the conventional, one enters the sixth stage.
Relying on this sixth stage, one destroys the obstacle of the mode of activity of views; having destroyed the obstacle of the mode of activity of views, one enters the seventh stage.

Relying on this seventh stage, one destroys the obstacle of not seeing the characteristic of cessation; having destroyed the obstacle of not seeing the characteristic of cessation, one enters the eighth stage.

Relying on this eighth stage, one destroys the obstacle of not seeing the characteristic of arising; having destroyed the obstacle of not seeing the characteristic of arising, one enters the ninth stage.
By relying on these nine stages, one destroys the obstacles to the six supernormal powers; having destroyed the obstacles to the six supernormal powers, one enters the tenth stage.
By relying on this tenth stage, one destroys all cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); having destroyed all cognitive obstacles, one uproots the fundamental mind and enters the stage of the Tathāgata.
“The stage of the Tathāgata attains ultimate purity because of three kinds of purification.
What are these three?
First, the purification of afflictions; second, the purification of suffering; and third, the purification of marks.”

"It is like gold that has been melted, refined, and forged; once it has been smelted and beaten, it is free from all dust and impurities. This is for the purpose of revealing that the essence of the gold was originally pure; thus, while the gold is pure, it is not the case that there is no gold."
“Just as the element of water, when still and pure, is free from further turbidity and filth, yet this demonstrates the inherent purity of the nature of water rather than the absence of water;
likewise, although the afflictions that originally arose within the *dharmakāya* are entirely purified, this purity of the *dharmakāya* does not mean it is without substance.”
"Just as when smoke, clouds, dust, and mist have all been cleared from the sky, that sky is pure, yet it is not the case that there is no sky;
likewise, because all sufferings have been utterly extinguished within the Dharmakāya, it is said to be pure, yet it is not the case that it lacks substance."

"It is, for example, like a person who, while asleep in a dream, sees a great flood of water sweeping over his body; he moves his hands and feet to swim upstream, and because his mental power does not falter or retreat, he succeeds in reaching the further shore from this shore. Once he has awakened from the dream, he no longer sees the water, nor the near or far shores."
Once the delusive thoughts of birth and death have been completely extinguished, this awakening is pure; it is not a state of non-awakening.
Likewise, when all delusive thoughts within the dharma-realm no longer arise, it is called "pure"; it is not a state of non-existence that is called "purity."
"Furthermore, good son!

This Dharma-body, because it is purified of the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa), is able to manifest the response-body (nirmāṇakāya); because it is purified of the karmic hindrances (karmāvaraṇa), it is able to manifest the transformation-body (saṃbhogakāya); and because it is purified of the cognitive hindrances (jñeyāvaraṇa), it is able to manifest the Dharma-body (dharmakāya)."
For example, just as lightning arises depending on space and light arises depending on lightning;
so too, the response body (nirmāṇakāya) arises depending on the dharma body (dharmakāya), and the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) arises depending on the response body.

Therefore, the purity of nature encompasses the Dharma-body; the purity of wisdom encompasses the Sambhogakaya; and the purity of samādhi encompasses the Nirmāṇakāya. These three purities are the suchness of phenomena, the non-differentiated suchness, the single-flavored suchness, the liberation-suchness, and the ultimate suchness.
Therefore, the essence of all Buddhas is one and not different.

"Good son! If there are good sons or good daughters who say that the Tathāgata is their great teacher, you should know that these good sons and good daughters fully know and fully see the body of the Tathāgata, for there is no separate body."
“Good son! Therefore, because all improper mental attention toward all objects has been completely severed, there are no two characteristics and no conceptual discrimination regarding this Dharma.”
“Within the non-dual characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*) practiced by the Noble Ones, through the power of that practice, all such various obstacles are completely eliminated.
As each obstacle is eliminated, so too is the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) rendered utterly pure.

Because the wisdom of the suchness-realm (*tathatā-dharmadhātu*) is purified, one thus fully attains and maintains all masteries; because all obstacles of those who have attained all masteries are entirely eradicated and all aspects are purified, this is the characteristic of the wisdom of suchness.”
To see in this way is called the noble vision; this is what is meant by truly seeing the Buddha.
Why is this? Because one sees suchness (tathatā) as it is.
Therefore, the Tathāgata perceives all Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, though they have already transcended the triple world, are unable to know or perceive the true realm when seeking it.

Thus, that which the Noble Ones do not know or see causes all ordinary beings to give rise to doubt and confusion, leading them to inverted conceptualizations; they are unable to cross over, just like a rabbit wishing to cross the great ocean.
Why is this? Because they are unable to penetrate the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!"

All Tathāgatas possess a non-conceptual mind that has attained great mastery over all phenomena, because they perceive through unimpeded and pure wisdom; this is their own unique domain, not shared with others.

Therefore, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they have not spared their own bodies or lives, performing what is difficult to perform, in order to attain this body.
Such a body is supreme and peerless; it is the most excellent of all states, inconceivable, transcending the realm of verbal expression;
it is quiescent, surpassing all fear.
“Good son! Thus one knows and perceives suchness:
it is neither born, nor does it age, nor does it die; its lifespan is limitless; it has no lying down to rest and no eating; body and mind are always in samādhi, without distraction or movement.”
If one gives rise to a contentious mind toward the Tathāgata, one will be unable to see the Tathāgata;
yet all that the Tathāgata speaks is beneficial, and those who hear it shall all receive liberation.
If there are wicked people, evil elephants, or predatory beasts with whom one does not encounter, yet one still engenders karma toward the Buddha, the retribution will be boundless.

"All Tathāgatas have no records of non-existence; they have no desire to know all realms of existence; they have no differentiated mind regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; and whatever the Tathāgata has prophesied is without exception certain."

In the four modes of deportment of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, there is nothing that is not encompassed by wisdom; among all phenomena, there is nothing that is not encompassed by compassion, and nothing that does not benefit all sentient beings.

“Good son! If there are good men or good women who hear, believe, and understand this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, they shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras; they will always be born among humans or devas and never become inferior. They will constantly have the opportunity to draw near to all Tathāgatas, listen to and receive the True Dharma, and will always be born in the pure lands of the Buddhas.”

Why is this? Because these profound dharmas have entered their ears, such sons of good family have been seen and prophesied by the Tathāgata as ones who shall attain non-retrogressive *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Since these sons of good family have had such profound dharmas pass through their ears, it should be known that these persons do not slander the Tathāgata, do not slander the True Dharma, and do not slander the Noble Saṅgha.

In order that all sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness may plant them, and that those who have already planted roots of goodness may cause them to increase and reach maturity, all sentient beings in all worlds are able to practice the six pāramitās.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Great Kings, and the assembly of devas rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra is preached in various lands and regions, there will be four kinds of benefits for those lands.
What are these four?

First, the king’s military forces shall be powerful and flourishing, free from enemies and pestilence; his life shall be long, and he shall enjoy auspicious peace and happiness as the True Dharma flourishes.
Second, the ministers and high officials shall be harmonious and free from contention, held in the king’s respect and affection.

Third, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the people of the realm and its cities shall practice the True Dharma, bringing great benefit; their lives shall be long, and they shall enjoy wealth, leisure, and peace, fully establishing themselves in all fields of merit.

Fourth, during the three periods of the day, the four great elements remain in harmony; these humans and devas increase their protective guardianship, treating all with impartial compassion and a heart free from malice, causing all sentient beings to take refuge with sincere hearts and to practice the path to Bodhi.
"Regarding these four kinds of beneficial merits, we shall all act for their benefit in every place.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good sons! It is so, it is so.
You all should practice this sutra in this manner, and then the Dharma will abide long in the world."
