Chapter Six: The Most Pure Ground of Dhāraṇīs (Part Three). Chapter Six: The Most Pure Ground of Dhāraṇīs. At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavyūha-asaṅgaprabhā-jvālā, together with immeasurable billions of followers, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha. They made offerings of various flowers, incense, precious banners, pennants, and canopies, and spoke these words:
"By how many causes and conditions is the bodhicitta attained?"
"What is this bodhicitta?
World-Honored One!
Regarding enlightenment, the present mind cannot be apprehended, the future mind cannot be apprehended, and the past mind cannot be apprehended."
Apart from bodhi, the bodhicitta is likewise unattainable. Bodhi is ineffable;
the mind, too, is without color, without marks, without substance, without activity, and is not something that can be produced.
“Sentient beings, World-Honored One, are likewise unobtainable and unknowable. How,
then, can the profound meaning of all dharmas be known?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
Bodhi is the performance of secret activities; it cannot be known."
Apart from bodhi, the bodhicitta is also unattainable.
Bodhi is ineffable, the mind is signless, and sentient beings are likewise unknowable.
Why is this? As it is with intention, so it is with the mind;
as it is with the mind, so it is with bodhi.
"As is the mind, as is bodhi, so too are sentient beings;
as are sentient beings, so too are all phenomena of the three periods of time.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have attained a mind that penetrates all dharmas; this is called bodhi and the bodhicitta.”
Awakening is neither past, nor future, nor present;
the mind is likewise, and sentient beings are likewise—within this, nothing can be apprehended.

Why is this? Because all dharmas are unarisen, awakening (*bodhi*) cannot be apprehended, nor can the name "awakening" be apprehended; sentient beings and the name "sentient beings" cannot be apprehended; śrāvakas and the name "śrāvaka" cannot be apprehended; pratyekabuddhas and the name "pratyekabuddha" cannot be apprehended; bodhisattvas and the name "bodhisattva" cannot be apprehended; buddhas and the name "buddha" cannot be apprehended; and neither practice nor non-practice can be apprehended, nor can the names "practice" or "non-practice" be apprehended.
To abide securely within all dharmas of tranquility and to give rise [to the mind] by relying upon all roots of merit and virtue—this is called the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
"For example, the precious King of Mountains, Sumeru, is called the cause of the dānapāramitā.
The second arousal of the mind is like the great earth, which supports each and every phenomenon; it is called the cause of the śīlapāramitā."
For example, the lion, the king of beasts with long manes on its chest, possesses great supernormal power; it strides alone without fear and has no dread of combat.
In this same way, the third mind explains the cause of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
For example, the wind-circle possesses the strength, vigor, and swiftness of Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, the fourth mind is non-retrogressive, and this is called the cause of the *vīryapāramitā*.
For example, a seven-jeweled tower has four stairways, and a cool breeze blows through its four gates.
In this way, when the various treasuries of meritorious dharmas within the fifth mind-stage are not yet fully perfected, this is called the cause of the dhyāna-pāramitā.

Just as the solar disc radiates intense and blazing light, so too does the sixth mind, for it is able to destroy the great darkness of birth and death; therefore, it is called the cause of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

For example, just as a great and wealthy merchant lord can fulfill all the heart's desires, so too the seventh mind can cause one to cross over the perilous and evil path of birth and death, and can cause one to obtain many jewels of merit; therefore, this is called the causal factor for the *upāya-kauśalya-prajñā-pāramitā* (the perfection of skillful means and wisdom).
Just as the moon is pure and full, so too,
because the eighth mind is fully endowed with purity regarding all objects of perception, it is called the cause of the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
For example, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King entrusts his military and precious ministers with the power of command, so too does the ninth mind skillfully adorn and purify the Buddha-field;
because its merits are universally pervasive and it extensively benefits all beings, this is called the cause of the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
It is, for example, like space and a universal monarch (cakravartin).

Likewise, because the tenth mind fully penetrates all objects and attains mastery over all phenomena by reaching the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka), it is called the cause of the perfection of wisdom (jñānapāramitā).
The Buddha said:
"Good son, such are the ten causes for the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
The Buddha said:
“Good son, the dānapāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is accomplished by relying on five kinds of dharmas.”
What are these five?

First, the faculty of faith; second, compassion; third, a mind free from seeking desire; fourth, the gathering and sustaining of all sentient beings; and fifth, the aspiration for the wisdom of all-knowledge.
"It is so, son of good family!
By relying on these five dharmas, the pāramitā of dāna can be brought to fulfillment.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! By means of these five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā). What are the five?

First, the purification of the three karmas; second, not acting as a cause or condition for the afflictions of any sentient beings; third, severing all evil paths and opening the gates to the path of goodness; fourth, transcending the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and fifth, because all merits and vows are fulfilled.
“Good son! By relying on these five dharmas, the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) can be accomplished.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience).
What are these five?

First, to subdue the afflictions of greed and anger; second, to disregard body and life while not giving rise to the contemplation of peaceful rest; third, to reflect upon past karma; fourth, to give rise to a mind of compassion in order to bring all sentient beings to maturity in their roots of merit and goodness; and fifth, to attain the profound patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! Furthermore, based on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the pāramitā of vīrya.
What are these five?

First, not dwelling together with any afflictions; second, not finding peace and happiness as long as merit is not fully perfected; third, never giving rise to weariness toward any difficult practices; fourth, desiring to benefit all sentient beings by accomplishing great compassion and gathering them in; fifth, aspiring to the stage of non-retrogression.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the *vīryapāramitā* (perfection of vigor).
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes the dhyāna-pāramitā.
What are these five?
First, to maintain all wholesome dharmas without dispersal;
second, to be liberated from birth and death, remaining unattached to either state;
third, to aspire to attain supernormal powers for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity in their roots of goodness.
Fourth, they resolve their minds to wash and cleanse the dharma-realm for the sake of purifying the mind;
fifth, they do so in order to sever all roots of affliction within sentient beings.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the dhyānapāramitā.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the prajñāpāramitā.
What are these five?
First, to serve and attend upon all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with wise and great intelligence, never feeling weary or satisfied;
second, to always delight in hearing the profound Dharma taught by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, never feeling weary or satisfied;
third, the supreme wisdom of the ultimate and conventional truths.
Fourth, regarding the afflictions of views and mental defilements (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *kleśa*), such superior wisdom is able to discern and sever them;
fifth, one attains complete mastery over all the dharmas of the five worldly sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*).
“Good son! This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! Furthermore, by relying on five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the pāramitā of superior wisdom in skillful means.
What are these five?
First, they thoroughly penetrate the intentions, afflictions, and mental activities of all sentient beings;
second, their minds fully comprehend the gates of immeasurable dharmas that serve as antidotes;
third, they possess great loving-kindness and great compassion, entering and emerging from them with mastery.
Fourth, they aspire to and seek the full cultivation, maturation, and fulfillment of the great *pāramitās*;
fifth, they aspire to and seek the thorough comprehension and integration of all Buddha-dharmas.
“Good son! This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the supreme wisdom-pāramitā of skillful means.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā). What are these five?
First, dwelling with a mind at peace and joy in the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and unceasing, neither existent nor non-existent;
second, contemplating all phenomena as most wondrous and all defilements as pure, the mind attains peaceful abiding;
third, transcending all marks, the mind is suchness—unconditioned, without activity, non-different, and immovable—settling the mind in suchness.
Fourth, one attains a state of settled abiding within the conventional truth for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
fifth, one is able to abide simultaneously in both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of aspiration.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Good son! By means of these five dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*). What are the five?
First, the power of wisdom that can comprehend the perilous and evil mental activities of all sentient beings;
second, the ability to cause all sentient beings to enter into the most profound Dharma;
third, the knowledge and vision of all sentient beings as they traverse through birth and death according to their respective causes and conditions.
Fourth, he possesses the power of wisdom to discern and know the three categories of all sentient beings;
fifth, because his teaching of the Dharma—whether for planting seeds, for ripening, or for liberation—is entirely through the power of wisdom in accordance with reality.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of power.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice and accomplish the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā).
What are these five?

First, the perfection of the wisdom that discriminates between good and evil regarding all phenomena; second, the perfection of the wisdom that distances oneself from and embraces black and white dharmas respectively; third, the perfection of the wisdom that feels neither aversion toward saṃsāra nor delight toward nirvāṇa; fourth, the perfection of the wisdom that attains ultimate liberation through the practice of great merit and the practice of great wisdom; and fifth, the perfection of the wisdom of consecration regarding the unique qualities of all Buddhas and the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! What is the meaning of *pāramitā*?
The excellence of practicing the path is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
The meaning of *pāramitā* is the fulfillment of profoundly deep wisdom;
the meaning of *pāramitā* is that the mind does not cling to phenomena, whether they are conditioned or unconditioned;
the meaning of *pāramitā* is the correct awakening and correct contemplation regarding the faults of saṃsāra and the virtues of nirvāṇa.
To embrace both fools and the wise is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
to be able to manifest various kinds of rare and wondrous Dharma-treasures is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
and the fulfillment of unimpeded liberative wisdom is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To correctly discern and know the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
that generosity (*dāna*) and the other perfections, as well as wisdom (*prajñā*), can cause one to reach the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
and that they can bring about the fulfillment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
The meaning of *pāramitā* is that which can bring to maturity the merit and roots of goodness of all sentient beings;

the meaning of *pāramitā* is the accomplishment of the Buddha-wisdom, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth at the cool terrace of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
the meaning of *pāramitā* is the ability to cross over birth-and-death and nirvana—which are both false views—without remainder.
To deliver and liberate all beings is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
to skillfully explain and subdue all outsiders who come to challenge and debate is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
to be able to turn the wheel of the Dharma in twelve aspects is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To be without attachment, without views, without affliction or entanglement, and without divergent thoughts—this is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
"Good son! At the first bodhisattva stage, these signs appear before one:
"The immeasurable and boundless treasuries of various kinds of jewels and other treasures throughout the trichiliocosm are all completely filled.
The Bodhisattva sees them all.
'O Son of Good Family!'"
When the Bodhisattva is in the second stage, these signs appear beforehand:
the ground of the trichiliocosm becomes as level as the palm of a hand, adorned with immeasurable and innumerable varieties of pure jewels of wondrous colors and ornaments.
The Bodhisattva sees them all.
"Good son! These signs appear before the Bodhisattva at the third stage:
"The Bodhisattva sees them all: themselves brave and strong, adorned with armor and weapons, capable of crushing and subduing all enemies and bandits. Good son!"
In the fourth stage of the Bodhisattva, these signs appear beforehand:
wind-circles from the four directions scatter various exquisite flowers, completely covering the ground.
The Bodhisattva perceives them all.
“Good son! These signs appear before the Bodhisattva on the fifth stage:
like a precious woman adorned with every ornament, her head is strewn with *tāna* flowers, and her body and head are embellished with exquisite jewels and necklaces.”
The Bodhisattva sees them all.
"Good son! These signs appear before the Bodhisattva in the sixth stage:

The lotus ponds made of the seven precious gems have four stairways with paths of golden sand; they are pure and free from impurity, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities. The ponds are adorned with *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers. Within these lotus ponds, one sports in person, experiencing joy and purity, with a coolness that is beyond compare.
The Bodhisattva sees them all.
"Good son! These signs appear before the Bodhisattva in the seventh stage:
Though they were destined to fall into hell on their left and right sides, by the power of the Bodhisattva, they did not fall; they suffered neither injury nor pain.
The Bodhisattva sees them all.
"Good son! These signs appear before the Bodhisattva at the eighth stage:
To the left and to the right, there was the Lion, the King of Beasts, with a shaggy mane upon his chest; all other beasts were utterly terrified of him.
The Bodhisattva saw them all.
"O Son of Good Family!..."
These signs appear before the Bodhisattva at the ninth stage:

a Wheel-Turning Sage King, surrounded and honored by immeasurable billions of followers, with a white parasol atop his head—adorned with immeasurable varieties of jewels—held over him to provide shade.
The Bodhisattva sees them all.
"Good son! These signs appear before the Bodhisattva at the ten stages:

The body of the Tathāgata is golden and resplendent, with immeasurable pure light fully perfected; surrounded by and reverently making offerings to immeasurable billions of Brahmā kings, he turns the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Wheel of Dharma.
The Bodhisattva sees all. "Good son,
why is the first stage named 'Joy'?"

Having attained the supramundane mind, which was previously unattained but is now for the first time realized, and having accomplished all that was wished for through great deeds and great functions, one experiences great joy and celebration; therefore, the first stage is called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
"Because all subtle transgressions and faults of violating the precepts are purified, the second stage is called the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Because the samādhi of immeasurable wisdom-light is unshakable and cannot be overcome, and because it serves as the basis for the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining, the third stage is called the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*)."

Because it can burn away afflictions and increase the radiance of the fire of wisdom, serving as the basis for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, the fourth stage is therefore called the "Blazing Stage" (Arciṣmatī).

"Because this mastery over the superior wisdom of the skillful means of practice is difficult to attain, and because the afflictions of views and mental disturbances cannot be subdued, the fifth stage is therefore called the 'Difficult to Conquer' (Sudurjayā) stage."

"Because the continuity of the practice of the Dharma is clearly manifested through the presence of signlessness and manifold reflection, the sixth stage is therefore called the Stage of Manifestation (Abhimukhī)."

"Because of the far-reaching cultivation of the untainted, uninterrupted, signless mental application, and the samādhi of liberation, this stage is pure, unobstructed, and unhindered; therefore, the seventh stage is called the 'Far-Reaching Stage' (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi)."

"Because one attains mastery through the cultivation of signlessness and right reflection, such that the activities of all afflictions cannot cause one to waver, the eighth stage is therefore called the Immovable Stage."

Because one attains mastery in expounding all various kinds of dharmas, being free from affliction and entanglement, and because wisdom increases with sovereign unimpededness, the ninth stage is therefore called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī).
"The Dharma-body is like space and wisdom is like a great cloud; because it can pervade and cover all things, the tenth stage is therefore named the Dharma-Cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi)."

"In the first stage (*bhūmi*), the desire to practice a path with signs is the obstruction of ignorance; the fear of birth and death is ignorance. Based on these two kinds of coarse minds, there is the obstruction of the first stage."

"Subtle transgressions are caused by ignorance; the various characteristics of karmic formations are caused by ignorance. Based on these two kinds of coarse minds, there are the obstacles of the second stage.
Because one attains benefits previously unattained, there is agitation caused by ignorance;
because one does not possess the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, there is [agitation] caused by ignorance."
Based on two kinds of coarse minds, these constitute the obstacles of the third stage:
the arising of a mind of craving and attachment toward the bliss of dhyāna-concentration due to ignorance;
and the craving for subtle and pure dharmas due to ignorance.
Based on two kinds of coarse minds, there are obstacles to the four stages:
first, the contemplation of desiring to enter nirvana; second, the contemplation of desiring to enter saṃsāra.
These contemplations of nirvana and saṃsāra have ignorance as their cause.
The unequal contemplation of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has ignorance as its cause.
Based on these two kinds of coarse minds, this constitutes the obstacle of the fifth stage.
"The continuity of the practice of dharmas manifests with perfect clarity; ignorance is its cause."
The characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) repeatedly arise in the mind with ignorance as their cause.
Based on these two kinds of coarse minds, there are obstacles to the sixth stage.
Subtle characteristics, whether manifest or unmanifest, constitute ignorance.
When one single-mindedly contemplates the desire to sever [afflictions] but has not yet attained the skillful means, there is ignorance.
Based on these two kinds of coarse minds, this constitutes the obstacle to the seventh stage.
It is ignorance that involves expending great effort regarding signless phenomena.
Attachment to signs and the lack of mastery over them constitute ignorance that is difficult to transcend.
Based on these two kinds of coarse mind, there is an obstruction to the eighth stage. [Regarding this stage:
there is ignorance consisting in the inability to maintain and uphold the immeasurable teachings, the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables, and the immeasurable analytical wisdom.
Lack of mastery over the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) is ignorance;
based on these two types of coarse mind, they constitute the obstacles of the nine stages.
Lack of attainment of the greatest supernormal powers (abhijñā) as one desires is ignorance;
The ignorance resulting from insufficient practice regarding the subtle and secret treasury constitutes the obstacle to the ten stages based on two kinds of coarse mind.
"The obstruction of subtle wisdom regarding all objects has ignorance as its cause."
The future is an obstruction because it does not arise again; it is the failure to attain the wisdom of non-arising, with ignorance as its cause.
This is the hindrance to the stage of the Tathāgata.
"It is so, son of good family!"

On the first Bodhisattva stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*); on the second stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); on the third stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); on the fourth stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); on the fifth stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); on the sixth stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); on the seventh stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of skillful means and supreme knowledge (*upāya-jñāna-pāramitā*); on the eighth stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*); on the ninth stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*); and on the tenth stage, one practices and inclines toward the perfection of gnosis (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
“Good son! The first production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is called the samādhi ‘Arising of the Wondrous Jewel,’ which is attained through its gathering;
the second production of the thought is the samādhi ‘Delightful Abiding,’ which is attained through its gathering; the third production of the thought is the [samādhi] ‘Difficult...’”
The first resolve is brought forth through the mastery of the samādhi of movement; the fourth resolve is brought forth through the mastery of the non-retrogressive samādhi;
the fifth resolve is brought forth through the mastery of the jewel-flower samādhi;
the sixth resolve is brought forth through the mastery of the sun’s perfect radiant flame samādhi; and the seventh resolve fulfills all vows as desired.
The eighth production of the thought of enlightenment is attained through the empowerment of the samādhi of the manifestation of present Buddhas;
the ninth production of the thought of enlightenment is attained through the empowerment of the samādhi of the treasury of wisdom;
and the tenth production of the thought of enlightenment is attained through the empowerment of the śūraṅgama-mārga samādhi.
“Good son! These are called the ten kinds of generating the mind of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Good son!”
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in this first stage (bhūmi), are born by relying on the power of merit through that which is called a dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the mantra, saying:
"Tadyathā" (The first character *tian* [天] is pronounced with a light *ke* [可] tone; the *ta* [他] at the beginning of each of the subsequent nine sections is all identical to this pronunciation). 1.
1. Pūrṇi (the final *ni* is pronounced as in this entry; the same pronunciation applies to the character *ni* throughout the subsequent nine articles).
2. Nara-ti (the *ti* is pronounced with a Wu dialect accent). 3. Tuhu, tuhuhu, tuhuhu. 4. Namyā-vadhu-riyu. 5.
Upasati-ri (the final *ri* is pronounced as in this entry). 6. Namyā-ba.
Candu-lu (7); Wu-yin-hu-di (pronounced *yu-duo-di*) Wu-yin-hu-di (8);
Duo-ba-duo-luo-shan (9); Dan-di-tu (10); Po-li-he-lan (11);
Gou-liu-liang (12); Suo-he-hu-ke (13). These are the latter nine chapters.
The character *ma-ha* is entirely the same sound as this; these are the twelve. "Good son!
This dhāraṇī is named 'Protected by Buddhas numbering more than the sands of one Ganges River. "

If a Bodhisattva of the First Ground recites and maintains this dhāraṇī mantra, they shall attain liberation from all fears, all wild beasts, all evil spirits, and the calamities and afflictions caused by humans and non-humans; they shall be freed from the five hindrances and never forget the mindfulness of the First Ground.
“Good son! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell securely and happily in these two stages, they give rise to what is called a *dhāraṇī*.
It is as follows: *Tadyathā*: (1) *ucchuṣmi*, (2) *ciri ciri*, (3) *uṣṭrā*, (4) *uṣṭrā-ni*, (5) *candra candra ucchuṣmi*, (6) *ciri ciri*, (7) *kroḍa kroḍa*, (8) *soka*. Good son!”
This dhāraṇī is named "Protected by Buddhas as Numerous as the Sands of Two Ganges Rivers.

When a bodhisattva on the second stage recites and maintains this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall attain deliverance from all fears, all wild beasts, all evil spirits, and the enmity of humans and non-humans; they shall be freed from calamities, misfortunes, and all afflictions, liberated from the five hindrances, and shall never forget the mindfulness of the second stage.
“Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives birth to this dhāraṇī called ‘Difficult to Conquer Great Power’ at this third stage.
Tadyathā: (1) *dantī* (2) *bandhantī* (3) *karañjī* (4) *gaurī* (5) *kiṃculī* (6) *tantulī* (7) *svāhā*. Good son!”
This dhāraṇī is named "Protected by Buddhas as Numerous as the Sands of Three Ganges Rivers.

When a Bodhisattva of the third stage recites and maintains this dhāraṇī-mantra, they shall attain deliverance from all fears, all predatory beasts such as tigers, wolves, and lions, all evil spirits, humans and non-humans, enemies and bandits, calamities and misfortunes, and all forms of affliction and harm. They shall be liberated from the five obstacles and never forget the third stage.
“Good son! A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives birth to this dhāraṇī called ‘Great Benefit and Difficult to Destroy’ in this fourth stage.
Tadyathā: (1) śiri śiri; (2) dhamini dhamini; (3) dharidhari; (4) śiriśirini; (5) vidhara-vase; (6) vasina; (7) vandaha-mati; (8) svāha. “Good son!”
This dhāraṇī is named "Protected by Buddhas as Numerous as the Sands of Four Ganges Rivers.

When a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage recites and maintains this dhāraṇī, they shall transcend all fears, all predatory beasts such as tigers, wolves, and lions, all malevolent spirits, and all enemies—whether human or non-human—including calamities, misfortunes, and various poisons. They shall be liberated from the five hindrances and never forget the mindfulness of the fourth stage.
“Good son! A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives birth to this dharani, which is adorned with various merits of this fifth stage.
Tadyathā: (1) hāri hārini; (2) carī carini; (3) karamaṇi; (4) saṃkaramaṇi; (5) sabhāṣaṇi; (6) śambhāṣaṇi; (7) siddham-bhāṣaṇi; (8) mohani; (9) svābhy-ūṣe; (10) soha. Good son!
This dhāraṇī is named "Protected by Buddhas as Numerous as the Sands of Five Ganges Rivers.

When a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage recites and upholds this dhāraṇī, they shall overcome all fears, all poisonous harms, tigers, wolves, and lions, all evil spirits, humans and non-humans, enemies and bandits, calamities and misfortunes, and all afflictions and injuries. They shall be liberated from the five obstacles and never forget the mindfulness of the fifth stage.
“Good son! This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to the dhāraṇī known as ‘Perfect Wisdom’ and others within this sixth stage.
Tadyathā: (1) viduri, (2) viduri.”
1. Marīṇi 2. Kāri kāri 3. Piḍu-tu-yū-ha-ti (the word *ti* is pronounced with the Wu dialect) 4.
Lū lū lū (the three characters *lū* are pronounced as above) 5.
Cū lū cū lū 6. Turubha turubha 7. Śa śa (the two characters *śa* are pronounced as above)
1. The same as above in sound: *zhāng-wo* (cut by *qiē*). 2. Its ninth: *po-lì-sā* (the second character cut by *shǐ*). 3. Its tenth: *sā-xiàng* (cut by *tuō*;
pronounce these two characters with an urgent, rolling tone). 4. *sī-dǐ* (the first character cut by *zhī-lǚ*). 5. Its eleventh:
*sà-pó-sā-tuó-nán* (the third character cut by *níng-gān*). 6. Its twelfth: *xī-chí-xiá-dǒu* (the first character cut by *zhí-lí*, the second by *xiāng-jia*). 10. Its tenth: *dǒu*.
*Samantatārapaṭi svāhā*. "Good son, this dhāraṇī is named 'Protected by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of more than six Ganges Rivers.'"

When a Bodhisattva of the sixth stage recites and maintains this dhāraṇī, they shall overcome all fears, all poisonous harms, tigers, wolves, and lions, as well as all evil spirits, humans and non-humans, enemies, calamities, and various afflictions. They will be liberated from the five hindrances and shall never forget the mindfulness of the sixth stage.
“Good son! In this seventh stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains birth in the dhāraṇī called ‘Superior Practice of the Dharma.

"Good son! This dharani consecration-verse of auspiciousness is named 'Protected by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of more than ten Ganges Rivers. "

When a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground recites and maintains this dhāraṇī mantra, they shall attain deliverance from all fears, all predatory beasts such as tigers, wolves, and lions, and all evil spirits, humans, non-humans, and other hostile thieves; they shall be freed from poison, harm, and calamities, and shall be liberated from the five hindrances while never forgetting the mindfulness of the Tenth Ground.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Lion-like Unobstructed Radiance immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“I pay homage to the One Beyond Analogy, Who expounds the profound meaning of signlessness.
Sentient beings have lost their vision; The World-Honored One is able to deliver them.”
Because the World-Honored One possesses the Buddha-eye, he does not perceive the characteristics of a single dharma;
with the unsurpassed Honored One’s Dharma-eye, he perceives the inconceivable meaning.
He cannot give rise to a single dharma, nor does he extinguish a single dharma.
Because of your vision of equality, you have reached the supreme state.
Because you do not diminish birth and death, I pray that the Honored One may realize nirvāṇa;
because you have transcended the views of these two dharmas, you have thus realized tranquility.
The wisdom of the World-Honored One is of a single flavor;
because he does not discriminate between the categories of the pure and the impure, he has attained unsurpassed purity.
The body of the World-Honored One is boundless; he does not utter a single word or syllable.
Because the entire assembly of disciples is satiated by the rain of Dharma;
because all conceptualizations regarding sentient beings are entirely absent,
the World-Honored One universally rescues those sentient beings who are suffering and distressed.
Suffering and pleasure, permanence and impermanence, self and non-self—
regarding such manifold meanings, the World-Honored One’s wisdom is unattached.
The world is neither one nor many, like an echo in an empty valley;
it neither passes over nor perishes—only a Buddha can fully comprehend this.
The dharma-realm is without discrimination; therefore, there is no distinct vehicle.
"For the sake of delivering sentient beings, I have distinguished and taught the three vehicles.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King Maheśvara rose from his seat within the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How rare and immeasurable!
The subtle and profound meaning of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* is ultimately complete and perfect; it is capable of bringing to fulfillment all Buddha-dharmas and all the benevolence of the Buddhas.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is. Good son!"
"It is as you have said,
noble son!
If one hears this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, all bodhisattvas shall not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Why is this? Good son!

For a Bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression, the maturation of the roots of goodness is the foremost seal; it is because of this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra—the king of all sūtras—that they are able to hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite it.
Why is this? Good son!

If all sentient beings have not yet planted roots of goodness, have not yet matured their roots of goodness, and have not yet drawn near to the Buddhas, they shall not be able to hear this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.

“Good son! By means of hearing and upholding this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, all karmic obstructions of these good sons and good daughters shall be completely extinguished, and they shall attain supreme purity. They will always behold the Buddhas and never be separated from the World-Honored One; they will always hear the wondrous Dharma and constantly listen to the True Dharma. They will be born into the stage of non-retrogression and will draw near to the Lion-like Victorious Ones without ever being parted.”
The *Dhāraṇī of the Ocean-Seal Producing Sublime Merits, Inexhaustible and Undiminished*;
the *Dhāraṇī of Thoroughly Penetrating the Mental Activities and Speech of All Sentient Beings, Inexhaustible and Undiminished*;
the *Dhāraṇī of the Sun’s Perfect Stainless-Phase Light, Inexhaustible and Undiminished*; the *Dhāraṇī of the Full Moon’s Phase Light, Inexhaustible and Undiminished*.

The *dhāraṇī* of the stream of merit that subdues all afflictions and phenomena; the *dhāraṇī* of the indestructible adamantine mountain that is inexhaustible, undiminishing, and shatters all solidity;
the *dhāraṇī* of the treasury of causes and conditions for explaining the unspeakable meaning that is inexhaustible and undiminishing;
and the *dhāraṇī* of penetrating the sounds of the rules of true speech that is inexhaustible and undiminishing.
The Bhikṣuṇī [possesses] the *Akṣayākṣīṇa-gaganāmala-cittacaryā-mudrā-dhāraṇī* and the *Akṣayākṣīṇa-anantabuddhakāya-prakāśana-dhāraṇī*.

“Good son! Because these various dhāraṇīs and others have been accomplished, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, within all the buddha-fields of the ten directions, speaks the various unsurpassed true dharmas through the bodies of emanation-buddhas. He remains unmoving within the suchness of phenomena (dharmatā), neither going nor coming; he is well able to mature the roots of goodness of all sentient beings, yet he perceives no sentient beings whatsoever who are to be matured.
He speaks various dharmas, yet within all verbal expressions he is unmoving, neither going, nor staying, nor coming.”

"It is able to manifest arising and ceasing while tending toward non-arising and non-ceasing; it teaches that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no coming or going, for all dharmas are without distinction.

Having spoken this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, thirty trillion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); immeasurable bodhisattvas did not regress from their resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); immeasurable and boundless bhikṣus attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*); and immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the bodhisattva mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The path that flows against the current of birth and death Is profound, subtle, and difficult to see.
Craving covers sentient beings; In the darkness of ignorance, they do not see."

At that time, the great assembly rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“Wherever this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* may be expounded and proclaimed, we, the members of this assembly, shall all go there to serve as listeners.”

This Dharma-preacher shall receive manifold benefits, peace, and freedom from obstacles, with body and mind at ease; we shall all provide him with offerings to the utmost of our ability, so that all listeners may be secure and happy.
In this land, there shall be no perils of hostile bandits or terrors; there shall be no fear of famine and no fear of non-human beings (*amanuṣya*), and the people shall flourish.
At this place where the Dharma is preached, all devas, humans, non-humans, and other sentient beings must not pass over it from above to defile the site where the Dharma is being taught.

Why is this? The place where the Dharma is preached is itself a stūpa; good sons and good daughters should make offerings to this place of preaching with various perfumes, flowers, silken fabrics, banners, and canopies.
We shall provide protection and benefit for you, eliminate all obstacles, and supply whatever you require as desired, ensuring that everything is fully provided.
The Buddha said, “Good sons! It is so;
you all should diligently practice this sutra, and then the Dharma will abide long in the world.”
The *Combined Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*, Fascicle Three: "The fear of birth and death is an obstacle to the first stage (*bhūmi*) because of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The obstruction regarding subtle transgressions and the various characteristics of karmic actions are obstacles to the second stage because of ignorance."

Because one fails to attain the benefits not yet attained due to the cause of agitation—namely ignorance—and because one lacks the cause for the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retention—namely ignorance—these two types of ignorance are said to be the obstacles of the third stage.
“Delighting in the bliss of meditative concentration and giving rise to a mind of craving and attachment, with ignorance as the cause—this is the obstacle of the fourth stage.

To have one intention of contemplating entry into nirvana and another intention of contemplating entry into saṃsāra—these contemplations of nirvana and these contemplations of saṃsāra have ignorance as their cause;
the unequal contemplation of saṃsāra and nirvana has ignorance as its cause.”
This is the obstacle to the fifth stage.
"The continuity of the activity of dharmas manifests clearly, with ignorance as its cause;
the characteristics of dharmas repeatedly enter the mind, with ignorance as their cause."
This is the obstacle to the sixth stage.
Subtle marks, whether manifest or unmanifest, have ignorance as their cause;
the failure to obtain the skillful means for severing them despite having cultivated one-flavored contemplation has ignorance as its cause.
This is the obstacle to the seventh stage.
It is that one exerts much effort regarding signless dharmas, with ignorance as the cause;
and that one is difficult to deliver because of the autonomous grasping at signs, with ignorance as the cause.
Based on these two kinds of coarse minds, there are obstacles to the eighth stage.

Because one has not yet been able to master the immeasurable preaching of the Dharma, the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables, and the immeasurable analytical wisdom— taking ignorance as the cause—
and because one has not yet attained mastery over the four unhindered analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)— taking ignorance as the cause.
Based on two kinds of coarse minds, these constitute the obstacles of the ninth stage:
the non-attainment of supreme supernormal powers as desired, caused by ignorance;
and the insufficiency in the cultivation of the subtle and secret treasury, caused by ignorance.
Based on two kinds of coarse minds, these constitute the obstacles to the tenth stage.
The obstruction consisting of subtle cognitive hindrances regarding all objective spheres has ignorance as its cause;
the obstruction whereby future hindrances do not arise again, yet the knowledge of their non-arising has not been attained, also has ignorance as its cause.
This is the obstacle to the stage of the Tathāgata.
