Chapter Seven: Praise (Part Four). Chapter Seven: Praise. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā Bhadrā:
“In the past there was a king named Golden Dragon Honored One (*Suvarṇanāga-guru*), who constantly praised with these words of praise all the Buddhas of the past,
future, and present: ‘I now revere, pay homage to, and praise the Buddhas of the ten directions of the past, future, and present.’”
The Buddhas are pure, subtle, wondrous, and tranquil; among all forms, they are the supreme form, radiant with golden light.
Among all sounds, the voice of the Buddha is the most excellent, like that of Great Brahmā, deep and far-reaching as the sound of thunder.
His hair is deep blue-black, with lustrous curls rising like flames; its color cannot be matched by bees, emeralds, or peacock feathers.
His teeth are pure white, like jade or snow; they illuminate his golden countenance with distinct and perfect alignment.
His eyes are long and wide, pure and stainless, like blue lotuses blooming and reflecting in the water.
His tongue is broad and long, its color a radiant crimson; its light shines forth like a flower in its first bloom.
The tuft of hair between the eyebrows is white as a conch or the moon, curling to the right with a lustrous sheen like pure lapis lazuli.
The eyebrows are fine and long, shaped like the crescent moon; their color is a brilliant black, surpassing even that of the king of bees.
The nose is high, round, and straight, like a cast gold ingot; subtle and supple, it stands at the center of the face.
This supreme mark of the Tathāgata is the most excellent in its sequence; he attains the true flavor of things, and none can equal him.
From each and every pore, a single hair grows in a clockwise curl; soft, fine, and deep blue-black, it is like the neck of a peacock.
At the very moment of birth, his body emits a great radiance that universally illumines immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions, extinguishing all sufferings within the three realms.
May all sentient beings receive complete happiness;
may hungry ghosts, humans, devas, and others likewise be secure and free from affliction,
as all immeasurable evil realms are entirely extinguished.
The color of his body is subtle and wondrous, like a mass of molten gold;
his countenance is pure and serene, like the full moon;
the radiance of the Buddha’s body is brilliant, like the sun first rising.
His gait and deportment were like those of a lion;
his long arms hung down, reaching below his knees when standing, like the branches of a *sāla* tree swaying in the wind.
His halo extended one fathom, illuminating the immeasurable, as if a hundred thousand suns and moons were gathered together.
The Buddha’s body is pure and sublime, free from all defilement; its radiance shines universally throughout all buddha-fields.
The Buddha’s light is majestic and lofty, its brilliant flames blazing intensely, capable of completely eclipsing immeasurable suns and moons.
The Buddha is a sun, a lamp, and a torch, illuminating immeasurable realms; he causes all sentient beings to follow the light and behold the Buddha.
Through the hundreds of thousands of karmic practices cultivated and accumulated from the beginning, and through the gathered merit, he adorns the Buddha-body.
His arms are long, slender, and rounded, like the trunk of an elephant king; his hands and feet are pure and soft, inspiring love and never-tiring devotion.
The Buddhas of the past and future are as numerous as motes of dust;
the Buddhas of the present are likewise so.
To all such Tathāgatas, I now pay homage; their bodies and speech are pure, and so too is their mind.
With exquisite flowers and incense, I offer worship and present them with hundreds of thousands of merits, praising and extolling them in song.
Even if one possessed a hundred tongues and were to praise the Buddha’s merits for a thousand kalpas, one could never exhaust them.
All the merits possessed by the Tathāgata in the present world are manifold, profound, and firm,
being the most subtle and supreme of all.
Even if one were to possess a thousand tongues and wished to praise a single Buddha, one could not exhaust even a small fraction of his merits;
how much less could one hope to extol the merits of all Buddhas?
Even if one were to fill the waters up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra),
one might still be able to count the number of drops with a single hair; yet there is no one who can know even a single merit of the Buddha.
I have now paid homage to and praised all Buddhas; my physical, verbal, and mental actions are entirely pure.
May all the immeasurable wholesome deeds I have cultivated lead all sentient beings to realize the Unsurpassed Way.
Thus the King of Men, having praised the Buddha, further made such immeasurable vows:
"If in a future age, throughout immeasurable and boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
in whatever place I may be born, may I always see the wondrous golden drum within my dreams."
I have heard the profound sound of repentance;
now I praise you whose countenance is pure. May I, in future lives, also attain such as this.
The virtues of all Buddhas are inconceivable; In hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they are extremely difficult to encounter.
I pray that in the future, throughout immeasurable ages, I may see them in dreams at night, And recount them as they truly are during the day.
Practicing the six perfections to rescue and deliver sentient beings, crossing over the sea of suffering,
and only then shall my own body attain the unsurpassed path, so that my world shall have no equal.
By virtue of this karmic fruit, in a future age, may he encounter Śākyamuni Buddha and receive his prediction of enlightenment;
and may my two sons, Jinaratna and Jinaśrī, always be born into my household and likewise receive their predictions together with him.
If there are sentient beings who have no protector or refuge, who are oppressed by manifold sufferings and have no place of reliance,
I shall, in the future, act as a great protector and a place of reliance for such as these,
able to eliminate their manifold sufferings and cause them all to be utterly extinguished.
Bestowing upon sentient beings all manner of goodness and peace;
in future ages, as I practice the path to enlightenment, I shall not calculate the number of kalpas, until the very limit of existence is exhausted.
By means of this golden light and the causes and conditions of repentance, may my ocean of evil,
my ocean of karma, and the great ocean of afflictions all be dried up without remainder;
and may my ocean of merit be fully accomplished.
The great ocean of wisdom is pure and complete.
With immeasurable merit, it aids the path to enlightenment, just as the great ocean is replete with precious jewels.
By the power of this golden light and the force of repentance, may the merit of Bodhi be unimpeded in its radiance.
With wisdom-light free from defilement, illuminating all with pure penetration, may my body’s light shine universally in future lives.
With the majestic power of merit, his radiant flames blaze intensely; within the three realms, he is most supreme and extraordinary.
Without any diminution, he shall deliver sentient beings, causing them to cross the ocean of suffering and further establish them in the great ocean of merit.
For many kalpas in future lives, I shall practice the path of bodhi, just as the Buddhas of the past practiced the path of bodhi.
The pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
and the immeasurable merit of the Supreme Buddhas.
"May I, in a future life, attain this extraordinary merit and pure land, just like the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
You should know with faith that the king at that time, the Venerable Golden Dragon, was none other than yourself.
At that time, the two sons, Jinaloka and Jinaprabha, are now your two sons, Rajaprabha and so forth.
"In immeasurable other sutras, emptiness has already been explained at length; therefore, herein,"
To explain it briefly:
the faculties of sentient beings are dull and they possess little wisdom; they are unable to extensively understand the immeasurable meaning of emptiness.
Therefore, regarding this honored sutra, I have spoken of it briefly through various causes and conditions and diverse, wondrous skillful means.
Out of great compassion for those of dull faculties, I now expound this sublime and wonderful scripture.
As I understand it, I know the intentions of sentient beings: this body is false and deceptive, like an empty village.
The six sense bases are a hamlet where the thieves of the fetters dwell; each exists in its own right, none knowing one another.
The eye-faculty perceives forms; the ear discriminates sounds; the nose smells various fragrances;
the tongue relishes flavors; the body-faculty greedily experiences all tactile objects;
and the mind-faculty discriminates all phenomena.
The six sense-faculties each take their own respective objects as conditions; they do not engage with the objects of other senses.
The mind is like a magical illusion, racing through the six sense-faculties, constantly deluded and discriminating among all phenomena.
Just as worldly people rush into an empty village, harmed by the six thieves yet foolishly unaware of how to avoid them;
so too does the mind constantly rely upon the spheres of the six sense organs, each knowing well the place where it lies in wait.
Following after forms, sounds, Odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, The mind dwells within the six sense-faculties,
Like a bird cast into a net. Wherever its mind may be,
It constantly abides among the various faculties, Pursuing the various sensory objects Without ever relinquishing them for a moment.
The body is empty and false, incapable of being nourished; it is devoid of dispute and contention, and likewise lacks a sovereign master.
Arising from the conjunction of various causes and conditions, it possesses no solidity or reality, being produced through the power of deluded conceptualization.
Earth, water, fire, and wind, combined and assembled, form [the body];
they increase and decrease according to the seasons and mutually harm one another, just like four snakes dwelling together in a single basket.
The four great venomous serpents, each with its distinct nature— two moving upward, two moving downward,
and likewise two in each of the directions— such as these great serpents are all extinguished without remainder.
The two serpents of earth and water are heavy by nature and sink downward;
the two serpents of wind and fire are light by nature and rise upward.
Receiving retribution according to karma, one wanders through the realms of gods, humans, and other destinies, following whatever actions one has performed.
Thus one falls into the three realms of existence.
Great and small impurities overflow externally; various worms arise within the body, which is devoid of anything lovely or delightful.
Cast away among the tombs, it is like a decayed piece of wood.
"Good daughter, you should observe:
all phenomena are thus; where is there a person or a sentient being?
Their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent; they exist only because of ignorance."
Thus these great elements, each and every one, are not real; they are fundamentally unborn, and their nature is without combination.
For this reason, I say that these great elements are fundamentally unreal from the beginning, existing only through combination.
The essential nature of ignorance is fundamentally non-existent; it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions of deluded thought.
Because it has no reality, it is conventionally designated as "ignorance"; therefore, I speak of it by the name "ignorance."
Craving, grasping, becoming, birth, old age, death, sorrow, and affliction— these manifold sufferings and karmic formations are inconceivable.
Birth and death are boundless, revolving without ceasing; fundamentally there is no arising, nor is there any combination.
Through unwholesome reflection, the mind creates its own course; I sever all views, fetters, and the like.
With the sword of wisdom, one tears asunder the net of afflictions; regarding the house of the five aggregates, one perceives it all as empty and quiescent.
One opens the gate of ambrosia, reveals the vessel of ambrosia, and enters the city of ambrosia.
Dwelling in the chamber of nectar, may you cause all sentient beings to partake of the flavor of nectar.
Blow the great Dharma conch, beat the great Dharma drum, kindle the great Dharma lamp,
and rain down the supreme Dharma rain.
I have now subdued all enmities and fetters, and raised aloft the supreme, subtle banner of the Dharma.
I deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death, forever severing the immeasurable suffering and afflictions of the three evil realms.
The afflictions burn fiercely, scorching all sentient beings;
they have no protector and no refuge.
With the nectar of immortality, cool and delicious in flavor, I shall satisfy these people and cause them to be free from their parching heat.
Throughout immeasurable eons, they have practiced all deeds with devotion, making offerings and showing reverence to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Firmly cultivating and accumulating the path to Bodhi, they seek the Tathāgata’s true Dharma-body.
The head, eyes, marrow, and brain; beloved sons and daughters;
wealth, treasures, pearls, necklaces, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and various other diverse objects.
If all the trees within the trichiliocosm were broken into counting-slips,
and the entire great earth were ground into fine dust, and these particles of dust filled all of space;
and if every sentient being possessed wisdom, and this wisdom were given to a single person—
Beings such as these are like motes of dust; one might calculate and know their number.
But the wisdom of the Tathāgata cannot be numbered; the wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata in a single thought-moment could not be exhausted even by calculation throughout incalculable eons.

Chapter Nine: Fulfilling Wishes by Relying on Emptiness (4) The Golden Light Sūtra, Chapter Nine: Fulfilling Wishes by Relying on Emptiness Translated by Paramārtha, Tripiṭaka Master of the Liang Dynasty At that time, the goddess Bhadramatī, Radiant with Wish-Fulfilling Jewels, rose from her seat amidst the great assembly. She bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee upon the ground, joined her palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha in verse:
“I ask the One who Illumines the World, The Most Honored among the Two-Legged Beings, Concerning the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Right Practice;
I pray only that you will deign to listen and grant me leave.”
The Buddha said:
“Good Goddess!
If you have any doubts, ask whatever you wish in your mind; I shall explain it to you in detail.”
"How do the bodhisattvas practice the correct conduct of enlightenment,
remaining free from both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, for the sake of benefiting themselves and others?
The Buddha said:
“Good Goddess!
One practices the dharma of bodhi by relying on the dharma-realm; one cultivates the practice of equanimity.
Good Goddess!”
"How does one practice the Dharma of Bodhi by relying on the *dharmadhātu* and cultivate the practice of equanimity?
O Good Goddess!

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) can manifest the *dharmadhātu*, and the *dharmadhātu* is the five aggregates; yet the five aggregates cannot be described, nor can that which is not the five aggregates be described."

Why is this? If the five aggregates were the dharma-realm, it would be the view of annihilation; if one were apart from the five aggregates, it would be the view of eternalism. To be free from these two extremes and not to cling to them, such that no fault can be found and what is seen is without name or mark—this is called explaining the dharma-realm.
“Good Goddess!
How can the five aggregates manifest the dharma-realm?
Good Goddess!”
In this way, the five aggregates do not arise from causes and conditions. Why is this?
If they were to arise from causes and conditions, would that which has already arisen arise, or would that which has not yet arisen arise?
If it has already arisen, by what causes and conditions would it arise?
If it has already arisen, it does not arise from causes and conditions.
If it has not yet arisen, it cannot arise.

Why is this? All dharmas that have not yet arisen are non-existent; they are without name and without mark, incapable of being known through calculation or analogy, and not produced by causes and conditions.
“Good Goddess!
For example, the sound of a drum arises in dependence upon wood, leather, the drumhead, and human effort.
This sound of the drum is empty; it is empty of the past, empty of the future, and empty of the present.”

Why is this? This sound of the drum does not arise from the wood, nor from the hide, nor from the mallet, nor from human effort; this sound does not arise within the three periods of time, and thus it is unarisen.
If there is no arising to be found, then there is no ceasing;
if there is no ceasing, there is nowhere from which it comes;
and if there is nowhere from which it comes, there is also nowhere to which it goes.
If there is no place to which it goes, it is neither eternal nor discontinuous;
if it is neither eternal nor discontinuous, then it is neither identical nor different. Why is this so?
If they were one and not different from the dharma-realm, then ordinary persons would perceive the ultimate truth and attain unsurpassed, peaceful nirvana;
however, this is not the case, and therefore they are not one.

If one says they are different, then the modes of practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would constitute attachment; as long as one has not attained liberation from the fetters of affliction, one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because all noble ones practice with identical wisdom regarding both conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; therefore, they are not different.
For this reason, the five aggregates do not exist [as inherently real], yet they are not non-existent, nor are they produced from causes and conditions.

Because it does not fall within the realm of the sages, it is beyond the reach of language; it is without name and without form, without cause and without condition, without objective realm and without analogy; it is eternally quiescent from beginning to end and primordially empty by nature.
Therefore, the five aggregates can manifest the dharma-realm. "O Goddess!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family desires to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should contemplate that the ultimate truth and conventional reality are not different; such a state is difficult to fathom. Without differentiating between the realms of the noble and the ordinary, and without abandoning the conventional or the ultimate, they should practice the conduct of bodhi by relying upon the dharma-realm."

At that time, having spoken these words, the Goddess Bhadra leaped for joy and rose from her seat. She bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, she prostrated herself with single-minded devotion and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“As has been explained above, I shall now train in the correct practice of bodhi.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, asked the goddess Ratnarcis within the great assembly:
“This bodhi-practice is difficult to cultivate; how is it that your mind has attained mastery in this bodhi-practice?”
Then the Goddess Subhadrā replied to the Brahmā King:
"Great Brahmā King!
If that which the Buddha has spoken is truly profound, such that all ordinary beings cannot perceive its flavor, it is the subtle and difficult-to-know realm of the sages."

If my mind may dwell in peace and happiness by relying upon this Dharma, then by the power of these true words, may all immeasurable and boundless sentient beings in the five turbidities of this evil world attain golden bodies and the thirty-two marks; may they be neither male nor female, sitting upon precious lotus flowers and experiencing immeasurable bliss; may celestial wondrous flowers rain down, and the various celestial musical instruments sound spontaneously without being struck; and may every form of offering be fully provided.

When the Good Goddess had spoken these words, all sentient beings in the five turbidities of this evil world became entirely golden in color, were endowed with the thirty-two marks, were neither male nor female, and sat upon precious lotus flowers experiencing immeasurable bliss.

It was like the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, free from all evil realms; rows of jewel trees stood in formation, and seven-jeweled lotuses filled the world. A rain of various seven-jeweled objects and exquisite celestial flowers fell, while divine music played.
The goddess Bhadramāyākārī, Resplendent with the Light of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, immediately transformed her female form into the body of a Brahmā.
Then, the Great Brahmā King asked the Bodhisattva Resplendent with the Light of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel:
"By what practices did you formerly cultivate the conduct of awakening?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
“Brahmā King!
If the moon in the water were able to practice the conduct of awakening, then I too would have already practiced the conduct of awakening.”
If one dreams of practicing the bodhisattva conduct, I too shall practice the bodhisattva conduct;
if one practices the bodhisattva conduct like a flame or dew, I too shall practice the bodhisattva conduct;
if one practices the bodhisattva conduct like an echo, I too shall practice the bodhisattva conduct.
When the Great Brahma King had heard these words, he spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"In reliance upon what do you speak these words? He replied:
“Brahmā King!
There is not a single dharma that possesses a real characteristic, because cause and effect are established in mutual dependence.
Brahmā King then addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"If that were so, all ordinary worldlings would surely attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva replied,
"With what intention do you say this?"
Brahmā King!
The foolish person is one thing and the wise person another; awakening is one thing and non-awakening another; liberation is one thing and non-liberation another.
Brahmā King!
Thus, all phenomena are equal and without distinction.
Within this dharma-realm, suchness is without variation; there is no intermediate state to be grasped, neither increase nor decrease.
“Brahmā King!

It is like a master illusionist skilled in the arts of illusion, together with his disciples, who takes earth, sand, grass, wood, leaves, and so forth from a crossroads, gathers them in one place, and performs various illusions so that people may see multitudes of elephants, multitudes of horses, multitudes of chariots, multitudes of armies, heaps of the seven treasures, and various storehouses.”
If there are sentient beings who are foolish and lacking wisdom, unable to reflect, and ignorant of the root of illusion, they may see or hear [such things] and think:
"What I have seen—the multitudes of elephants, horses, and so forth—is real, just as it was seen and just as it was heard."

Each person, according to their ability and strength, clings to their own view, declaring it to be the truth while asserting that others' views are not real, without subsequently reflecting upon them.
A person of wisdom, however, is able to reflect and understand the illusory nature of these things; whether seeing or hearing them, they reflect thus:
"As I see them, this multitude of elephants, horses, and so forth are not real; there is only an illusion that deludes the eyes."
In this context, what are called the multitudes of elephants, horses, and so forth, as well as the various treasuries and granaries, exist only as names and have no substantial reality—
just as I have seen them and just as I have heard them.

According to their ability and strength, these wise people do not cling to what they have seen, nor do they claim, "This alone is the truth, while for others it is not real," nor do they fail to reflect upon it later.

When such wise people employ worldly speech, it is entirely because they wish to lead others to understand the true meaning; this is not the case when one reflects based merely on what has been seen or heard.
“Thus it is, Brahmā!

If there are sentient beings—foolish worldlings who have not yet attained the supramundane noble wisdom—and thus do not know that all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*) and ineffable, these foolish worldlings, upon seeing or hearing phenomena that are either conditioned or unconditioned, form this thought:
‘These phenomena truly exist, just as I have seen them and just as I have heard them.’”

These ordinary worldlings, according to what they have seen and heard, cling to their perceptions according to their ability and strength, declaring, "This alone is true; all else is false," and subsequently fail to reflect upon it again.

If there are sentient beings—who are not ordinary worldlings, who have already seen the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and who have attained supramundane noble wisdom—and who know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are suchness (*tathatā*) and ineffable; these noble ones, whether seeing or hearing the dharmas of practice or non-practice, according to their capacity and strength, do not cling to what they see, do not claim it to be the truth while asserting others' views to be false, and do not subsequently engage in further deliberation.

"There are no real dharmas of practice, nor are there any real dharmas of non-practice; as I have seen and as I have heard, these are merely the products of false conceptualization regarding the characteristics of practice and non-practice, or the wisdom of persons."
This state is called "conditioned" or "unconditioned" phenomena; it exists only as a name and has no substantial reality.
It is just as I have seen it, just as I have heard it.

According to their ability and strength, they do not cling to their own views, nor do they claim that what they say is the absolute truth while what others say is false, nor do they fail to reflect further upon it later.
These noble ones conform to worldly conventions in their speech, desiring only to lead others to understand the true meaning.
Thus it is, Brahmā!

Because these noble ones perceive through their noble wisdom, they understand that the ineffable Dharma is subsumed within suchness, whether as conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena. This Dharma-suchness is designated by various names for the sake of being realized and known by others.
Then the Great Brahma King asked the Bodhisattva Jewel-Light Radiance:
"How many sentient beings are able to understand and master such subtle, profound, and correct Dharma?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Brahmā King!
As many as there are individuals among the various phantom-like transformed beings, so many sentient beings are able to understand and penetrate this profound Dharma."
The Brahma King spoke again:
"If this illusory person is non-existent, from where could such mental factors arise?
The Bodhisattva replied:
“Brahmā King!
Thus, this dharma-realm is neither existent nor non-existent; thus, sentient beings are able to understand and penetrate this profound meaning.
At that time, Brahmā King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Bodhisattva Jewel-Radiance is inconceivable; he has thoroughly realized such profound meaning.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Brahmā King! It is just as you have said."

"Why is this? It is because the Bodhisattva Maṇiratnaprabhāsa has already instructed the Brahmā King in the practice of contemplating the Dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Thereupon, the Great Brahmā King and the assembly of Brahmās rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Maṇiratnaprabhāsa, speaking these words:
“Rare, indeed, rare!
Today we have been able to behold the Great Teacher and hear the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having attained unimpeded mastery over all dharmas, addressed the Brahma King, saying:

“This Bodhisattva Maṇiratnaprabhāsa shall, in a future age, attain Buddhahood under the name of Tathāgata Guṇaratnārciśrīgarbha, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He shall preach this subtle and wondrous Sūtra of the Golden Light, whereby three thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas will attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; eight thousand koṭis of devaputras will attain stainless purity and achieve the pure Dharma-eye regarding the Dharma; and immeasurable and innumerable kings, ministers, and subjects will attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.”

Five billion bhikṣus who were practicing the bodhisattva path and were about to retreat from the resolve for awakening, upon hearing the Dharma preached by the Bodhisattva Ratnārcis, attained firm, inconceivable, and fulfilled vows; they once again gave rise to the mind of awakening, each disrobing to make an offering to the Bodhisattva, and once more resolved upon the unsurpassed, supreme progress toward enlightenment.
Having generated the supreme mind of advancement, they made this vow:
"May all our merits and roots of goodness never decline, and may they be dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

“Thus, these bhikṣus, practicing in reliance upon these merits, shall achieve accomplishment after ninety great kalpas. These bhikṣus will emerge from birth and death, and the Buddha will grant them this prediction:

‘After thirty asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall become buddhas named King of Difficult-to-Conquer Radiance (Duṣprasahaprabharāja). Your land shall be named Stainless Light (Vimalaprabhā). Simultaneously, you shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and you shall all share the same title: Buddha King of the Interspersed Array of Vows (Praṇidhānavyūhavyatikīrṇarāja).’”
At that time, the Buddha told the Brahma King:
"This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, when correctly heard and correctly listened to, possesses great supernormal power.
O Brahma King!"

If for hundreds of thousands of great kalpas one practices the six pāramitās without skillful means, yet there is a son or daughter of good family who has already heard this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, and having transcribed it, recites and reads it once every half-month, then this accumulation of wholesome merit cannot equal even one hundred-thousandth part of the former merit; it is beyond reach even by calculation or analogy.
Brahmā King!
For this reason, I shall now cause you to study, uphold, and extensively explain it for others. Why is this?

Regarding such profound and subtle sūtras as these, when I practiced the bodhisattva path, I was like one in the midst of battle who does not begrudge his own body or life; thus, I attained mastery of this sūtra, receiving, upholding, reciting, and explaining it for others.
“Brahmā King!
It is like a wheel-turning sage king: as long as the king remains in the world, the seven treasures do not perish;
once the king has passed away from the world, all seven treasures naturally come to an end.”
"Brahmā King!
If this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* exists in the present age, the great and true jewel of the Dharma will not perish at all.

Therefore, you should rely upon the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* to hear it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, explain it for others, and cause others to transcribe it. Within these meritorious deeds, you should practice the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), not begrudging your life nor fearing weariness. My disciples should thus diligently train themselves."

At that time, the Lord of Devas, the Great Brahmā Heavenly King, together with immeasurable hosts of Brahmās, Śakra, the Four Kings, and the yakṣa hosts, rose from their seats. Baring their right shoulders and placing their right knees upon the ground, they joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We shall all protect and circulate this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*. If the Dharma-preachers who expound this teaching encounter any difficulties, we shall eliminate them, causing them to be endowed with all virtues, to be perfect in physical appearance and flavor, to possess unimpeded eloquence, and to have their bodies and minds open and serene; we shall cause all those in the assembly to be joyful.

If there are famines, enemies, bandits, or the terrors of non-human beings in this land, we shall ward them off, so that its people may be prosperous and at ease—all through the power of our grace as the Four Kings."
If there are those who make offerings to this sutra scroll, I shall likewise provide them with great protection, no different from that which I provide for the Buddha.
*Combined Edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Scroll Four;
*Combined Edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Śīlabhadra of Daxingshan Monastery during the Sui Dynasty, based on the translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of North Liang. Chapter Ten:

The Four Heavenly Kings (V). Chapter Ten: The Four Heavenly Kings. At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, and the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*—the king of all sūtras—is protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; it adorns the profound and wondrous merits of bodhisattvas, is constantly revered by the various devas, causes the hearts of the celestial kings to rejoice, and is praised by the World Protectors.”

This sutra can illuminate all the celestial palaces; this sutra can bestow happiness upon sentient beings; this sutra can cause the rivers of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals to parch and dry up; this sutra can eliminate all fears; this sutra can repel enemies and bandits from other regions; this sutra can remove the calamity of famine and high grain prices; this sutra can cure all epidemics; this sutra can extinguish the portents of malevolent stars; and this sutra can dispel all grief and affliction.
To state the essentials:
this sutra can extinguish the immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings.
World-Honored One!

When this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra is being extensively proclaimed before a great assembly, we—the four kings and our retinues—having heard this unsurpassed flavor of the nectar-like Dharma, shall increase our physical strength, our mental vigor and sharpness, and be endowed with all majestic virtues.
“World-Honored One!
We four kings can preach the true Dharma and practice the true Dharma, serving as Dharma-kings of the world to govern it according to the Dharma.
World-Honored One!”

We, the four kings, along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, shall govern the world according to the Dharma, warding off all evil spirits and those who consume vital energy.
“World-Honored One!

We, the four kings, the twenty-eight classes of spirits and ghosts, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of spirits and ghosts, with our pure divine eyes that surpass those of humans, shall constantly observe and protect this Jambudvīpa.”
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, we are called the World-Protecting Kings.

If in this land there should be various depletions, enemy invaders crossing the borders, famine, pestilence, or various kinds of hardships, and if there should be a bhikṣu who upholds this sutra, we four kings shall together exhort him so that, by our power, he may quickly go to those regions—cities, towns, and districts—to widely proclaim and disseminate this subtle and wonderful *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, causing all such various hundreds of thousands of depleting matters to be completely extinguished.”
“World-Honored One!

Just as with the territories belonging to various kings, if a holder of this sutra should arrive in their kingdom, that king ought to go to that person’s place to hear and receive such a subtle and wondrous scripture.”
Having heard this, we shall rejoice and further protect, keep in mind, and revere such a person.
World-Honored One!
We, the four kings, shall again diligently protect this king and the people of his realm with a devoted heart, eliminating their decline and afflictions so that they may attain peace and security.
“World-Honored One!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who receive and uphold this sutra, and if there are kings among men who are able to provide for them and bestow upon them all that brings peace and comfort, we four kings shall likewise cause these kings and all the people of their nations to be secure and at ease, fully endowed with freedom from affliction.”
"Blessed One!

If there are members of the fourfold assembly who uphold, receive, read, and recite this sublime sūtra, and if any human kings are able to make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise them, we, the Four Kings, shall likewise cause such human kings to always receive the foremost offerings, reverence, honor, and praise among all kings, and shall cause other kings to look upon them with admiration and envy, praising their virtue."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Four Heavenly Kings who protect the world, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

You Four Kings, in the past, have already made offerings to, paid respect to, honored, and praised immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas. Under those Buddhas, you have planted various roots of goodness, preached the True Dharma, practiced the True Dharma, governed the world according to the Dharma, and served as kings of men and gods."

Today you have brought long-term benefit to all sentient beings; practicing great compassion, you bestow upon them all instruments of happiness, able to restrain all evils and diligently provide all that is wholesome.

For this reason, if there is a king who is able to make offerings to and revere this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra, you should truly protect and sustain him in such a manner, extinguishing his suffering and distress and bestowing upon him peace and happiness.

If you, the Four Kings, along with your retinues and immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities, can protect and keep such a sutra in mind, you will thereby be upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
When you, the four kings, along with the other hosts of devas and hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities, engage in battle with the asuras, you gods shall always achieve victory.
If you are able to protect and keep this sutra in mind, you will be able to completely eliminate and subdue all sufferings, namely those caused by enemies and bandits, famine, and pestilence.

If any members of the fourfold assembly can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, you should also diligently protect them with a devoted heart, in order to remove their decline and affliction and bestow upon them peace and happiness.
At that time, the Four Kings again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra will circulate in future ages wherever it may be—in kingdoms, cities, districts, or villages—at whatever place it arrives. If kings govern their realms according to celestial laws and are further able to reverently and wholeheartedly listen to and receive this sublime sūtra, and if they furthermore honor, make offerings to, and provide for the fourfold assembly who uphold this sūtra, then by these causes and conditions, we shall from time to time hear such a subtle and wondrous sūtra. Having heard it, we shall immediately gain an increase in physical strength, our minds will become courageous and vigorous, and we shall be endowed with all majestic virtues.”
Therefore, we and immeasurable spirits shall constantly remain invisible and provide protection wherever this sublime scripture circulates, ensuring that no obstacles arise;

we shall also protect and keep in mind those kings and their subjects who listen to this sutra, removing their afflictions and hardships so that all may dwell in peace and security, and causing enemies and bandits from other regions to retreat and disperse.
World-Honored One! When a king who rules over men hears this sutra, the hostile enemies of neighboring states may conceive such a thought:
"We shall assemble the fourfold army to destroy that kingdom.
World-Honored One!

By the majestic spiritual power of this sutra, at that time, neighboring enemies or other adversaries shall create obstacles and difficulties; they shall incite various forms of decline, affliction, calamities, and pestilence within its borders. When those enemies have thus instigated such evils, they shall assemble the four divisions of their army and set out toward this land intending to punish it. At that time, we, together with our retinues and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities, shall conceal our forms and provide protection and assistance, causing those enemies to naturally retreat and disperse, and giving rise to various terrors and obstacles.
"If even the military forces of that country cannot reach there, how much less could they possibly cause any destruction?
At that time, the Buddha praised the Four Heavenly Kings and the others:
"Excellent, excellent!"

"You Four Kings are indeed able to protect my cultivation of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* kalpas, as well as those human kings who uphold this sutra and reverently make offerings to it, by eliminating their misfortunes and afflictions and causing them to dwell in peace and happiness.

Furthermore, you are able to protect palaces, residences, cities, towns, villages, kingdoms, and frontiers, even driving back all enemies and bandits so that their decline and distress are extinguished and they attain security.
You shall also cause all kings within Jambudvīpa to be free from calamities, decline, strife, and litigation."
"O Four Kings, you should know that in this Jambudvīpa there are eighty-four thousand cities,
towns, and villages, and eighty-four thousand human kings. Each enjoys pleasure and happiness within his own kingdom,
each attains sovereignty over his own land, and each is individually satisfied with their own wealth and treasures, without [needing] one another."
As for the seizing and plundering [of others], they receive retribution in accordance with the karma they have cultivated in previous lives;
they do not give rise to evil thoughts or greed for other kingdoms, but each gives rise to a mind of mutual benefit,
a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of peace and happiness, a mind free from contention, a mind free from destruction, and a mind free from bondage.

The people of Chu were so heartened that each found joy within themselves; the relationship between superiors and subordinates was as harmonious and concordant as water and milk, their hearts filled with mutual affection as they increased their roots of goodness.

For these reasons, this Jambudvīpa will be peaceful, secure, and prosperous; its population will flourish, the earth will be fertile, and the Yin and Yang will be harmoniously balanced. The seasons will not deviate from their order, the sun, moon, and constellations will not fail in their regular courses, and wind and rain will arrive at their proper times. Free from calamities and misfortunes, the people will be abundant and self-sufficient in wealth; their minds will be free from greed and stinginess as well as envy. They will practice the ten wholesome deeds equally, and upon the end of their lives, many will be reborn in the celestial palaces of the heavens, increasing and filling the ranks of the devas.

“If, in future ages, there are kings who listen to this sutra, and who provide offerings, respect, and uphold it together with the fourfold assembly, then those kings will bring peace, happiness, benefit, and welfare to you, the Four Kings, as well as to your retinues and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities.”
For what reason?

If you, the Four Kings, should from time to time hear this sutra, you will have already obtained the water of the True Dharma and partaken of the flavor of ambrosia; your physical strength will increase, your minds will become courageous and sharp, and you will be endowed with all majestic virtues.
If these kings of men can listen to and receive this scripture with a sincere heart, they will have already been able to make offerings to me;
if they make offerings to me, they are making offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
and if they can make offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they shall obtain an immeasurable and inconceivable accumulation of merit.

By these causes and conditions, these kings of men shall receive protection, as shall their queens, concubines, ladies of the inner court, retinues, and princes; their decay and afflictions shall be extinguished, and their joy shall flourish.

Their palaces and halls shall be peaceful, secure, and pure, free from all calamities and portents; the deities who protect their dwellings shall increase in majesty and virtue, and they too shall experience immeasurable delight and happiness.
All the people within these lands shall enjoy the various pleasures of the five senses, and all evil matters shall be entirely extinguished.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

In future ages, if there should be a king who wishes to protect his own person, as well as his queen, concubines, court ladies, and princes; who desires for his palace and residence to have the foremost protection; whose reign is most preeminent; who possesses the inconceivable merits of a king; who wishes to gather immeasurable stores of merit; and whose realm is free from enemies and bandits from other regions, and devoid of all anxieties, afflictions, and painful matters.”
"World-Honored One!

Such a king of men should not be negligent or allow his mind to be distracted; he should give rise to a heart of reverence and humility. He should adorn his foremost, most subtle, and most excellent palace with various fragrant liquids used to sprinkle the ground, scatter various flowers, and arrange a great Dharma-seat—a lion-throne—further embellished with immeasurable rare and extraordinary treasures, and hung with various countless, subtle, and exquisite banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies."

One should bathe and purify oneself, anoint the body with fragrances, put on fine and clean robes, and adorn oneself with necklaces. Sitting upon a small and low seat, one should not be haughty or self-exalting; casting off self-importance and remaining free from negligence, one should humble oneself, eliminate pride and arrogance, and listen to such a sublime scripture with right mindfulness, regarding the teacher of the Dharma as the World-Honored One.

Furthermore, within the palace, he gave rise to a heart of compassion for the queens, princes, court ladies, and retinue; with a serene countenance, he spoke to them and exhorted them to provide various articles of offering to honor the Dharma Master.

At that time, having thus exhorted and transformed others, the king immediately gave rise to immeasurable joy and happiness; his heart was filled with delight, and he redoubled his self-exertion without succumbing to weariness, performing much that was beneficial and conceiving even greater reverence for the Dharma-preacher.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings:

"At that time, the King of Men should don pure, white, and fresh garments, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments in perfect order; holding a subtle and exquisite white silk canopy, his attire and deportment remaining constant and proper, he should personally go out to welcome the one who preaches the Dharma."

Why is this? Because for such a king, with every single step he takes, he performs an offering that encounters hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; furthermore, he transcends the hardships of birth and death for as many eons as there are steps, and in future ages, for that same number of eons, he shall constantly receive the consecration and attain the rank of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).
With every step taken, one shall likewise attain such merits in the present life: inconceivable power of mastery;

constant possession of the most excellent and exquisite palaces of the seven treasures belonging to humans and devas; an increase in lifespan in every place of birth; eloquence and clarity of speech; being trusted and relied upon by others; freedom from fear or apprehension; great renown; constant veneration by humans and devas; enjoyment of supreme and wondrous pleasures among devas and humans; attainment of great influence; fullness of majestic virtue; a subtle and exquisite physical form, foremost in beauty and dignity; constant encounter with the Buddhas; meeting with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); and the complete accomplishment of an immeasurable accumulation of merit.
“O you Four Heavenly Kings!

Thus, when a king of men perceives such various and immeasurable merits and benefits, he ought to personally go forth to welcome the Dharma Master, whether for the distance of one yojana or even up to a hundred thousand yojanas.”
One should conceive the thought of a Buddha toward the Dharma-preacher and reflect thus:
"Today, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, with his perfect wisdom, has entered my palace to receive my offerings and preach the Dharma for me;
having heard this Dharma, I shall not regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Ti, you have already encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas; you have already made offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
you have already attained the ultimate cessation of the sufferings of the three evil realms.
I have now planted the causes for becoming a hundred thousand immeasurable Wheel-Turning Kings, Śakras, and Brahmās, and I have planted boundless roots of goodness."
Having caused immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings to cross over birth and death,
and having accumulated immeasurable and boundless masses of merit, his harem and retinue have already obtained protection for their palaces and residences,
and all misfortunes have been completely extinguished; in his realm there are no enemies, thieves, or thorns, nor any hostile adversaries from other regions.
“...they shall not be able to invade or oppress. “O you Four Kings!

Thus, a king of men should provide such offerings to the True Dharma, and should listen to and receive this sublime sutra with purity, as well as honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising it.”

The fourfold assembly who uphold this sutra should likewise dedicate their share of the most supreme merit thus obtained to you and your retinues, as well as to the devas and spirits. By accumulating such wholesome merits, they shall in this present life constantly obtain immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable benefits of mastery; endowed with full majesty, power, and accomplishment, they shall be able to subdue all evils through the True Dharma.
At that time, the Four Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If in future ages there are kings who thus revere the True Dharma, who with a sincere heart listen to and receive this sublime sutra, and who revere, make offerings to, respect, and praise it; and when the fourfold assembly upholds this sutra, adorns their dwellings, sprinkles the ground with fragrant water, and listens to the preaching of the Dharma with single-minded right mindfulness—then we, the Four Kings, shall also be present among them to hear this Dharma together. We pray that for the sake of their own benefit, these kings will bestow upon us even a small portion of the merit they have attained.”
“World-Honored One!

When these kings of men, for our sake, burn various kinds of incense as an offering to this sutra at the place where the Dharma-preacher sits, that wondrous fragrance reaches our celestial palaces in a single thought-moment. That fragrance immediately transforms into a fragrant canopy; its scent is so subtle and exquisite, and its golden brilliance so radiant, that it illuminates our palaces, the palaces of Śakra, and the palaces of Brahmā.”

The Great Eloquence Deva, the Merit Deva, the Earth-Sustaining Firm Goddess, the Great General Vaiśravaṇa of the Kumbhāṇḍas, the Great Generals of the twenty-eight divisions of spirits and deities, Maheśvara, Vajrapāṇi, the Great General Maṇibhadra, and Harītī surrounded by her five hundred sons; the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Sāgara, and suchlike multitudes—from their respective palaces, each heard this wondrous fragrance and beheld the light of the incense-canopy shining everywhere, as that light of the incense-canopy also illuminated all the palaces of the devas.
The Buddha told the Four Kings:
"This radiance from the fragrant canopy does not merely reach your palaces, O Four Kings. Why is this?"

When these kings of men hold incense burners in their hands to make offerings while reciting this sutra, its fragrance spreads everywhere; in a single thought-moment, it reaches throughout the trichiliocosm—ten billion suns and moons, ten billion great oceans, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion Great Iron Ring Mountains, small Iron Ring Mountains, and all the kings of mountains; ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion Four Heavenly Kings, ten billion Trāyastriṃśa Heavens, and so on, up to ten billion Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heavens.

In this great trichiliocosm, the palaces of the ten billion Trāyastriṃśa heavens, as well as those of all the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, were entirely filled with clouds of various fragrant incense smoke; the golden light from these canopies also illuminated the palaces.
In this way, all the various clouds of incense smoke throughout the trichiliocosm are due to the majestic spiritual power of this sutra.

When these kings of men hold incense burners in their hands to make offerings to the sutra, the various fragrances not only pervade this trichiliocosm, but in a single moment of thought, they also pervade hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and boundless Ganges Rivers in the ten directions; furthermore, they form canopies of fragrance in the void above those Buddhas, and their golden light shines everywhere in the same manner.

When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, heard this wondrous fragrance, saw this fragrant canopy and golden light, and had performed such supernatural transformations throughout worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they praised the speaker of the Dharma with one voice:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Mahāsattva!
Since you are able to widely proclaim and disseminate such a profound and subtle sūtra, you shall thereby accomplish an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable accumulation of merit."

"If there are those who hear this profound sutra, the merit they obtain will not be small; how much more so for those who uphold, read, recite it, and for the sake of other sentient beings, reveal, analyze, and expound its meaning?"
Why is this? Good son!

If immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas should hear this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra, they will immediately become non-retrogressive from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Buddhas currently residing in the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, spoke with one voice, saying:
"O son of good family!

In a future age, you shall certainly attain the seat of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree; most honored and most supreme within the three realms, you shall transcend all sentient beings. Through the power of diligent cultivation, you shall undergo various ascetic practices, skillfully adorning the site of enlightenment. You shall be able to destroy the heterodox arguments of those outside the path throughout the trichiliocosm, subdue all Māras, enemies, and malevolent spirits, and awaken to the foremost tranquility of all dharmas—the pure, stainless, profound, and unsurpassed path of Bodhi.

"Good son! You have already been able to sit upon the Vajra Seat, turn the twelvefold wheel of Dharma—profound and praised by all Buddhas—which is unsurpassed; you have been able to beat the unsurpassed, greatest drum of Dharma; you have been able to blow the unsurpassed, most exquisite conch of Dharma; you have been able to raise the unsurpassed, most victorious banner of Dharma; you have been able to light the unsurpassed, most brilliant torch of Dharma; you have been able to rain down the unsurpassed nectar-rain of Dharma; you have been able to sever the immeasurable knots of enmity that are the afflictions; you have been able to cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of beings to cross the shoreless and fearsome great ocean of birth and death; you have been able to liberate them from the boundless cycle of saṃsāra; and you have again encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* can bring about various kinds of immeasurable merits in both the future and the present."

Therefore, if a king of men hears this subtle and wondrous sutra, he shall have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of immeasurable Buddhas.

Out of my reverence for this king of men, and because I perceive immeasurable merit and benefit therein, we—the four of us kings, our retinues, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of spirits—shall, upon seeing these various auspicious omens such as clouds of incense smoke and canopies of fragrance within our own palaces, conceal ourselves and remain invisible. For the sake of hearing the Dharma, we shall go to the palace where this king resides and to the place where the Dharma is being preached.

Mahābrahmā, Śakra-devendra, Mahāprajñā-devī, Puṇya-devī, the Earth Goddess Dhṛtarāṣṭrā, the Great General Vaiśravaṇa and the other twenty-eight generals of the spirits and ghosts, Maheśvara, Vajrapāṇi, the Great General Maṇibhadra, Hārītī surrounded by her five hundred sons, the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Sāgara, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of spirits, ghosts, and devas—all these assemblies, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, each concealed themselves and did not manifest their bodies as they arrived at the palace where this human king resided and where the Dharma was being preached.
“World-Honored One!

We, the four kings, along with our retinues and immeasurable spirits and deities, shall all with one mind regard this king as a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra). Together we shall practice a single course—a course of wholesome correspondence—acting as unsurpassed donors of the Great Dharma, and thereby satisfy us with the flavor of ambrosia.”

"We should protect this king, removing his misfortunes and afflictions so that he may attain peace and security; we shall cause all evil calamities and disasters concerning his palace, kingdom, and cities to be completely extinguished."
“World-Honored One!
If there is a king who, regarding this sutra, gives rise to a mind of renunciation and takes no pleasure in hearing it; whose heart has no desire to revere, make offerings to, honor, or praise it;
and if among the fourfold assembly there are those who uphold, read, recite, or explain it, whom he likewise cannot revere, make offerings to, honor, or praise;”

If we—the four kings, our retinues, and immeasurable spirits—were unable to hear this True Dharma, we would turn our backs on the flavor of the nectar of immortality, lose the great benefit of the Dharma, lack power and majesty, cause the celestial hosts to diminish, and increase those in the evil realms.
"World-Honored One!
We four kings and immeasurable spirits and deities shall abandon that land;
not only we, but also the immeasurable ancient virtuous deities who protect the land shall all depart."

Once we gods and various spirits have departed, that land shall experience all manner of calamities and anomalies. All the people will lose their virtuous minds; there will be only bondage, anger, strife, mutual destruction, and many epidemics. Comets will appear as portents, meteors will fall, and the five planets and various lunar mansions will deviate from their regular courses. Two suns will appear simultaneously, and the sun and moon will undergo eclipses. White and black evil rainbows will appear repeatedly. The earth will quake and emit great sounds; foul winds and torrential rains will occur every day. Grain and rice will become exceedingly expensive, leading to famine and starvation. There will be many invading enemies and bandits from other regions plundering the land, and the people of that country will suffer much distress; there will be no place in that land that is pleasant or delightful.
World-Honored One!

When we, the four kings, along with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of spirits and ghosts, as well as the long-standing benevolent deities who protect the lands, depart and distance ourselves, such immeasurable evil matters as these will arise.
“World-Honored One!

If there is a king who wishes to protect himself and his kingdom so that they may enjoy great peace and happiness; who wishes to cause all sentient beings within his realm to fully achieve and possess joy; who wishes to subdue all external enemies; who wishes to protect all territories; who wishes to govern his realm with the True Dharma; and who wishes to eliminate the fears of sentient beings—World-Honored One!”
These kings of men and others should certainly listen to this sutra, and they should also respectfully make offerings to, read, recite, and uphold those who do so.

By means of the roots of goodness from this Dharma-food, we—the four kings and immeasurable spirits—shall partake of the unsurpassed flavor of the nectar of the Dharma, increase our physical strength, sharpen our mental vigor and resolve, and cause the various devas to flourish.
Why is this? Because this king of men listens to and receives this sutra with a sincere heart.

"World-Honored One, it is like the discourses on the transcendence of desire spoken by the Brahma heavens, the various excellent discourses of Śakra Devānām Indra, and the discourses of the seers and immortals who possess the five supernatural powers."

Although Brahmā, Śakra-devendra, and those with the five supernatural powers may possess hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of immeasurable superior discourses, this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the most supreme among them all.

Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata has preached this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* for the sake of sentient beings; to cause all kings among men within Jambudvīpa to rule by means of the True Dharma; to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings; out of a desire to protect all sentient beings; wishing to ensure that sentient beings are free from all suffering and affliction; wishing to eliminate the thorns of enemies and bandits from other regions; wishing that all evils turn their backs and do not approach; and wishing to ensure that the land is free from distress and that there is no litigation or dispute through instruction in the True Dharma.
Therefore, O Kings of Men, each within your respective realms should kindle the torch of Dharma and cause the True Dharma to blaze forth, thereby increasing the hosts of devas.

By this cause and condition, we—the Four Great Kings, along with immeasurable spirits, ghosts, and the various celestial benevolent deities within Jambudvīpa—shall partake of the nectar of immortality; our enjoyment of the flavor of the Dharma shall be sufficient, and we shall attain great majesty and virtue, as well as fullness of vigor and power.

Within Jambudvīpa, there shall be peace, stability, and abundance; the population shall flourish, and people shall dwell in that place in happiness. Furthermore, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of inconceivable nayutas of kalpas in future lives, they shall constantly experience the most subtle and supreme bliss, and they shall encounter immeasurable Buddhas to plant all manner of roots of goodness, after which they will realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Such immeasurable merits as these have all been taught by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Tathāgata surpasses hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Brahmās and others by virtue of the power of his great compassion;
he also surpasses immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Śakras, the Indras, by virtue of the power of his ascetic practices.
Therefore, for the sake of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata expounds this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra*.

Should all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, as well as the kings of men, engage in worldly or supramundane affairs of state, or compose worldly treatises, they shall do so by means of this sūtra—desiring to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings—the Śākya Tathāgata has manifested this scripture and caused it to be widely proclaimed and circulated.
“World-Honored One!
For these reasons, these kings of men should certainly listen to and receive this sutra, and they should make offerings to it, honoring, respecting, and praising it.”
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"You Four Kings, along with your retinues and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of spirits and deities!"

If these kings of men can listen to this sutra with a sincere heart, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising it, you four kings should properly protect them, extinguishing their misfortunes and afflictions and bestowing peace and happiness upon them.

If there is anyone who can widely proclaim and disseminate such a sublime scripture—performing great Buddha-work among gods and humans and bringing vast benefit to immeasurable sentient beings—you four kings must certainly protect such a person. Do not allow them to be disturbed by external conditions; let their minds be tranquil and peaceful so they may experience happiness, and enable them to continue to widely proclaim this sutra.
At that time, the Four Kings rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined before the World-Honored One, praised him in verse:
“The Buddha-moon is pure, Complete and adorned;
The Buddha-sun shines brilliantly, Radiating a thousand rays of light.”
The face and eyes of the Tathāgata are most supreme, bright, and pure;
his teeth are white and stainless, like the roots of a lotus flower;
his merit is immeasurable, like the great ocean.
The ocean of wisdom is boundless, and the waters of the Dharma are complete; the hundreds of thousands of samādhis are without deficiency.
The soles of his feet are level and full, manifesting the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel; the webbing between his toes is like that of the king of geese.
His radiance blazes forth, like the king of jewel mountains.
Subtle and pure, like refined gold;
with all inconceivable merit, you are a mountain of Buddha-virtues—to you I now pay homage.
Like empty space, it manifests forms in response to things;
like the moon reflected in water, it is without obstruction; like a mirage, like a transformation.
"Therefore, I now prostrate before the Buddha-moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras, is most profound and supreme."
This unsurpassed teaching,
proclaimed by the World-Honored One who possesses the ten powers, you four kings should diligently protect.
For these reasons, this profound and wondrous scripture can bestow immeasurable happiness upon sentient beings.
For the sake of the peace, happiness, and benefit of all beings, it shall circulate for a long time within Jambudvīpa.
They are able to extinguish all the evil realms and immeasurable sufferings within the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.
Within Jambudvīpa, all kings of men will give rise to a heart of compassion and govern the world through the True Dharma.
If one can disseminate this wondrous sutra, then that land will be peaceful, secure, and abundant;
all sentient beings therein shall experience complete happiness.
If there is a king who desires to cherish his own person and his kingdom,
wishing for them to be prosperous and flourishing, he should with a sincere heart bathe himself in purity and go to the place of the Dharma assembly to listen to and receive this scripture.
All virtuous deeds subdue all internal and external enemies and adversaries,
and are further able to eliminate immeasurable fears.
These kings of sutras can bestow peace and happiness upon all immeasurable sentient beings.
They are like a jewel tree standing within a person's home, which is able to produce all manner of precious treasures.
This sublime sūtra is likewise so; it is able to give birth to all the merits of kings.
Just as clear, cool water can eliminate thirst and exhaustion;
this sublime sūtra is likewise so, able to eliminate the thirst for merit among kings.
Just as a casket containing rare jewels and extraordinary objects is held entirely in one's hand and may be used at will;
so too is this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, which can, according to one's desire,
bestow the Dharma-jewels upon all kings.
This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, this subtle and wondrous sūtra, is constantly honored and made offerings to by all the devas;
it is also protected and sustained by the majestic power and authority of the World-Protectors, the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
The Buddhas of the ten directions always keep this sūtra in mind; should anyone expound it, [they shall be protected].
They praised him, saying, "Excellent!
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of immeasurable spirits and deities came from the ten directions to protect this person.
If there are those who hear this wondrous sutra, their hearts will give rise to joy, leaping for immeasurable delight.
Within Jambudvīpa, the immeasurable multitudes will all rejoice and assemble to listen to this Dharma.
"By listening to this sutra, they shall possess all majestic virtues, increase the hosts of devas, and augment their vital essence and physical strength.
At that time, having heard these verses, the Four Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Since ancient times, I have never before heard such a subtle and profound Dharma of quiescent extinction.

Having heard this, my heart was filled with both sorrow and joy; tears flowed profusely, my entire body trembled, and my limbs were suffused with bliss. Furthermore, I attained immeasurable, inconceivable, and perfect wondrous happiness.

Having made offerings by scattering celestial māndārava flowers and mahāmāndārava flowers upon the Tathāgata, and having thus performed such worship of the Buddha, he addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“We four kings each have five hundred spirits who shall constantly follow and protect this preacher of the Dharma.
