*Combined Edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Volume Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Śīlabhadra of Daixingshan Monastery during the Sui Dynasty, in conjunction with Śikṣānanda. Chapter Eleven:
The Silver-Lord Dhāraṇī (Part Six). Chapter Eleven: The Silver-Lord Dhāraṇī. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“Śāriputra! These bodhisattvas cultivate all dharmas—namely, the mothers of the bodhisattvas, the former practices of the bodhisattvas, and the integrations of the bodhisattvas—and there is a fundamental dharma called the *Dhāraṇī of Non-Attachment*.
When he had spoken thus, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
regarding what is called ‘dhāraṇī,’ what is the meaning of the term ‘dhāraṇī’?”
Is it a dhāraṇī? Or is it not a dhāraṇī?
World-Honored One!
"Is it localized? Or is it non-localized?
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
Just as you have set out in the Mahāyāna,
have faith and understanding in the Mahāyāna, and increase your strength in the Mahāyāna, so it is as you have said."

That dhāraṇī is neither spatial nor non-spatial; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma; it is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is neither a thing nor a non-thing; it is neither a condition nor a non-condition; it is neither activity nor non-activity. There is no dharma that arises therein, nor is there any that ceases; it exists solely for the benefit of bodhisattvas.

Thus it is said that this dhāraṇī constitutes the path, the union, the power, and the abiding; namely, the various merits of the Buddha, the Buddha’s precepts, the Buddha’s training, the Buddha’s secret intent, and the Buddha’s manifestation—namely, the root of the Dharma, called the *Anupalip-dhāraṇī* (The Dhāraṇī of Non-Attachment).
When he had spoken thus, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
we pray that you will expound this for us.”

Sugata! We pray that you will expound this dharma-text of the dhāraṇī, so that bodhisattvas, having dwelt within it, shall become non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; shall achieve the eloquence of the nature of phenomena based on right vows and non-reliance; and shall attain the rarefied path of self-abiding, namely, by virtue of obtaining this dhāraṇī.
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!”
"So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī should be said to be like a Buddha."
Śāriputra!
If there are those who make offerings to, revere, serve, and provide for a bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī, they should regard it as making offerings to a Buddha.

Śāriputra! If there should be those who hear this dhāraṇī, or uphold it, or believe and understand it, they should be honored in this same way; not being separated from the bodhicitta, they are no different from the Buddha.
Śāriputra! This is the dhāraṇī: "Tadyathā:

(1) sandhārani, (2) uttarani, (3) samprati-kṣipra-citta, (4) sunama, (5) supratīśatā, (6) niśraya-vara, (7) satya-pratijñā, (8) su-aruha, (9) jñānamati, (10) utpādani, (11) apamanani, (12) abhiṣṭhāpani, (13) abhiprīyāhara, (14) śubhapati, (15) suniśrita, (16) bhūkuṃbha, (17) abhyavadata, (18) svāhā. Śāriputra!
This is a dhāraṇī phrase called "Non-attachment.

Once it has been correctly established and correctly received, if a bodhisattva maintains it, whether for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or a hundred thousand kalpas, they shall not abandon their vows; that person’s body will be able to subdue swords and weapons, poisons, and evil beasts—all of which they can subdue.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

This *adhyālambana-dhāraṇī* (Dhāraṇī of Non-Attachment) is the mother of all Buddhas of the past, the mother of all Buddhas of the future, and the mother of all Buddhas of the present; that is to say, the fundamental nature of phenomena is named the *adhyālambana-dhāraṇī*.

Śāriputra! Suppose there were ten *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms filled with the seven precious jewels, and one were to offer them to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as well as providing them with the most excellent garments and food, making such offerings to those Buddhas for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; yet if one were to hold even a single phrase from this Dharma-text of the *Dhāraṇī* of Non-attachment, the merit produced in this life would exceed that by far.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Because this Dharma-source of the *adhyālambana-dhāraṇī* is the mother of all Buddhas.

12. Chapter on Mahāprajñādevī (6). Chapter Twelve: Mahāprajñādevī. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang. At that time, the goddess Mahāprajñā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I shall augment the power of eloquence of this preacher of the Dharma, causing his preaching of the Dharma to be adorned and enabling him to skillfully attain great wisdom in its proper sequence.

If there are errors in the text or discrepancies in the meaning of the phrases within this sutra, I can cause this bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma to recover them in their proper order, and I can grant him dhāraṇī so that he does not forget them.

If there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, this Dharma-preacher, for their sake, shall extensively expound and disseminate this sublime sūtra throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted.

Furthermore, may immeasurable and boundless sentient beings hear this sutra; may they all attain a mass of fierce and inconceivable great wisdom, the retribution of incalculable merit and virtue, skillful understanding of immeasurable and diverse expedient means, excellence in eloquently expounding all treatises, proficiency in the various arts and crafts of the world, the ability to transcend birth and death and attain non-retrogression, and the certain and rapid attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“From here on, Yaśogupta continued the translation to supplement it: ‘I now wish to further explain the method for bathing with incantations and medicinal herbs. If there are bhikṣus who uphold this sūtra, or any sentient beings who deeply delight in hearing this scripture—for the sake of such persons as these, it can eliminate all calamities and anomalies caused by malevolent stars; it eliminates pestilence and disease, as well as the suffering of birth and death; it eliminates harsh speech, strife, and legal disputes with government officials; it eliminates evil dreams while sleeping at night, obstacles and hindrances caused by malevolent spirits, and curses cast by sorcery or bewitchment; all such evil obstructions shall be completely extinguished.’”
If there are any sentient beings who hear and receive this sutra and its Dharma, they should recite and uphold this mantra, and use it to consecrate medicinal decoctions for bathing their bodies.
For this reason, I shall now explain the method for preparing these medicinal mantras:

Gather equal portions of the following medicinal herbs: fine *changpu* (Acorus calamus), realgar, *mushuxiang* (Trigonella corniculata), *shilishe* (*Erythrina variegata*), *gan.songxiang* (Pinus massoniana resin), *shami* (*Zizyphus jujuba*), *caohuoxiang* (Cymbopogon citratus), *songgaocao* (Cnidium officinale), *shenxiang* (Aquilaria agallocha), cinnamon bark, clove, *fengxiang* (Cinnamomum tamala), *baijiaoxiang* (Balsamodendron mukul), *anxixiang* (Boswellia serrata), *aluosu* (*Pterocarpus marsupium*) decoction, *linglingxiang* (Nardostachys jatamansi), *ainaxiang* (Aquilaria malaccensis), *zhantanxiang* (Santalum album), stone realgar, *qingmuxiang* (Tabernaemontana coronaria), saffron, *fuzi* (Aconitum carmichaelii), mustard seeds, *suoshi* (*Cyperus rotundus*), honeyed saffron root, *naluotuo* (*Cassia fistula*), and *caolonghua* (*Mesua ferrea*). Once these have been collected, blend them together on a day when the moon is in the lunar mansion of *Gui* (Mṛgaśiras) and grind them into a paste. Having finished grinding, recite this mantra over it one hundred and eight times, and the mantra is as follows:

*Tadyathā sudhi kṛti kāmadāśa-aru-kare ciha-aru-kare ci indra-jale śakradale vaśati le abaddha kasgai-na ku-du-ku kapila-kapila-mate śīla-mate santī-totu-mabati śiri śiri satye yasatye svāhā.* Smear the ground with cow dung to a length and breadth of seven cubits to form a *maṇḍala*. Scatter flowers within the *maṇḍala* so that they completely cover the ground, and hang silk banners and canopies.
Place bowls made of gold and silver filled with stone-honey syrup, grape syrup, honey syrup, and milk outside the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
At each of the four corners, station one person wearing a helmet and armor, holding weapons, standing in concealment.

Furthermore, four young girls, each dressed in clean garments and holding flower-filled vases, should also stand at the four corners of the maṇḍala, burning resin incense as an offering that must not be interrupted.

Furthermore, one should prepare divine banners of five colors, place jeweled poles at the four corners, and provide musical performances with the five kinds of sounds. Fill new, clean vessels with fragrant water and place them within the ritual site; having first performed the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), one should then perform the ritual ablution.
He spoke this boundary-binding mantra, saying:
“Tadyathā | Arajī | Nayāye | Hili śili | Ki ki li | Svāhā. He recited this mantra over water twenty-one times and scattered it in the four directions.

Furthermore, it is taught that there are mantras for the medicinal bath and mantras for the body. First, one should recite the mantra over the body one hundred and eight times, and then recite the mantra over the medicinal water one hundred and eight times; with this water, one should bathe the body.
"Tadyathā | sagacche | vigacche | vigatavati svāhā. Having finished bathing after reciting the mantra, the practitioner shall make a great vow for that person:

"May the deities and stars of the four directions protect their life and body; may they always be at peace and auspicious, free from all obstacles and difficulties; may they have no fear of malignant stars, calamities, or portents; may the four elements be secure and healthy, free from all illness; and may every fear be entirely dispelled and healed."
He further spoke the incantations for the body and the incantations for the aspiration:

“Sami visami svāhā | sagati vigati svāhā | sagara sambudhye svāhā | gandhamadane svāhā | nīlagandhāye svāhā | aparājite vīryaye svāhā | himavatsambudhye svāhā | animiṣabhogadhārāye svāhā | Namo bhagavate varuṇadevanamaskṛtāya mahatvayi sthitodumbarapāṇḍarāṅgama-anuvrajatu svāhā. Thereupon, the Great Eloquence Goddess addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold, recite, copy, circulate, and practice according to the Dharma—whether in cities, villages, wilderness areas, open grounds, stūpas, temples, monastic quarters, or the dwellings of laypeople—I, together with my retinue, shall come to their place of practice accompanied by celestial music. I shall eliminate all illnesses, all calamities caused by malevolent stars, and all portents; I shall eliminate all suffering of pestilence and birth-and-death; I shall eliminate all evil speech, strife, and litigation with government officials; I shall eliminate all bad dreams during sleep at night; I shall eliminate all obstacles and hindrances caused by malevolent spirits; I shall eliminate all curses, sorcery, and incantations; and I shall eliminate all evil obstructions.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, they will swiftly transcend all afflictions, enter the stage of non-retrogression, and proceed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; by means of these merits, they shall quickly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the goddess Mahāprajñā, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
goddess Mahāprajñā!"

It is able to contemplate virtuous deeds for the sake of all sentient beings and to bestow fearlessness upon them; it explains the efficacy of this mantra-medicine for all beings, thereby benefiting all sentient beings.
Thereupon, the goddess Mahāprajñā prostrated herself before the Buddha three times and returned to her original seat.
At that time, the brahmin Kauṇḍinya, by means of his power of incantations, addressed the goddess Mahāprajñā:
"One should likewise pay homage to the goddess Mahāprajñā."
His name reaches all throughout the world, and he dwells eternally within the mountains;
gods, nāgas, and spirits—all pay him reverence. He constantly wears garments of grass and stands upon one foot;
all the devas come to his presence, desiring to invite the celestial deity.
May I bestow upon all sentient beings wisdom, eloquence in speech,
and the ability to speak with virtuous words. Tadyathā...

Lokāśiṣṭe lokapriye kṣitavara-te vimamukhe.
Śūli carā parādite aparādite gadāpudī namuci namuci mahatī pāradī kāri kṣaṇa.
Namaḥ sākāṃmamamabudhe aparājiteha tathāgata dhvaja-satvara śalukīcanda.
Rāvaṭaka Kāpiyāḍi Sutratiṭṭha Mahāparopavihili Mili.
Heḷi mili vicara duma-ma-budi-iva-namaśca bhagavate.
Viyatī sarasavati karaci jiu lihe li mi li he li mi li apāhme mi mahati.

Vibhūtasaññāṇa, Dhammasaññāṇa, Saṅghasaññāṇa, Indrasaññāṇa, Varuṇasaññāṇa, Yeluki-saññāṇa, Vatīna-ñisaphasaññāṇa, Saññāṇavajjīṇa. Svāhā! Meme mahatī-viṣṭā-tathā. Hiri miri hiri hiri vi-cara du-bhate. Mama namo bhagavate mahatī-viśrā-svāhā. Kṣitindra-maṇḍala-pate svāhā. At that time, the Brahmin Kauṇḍinya praised the Great Eloquence Goddess with these verses:
"All you spirits and deities, Now listen with a sincere heart:”
I now wish to praise the Great Sage, the Goddess of Eloquence.
Among all women, the Goddess of Eloquence is the most honored;
among the devas, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, and so forth—
Among all the noble ones in the world, he is the most honored of all.
Adorned with manifold merits, his body is graced with the marks of wisdom and virtue;
his eyes are like the *utpala* lotus.
Just as the seven-jeweled gem is extremely rare to behold in this world, I now wish to praise the most profound and supreme speech.
It bestows certainty upon all beings; it is the most excellent, the highest, and unsurpassed.
With marks and signs so dignified and majestic, they nourish all sentient beings; their physical form is pure like a lotus flower.
Their eyes are long and elegant, surpassing all others; their body is upright and handsome, never tiring to behold.
Adorned with various marks and signs of excellence, their radiance is pure like the light of the moon.
Wisdom pervades all things; with powerful memory and non-forgetfulness, he is able to maintain total retention (dhāraṇī).
Riding upon a lion while manifesting in human form, his body possesses eight arms that adorn his person.
To all sentient beings who behold him, he is like the full moon; his speech is eloquent and clear, and his voice is subtle and wondrous.
His wisdom is profoundly deep and inconceivable, and by means of this wisdom, he is ever-perfect.
Able to grant all the aspirations of sentient beings, he is the most honored among all multitudes;
Śakra, the asuras, and the various devas, gandharvas, yakṣas,
and the entire great assembly constantly offer praise.
"May we, [Name] and others, reverently make offerings with a pure and earnest mind.
By virtue of this aspiration, may all be auspicious, and may there be constant protection in places of fear.
"By reciting these seven-syllable verses with purity, I shall cause all such persons to fulfill their vows;
whatever they require, I will provide so that they lack for nothing.
Having spoken these verses, he caused the entire assembly to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Śrīdevī (6) The Sutra of Golden Light, Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Śrīdevī Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty At that time, Śrīdevī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I shall provide this Dharma-preacher with whatever he requires—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other assets—so that he lacks for nothing, his mind remains settled, and he may dwell in joy day and night, contemplating the chapters and verses of this sutra with right mindfulness and discerning its profound meaning.

If there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, this Dharma-preacher, for their sake, shall widely proclaim and disseminate this sublime sūtra throughout Jambudvīpa so that it may not be interrupted.

After these sentient beings have heard this sutra, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas in future ages, they shall constantly experience happiness among devas and humans, encounter various Buddhas, swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and completely exhaust the sufferings of the three evil realms without remainder.
“World-Honored One!

I have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of the past Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, World-Honored One named Ratnakusumaguṇasāgaravaiḍūryakanakaparvata-avabhāsa.”

Therefore, wherever I turn my thoughts, wherever I cast my gaze, and wherever I go, may immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings receive all manner of happiness; may they lack nothing in terms of clothing, food and drink, the necessities of life, or gold, silver, the seven treasures, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, jade, and conch shells.

If there is anyone who can recite this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and who three times calls my name while burning incense as an offering; and having made offerings to the Buddhas, further presents me with flowers, incense, and various delicious foods, scattering them in all directions—know that such a person will be able to gather wealth and precious goods.

By these causes and conditions, the essence of the earth increases; the Earth Deities and all the devas are filled with joy. The sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, and fruits of the sown grains flourish and grow lushly, and the Tree Deities rejoice as they produce immeasurable varieties of things.
"At that time, out of my compassionate concern for all sentient beings, I provided them with many necessities of life.
World-Honored One!

To the north of here, King Vaiśravaṇa has a city named Amanḍa. In that city there is a park named Puṇyapuṣpaprabhāsa; within this park is a most excellent garden called Suvarṇadhvaja, exquisitely adorned with the seven treasures. This is my usual place of residence."

If there are those who wish to increase their wealth and treasures, these persons should, within their own dwelling place, sweep and sprinkle it clean, bathe their bodies, put on fresh white garments, and anoint themselves with exquisite incense. For my sake, they should wholeheartedly recite the name of that Buddha, the World-Honored One Ratnakusuma-vaidūrya, three times; they should prostrate, make offerings, burn incense, and scatter flowers. They should also recite the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* three times, make vows with utmost sincerity, and separately offer various fragrant flowers and delicious foods to me, scattering them in all directions.
At that time, these verses should be recited: “Vārīpūrṇa-cāri-samantadharṣaṇi.”
Mahā-vihāra-gati samanta-vināyaka mahā-kāli-pati.
Vasami sarvatathāgata-samanta-bhūri-pūre.
Ayanadhamate mahāvidubhite mahāmaitreyasaṃgīte.
Hite śi-sa-bha-ki hite samanta ā-thā a-nu-sa-raṇi.

[The following eight lines of mantra are newly translated; they were also spoken by Śrīdevī, yet differ from the old version. As it is not known which is correct or incorrect, both are written out here. Namo to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Namo to all Bodhisattvas.
Homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva and the others.
"I shall now proclaim a divine mantra: Tadyathā..."
Pāripūrṇa-cārī samantadharṣaṇi mahāvihāragati.
Samantavidyānagati mahākāśyapa paripūrṇe sarvavidye samantasupariti pūriṇa āyana dharma-dharmamahāgupti.
*Mahāmaitrī-tirava-saṃkṣipte-te-he-te-si-saṃkṣihe-te-samanta-ātā-hanu-parani-svāhā.* This consecration mantra is definitive and auspicious; it is true and not false.

Sentient beings of equal conduct and those with middling roots of goodness should receive, uphold, recite, and master it. For seven days and seven nights, they should observe the eight precepts, purify their minds morning and evening, and make offerings of incense and flowers to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Constantly dedicating [the merit] for themselves and all sentient beings toward the fulfillment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should make this vow:
"May all that I seek be auspicious.

He shall personally clean and sweep his own dwelling, whether it be his private residence or a forest hermitage; he shall smear the ground with fragrant mud, burn exquisite incense, and arrange pure and fine seats, scattering various flowers and perfumes upon the ground to await me.

At that time, in the space of a single thought-moment, I entered his residence and sat upon his seat; from that day and night forth, I ensured that this household—whether in a village, a monastery, or an open space—lacked for nothing: whether money, gold and silver, precious gems, cattle and sheep, or grain and rice—all necessities were fully provided, and everyone experienced complete happiness.

If you can dedicate the most excellent portion of the roots of goodness you have cultivated to me, I shall never distance myself from that person for the rest of my life; wherever they dwell, I will protect and mind them with a sincere heart, and I will cause whatever they seek to be accomplished.
One should with a sincere heart pay homage to these various Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, whose names are:

Ratnottama Tathāgata; Vimala-jvalana-ratna-prabhāsa-rāja-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata; Suvarṇa-jvālā-prabha Tathāgata; Suvarṇa-śata-prabhā-saṃbhāra-garbha Tathāgata; Suvarṇa-parvata-ratna-cchattra Tathāgata; Suvarṇa-kusuma-jvālā-prabha-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata; Maholkā Tathāgata; and Ratna-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata.
One should also reverently pay homage to the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇaprabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Nityapralāpa, and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
One should also pay homage to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya in the east, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu in the south, Amitāyus Buddha in the west, and the Buddha Svaraghoṣa in the north.

Chapter 14: The Chapter on the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā (6). *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang. At that time, the earth goddess Sthāvarā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

World-Honored One! Whether in the present world or in future worlds, wherever this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* may be—whether in cities or villages, in mountains, marshes, or desolate places, or within royal palaces and residences—there it shall be.
Wherever this sutra is circulated, one should arrange lion thrones within that location and have the Dharma-preacher sit upon them to extensively expound and proclaim this sublime sutra.

I shall always serve as a guardian therein, concealing my body beneath the Dharma seat and supporting its feet upon my head; having heard the Dharma, I shall partake of the nectar-like flavor of the unsurpassed Dharma, thereby increasing my vital strength.

This great earth, sixteen hundred and eighty thousand yojanas deep, from the adamantine foundation up to the surface of the sea, has fully attained the growth and perfection of all flavors; its rich soil is more fertile and lush than it is today.

For this reason, within Jambudvīpa, medicinal herbs, trees, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits flourish and grow luxuriantly, fully endowed with beautiful colors, fragrant scents, and excellent flavors.

Once sentient beings have eaten, their lifespan increases; their physical strength, eloquence, and tranquility flourish; their six sense faculties become fully developed and keen; and their majestic virtue and countenances become upright, dignified, and extraordinary.
Having accomplished these various things, one’s undertakings are largely successful, and one possesses great power, diligence, and valor.
"Therefore, World-Honored One! [he said.]

Within Jambudvīpa, there will be peace, security, abundance, and joy; the population will flourish, and all sentient beings will experience much happiness, their minds satisfied and their wishes fulfilled according to their desires.

Once these sentient beings have attained such majestic power and great strength, they will be able to make offerings to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* and to respectfully honor and provide offerings to the fourfold assembly who uphold the sūtra. At that time, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to experience happiness, I shall go to their place and request the speaker of the Dharma to widely proclaim such a wondrous scripture.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!

When this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is expounded in detail, the majestic virtue obtained by myself and my retinue will be twice as great as usual; our physical strength will increase, and our minds will become courageous and sharp.
“World-Honored One!
Having partaken of the unsurpassed flavor of the nectar of immortality, the land of Jambudvīpa—extending seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth—has become twice as fertile as usual.”
“World-Honored One!
This great earth, upon which sentient beings rely, is able to increase all things necessary for their needs;
having increased all things necessary, it enables all sentient beings to use them as they wish and experience happiness.”

Various kinds of food and drink, clothing, bedding, palaces, houses, trees, groves, rivers, ponds, springs, and wells—all such things as these are fully provided, depending upon and supported by the earth.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
These sentient beings, in order to repay my kindness, should form this thought:
"I shall certainly listen to and receive this sutra, and I shall make offerings to it, honor it, respect it, and praise it."

Having formed this thought, they immediately depart from their dwelling—whether it be a city, a village, a house, or an open space—and proceed to the site of the Dharma assembly to hear and receive this sutra.
Having heard and received [this teaching], they returned to their respective dwellings and, each congratulating the others, spoke these words:

"We have now heard this most profound and unsurpassed sublime Dharma; we have already grasped an inconceivable accumulation of merit, encountered immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, attained liberation from the retribution of the three evil realms, and shall henceforth be constantly born among devas and humans to experience happiness."

"World-Honored One! If these sentient beings, each in their own dwelling place, were to expound this sutra for others—whether by explaining a single parable, a single chapter, or a single causal narrative; or by praising a single Buddha, a bodhisattva, or even a single four-line verse, down to a single phrase, or by uttering the title of this sutra—"
Wherever these sentient beings dwell, that land shall be fully endowed with excellence; its soil shall be rich and fertile, surpassing all other lands.
Whatever things grow from the ground shall all attain increase, flourishing and expanding extensively.
It shall cause all sentient beings to experience happiness, abound in wealth and treasures, delight in practicing generosity, and always maintain a firm mind of deep faith in the Triple Gem.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Earth Deity Drdha:
"If there are sentient beings who hear even a single phrase of the meaning of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, when their lives end among humans, they will be reborn at will in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
"Earth Deity!

If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of making offerings to this sutra, adorn their dwellings—even by hanging up a single banner, a single parasol, or a single robe—they shall, upon the end of their lives, be reborn in those naturally occurring palaces of the seven treasures belonging to the six heavens of the desire realm."
"O Earth Deity!

Within each of those palaces made of the seven precious gems, there are naturally seven celestial maidens who enjoy one another’s company, constantly experiencing inconceivable and subtle bliss day and night."
At that time, the Earth Deity addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By these causes and conditions, whenever a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma sits upon the Dharma-seat, I shall constantly guard and protect him day and night without departing, concealing my form beneath the Dharma-seat and placing his feet upon my head.”
"Bhagavān!

If there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, this Dharma-preacher, for their sake, shall widely proclaim and disseminate this sublime sūtra throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted."

After these sentient beings have heard this sutra, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas in future ages, they will constantly experience happiness among devas and humans; they will encounter various Buddhas, swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and completely sever the sufferings of the three evil realms without remainder.

Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on the Spirit-General Vaiśravaṇa (6). *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on the Spirit-General Vaiśravaṇa. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty. At that time, the Great General Vaiśravaṇa, Lord of the Spirits, together with the spirits of the twenty-eight divisions, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees upon the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [...]”

This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra—whether in the present age or in future ages, wherever it may be found—be it in cities or villages, mountain retreats or wildernesses, or within royal palaces and residences—in whatever place this sūtra is circulated, I shall go to that location together with these twenty-eight classes of great spirits and ghosts. Concealing our forms, we will follow and protect the preacher of this Dharma, extinguishing all evils and ensuring their peace and security.

As for the assembly listening to the Dharma—whether men, women, boys, or girls—who hear even the name of a single Tathāgata, the name of a single Bodhisattva, or the title of this sūtra within this scripture, and who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, I shall attend upon them, guard them, and protect them, completely extinguishing their evils and causing them to attain peace and security;
and it shall be likewise for kingdoms, towns, cities, royal palaces, houses, and empty dwellings.
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition am I named the Great General of the Kumbhāṇḍa Spirits, Saṃjñeya?
Indeed, World-Honored One!”
I shall personally realize this for myself.
World-Honored One!

I know all dharmas, I know all conditioned dharmas, and I have fully understood all dharmas. I know the specific distinctions of dharmas and abide in accordance with the nature of all dharmas as they truly are; within all dharmas, I encompass all dharmas.
World-Honored One!

I now directly perceive the inconceivable light of wisdom, the inconceivable torch of wisdom, the inconceivable practice of wisdom, the inconceivable accumulation of wisdom, and the inconceivable realm of wisdom.
"Bhagavān!
Regarding all phenomena, I have right understanding, right contemplation, attained right discernment, correctly understood conditions, and am rightly able to awaken to them.
Bhagavān!"
For this reason, he is named the Great General Vaiśravaṇa.
“World-Honored One!

I, the Great General Vaiśravaṇa, shall cause the speaker of the Dharma to have adorned speech and uninterrupted eloquence; the vital essence of all flavors shall enter through his pores, filling and strengthening his physical power; his mind shall become courageous and sharp, achieving inconceivable wisdom and entering into right mindfulness. May such matters as these be fully perfected for him, so that his mind knows no weariness or fatigue, his body experiences various joys, and his heart attains great gladness.”
For this reason, one is able to extensively expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.

If there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the person who preaches the Dharma shall, for the sake of these beings, widely proclaim and disseminate this wondrous sutra within Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted.

When immeasurable sentient beings have heard this sutra, they shall attain an inconceivable accumulation of wisdom and gather an inconceivable accumulation of merit. In future ages, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas among humans and devas, they shall constantly experience happiness; in future ages, they shall encounter various Buddhas, swiftly realize and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and all sufferings and the realms of the three evil destinies shall be forever extinguished without remainder.

“Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnakusumaguṇasāgaravaiḍūryakanakaparvatejaprabhāsa; homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, whose body is adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of ornaments, who brilliantly upholds such a subtle and wondrous Dharma-torch;
homage to Mahādevī Guṇavatī, who possesses supreme majesty and accomplishes all matters; homage to Mahāprajñādevī, who has achieved immeasurable wisdom and merit.”

Chapter 16: On Right Discourse (6). *The Golden Light Sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen: On Right Discourse. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Earth Deity Dṛḍhā:
"In the past, there was a king named Baladharavimala."
That king had a son named Śraddhālakṣaṇa, who was soon to receive the consecration and rule over the kingdom.
At that time, the father-king addressed his crown prince Śraddhālakṣaṇa:
"In this world there is a True Treatise for the skillful governance of a kingdom."
In the past, I was once a crown prince; before long, I too was to succeed to the throne of my father, the king. At that time, my father the king also taught me this Right Discourse.

By means of this doctrine, I have well governed the kingdom for twenty thousand years; never for a single thought-moment have I acted contrary to the Dharma, nor have I harbored any attachment toward my own kinsmen.
“What is called the Right Discourse for Governing the World?
O Earth Deity!
At that time, King Baladhararāja spoke these verses to Prince Śraddhālakṣaṇa:”
"I shall now proclaim the true discourse for all kings, for the benefit of sentient beings and to sever all doubts.
May all sovereigns of men and all celestial kings of the gods rejoice and listen attentively with palms joined."
The various kings, having gathered together on Vajra Mountain, along with the four world-protectors, rose and questioned the Brahmā King:
"O Great Teacher, Honored Brahmā!..."
Sovereign among the gods, you are able to eliminate doubt; please sever it for me:
how is it that such a person is called a "god"?
How is it that a king of men is further called a son of heaven?
Born among humans and dwelling in a royal palace, he rules the world with the True Dharma; for this reason, he is named a "heavenly being."
After the Four World-Protecting Kings had asked about this matter,
the Honored Teacher Brahmā then spoke these verses:
"I must, for the sake of all sentient beings, proclaim and expound upon it."
First, regarding the most excellent discourse:
because he accumulated karma through causes, he was born among human beings; as a king who rules over a realm, he is therefore called a "King of Men."
While dwelling within the womb, he is protected by the devas;
or perhaps they protect him first, and only then does he enter the womb.
Although he is among humans, he is born as a king of men; because he is guarded by the devas, [he is thus distinguished].
Furthermore, they are called "Heavenly Son" (devaputra);
for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven each bestow a portion of their own merit upon this person, and thus he is called "Heavenly Son."
Empowered by supernormal powers, they attain mastery; they remain far removed from unwholesome dharmas, preventing them from arising.
They abide securely in wholesome dharmas, cultivating them until they flourish and expand, thereby enabling sentient beings to be reborn in the heavens in great numbers.
Half are called kings of men, and also called musicians; they are rākṣasa executioners who can ward off all evils.
They are also called parents, who instruct and teach the cultivation of goodness and manifest the retribution of karmic results.
Protected by the various devas, they experience the fruits of good and evil deeds in both the present and the future.

Protected by the various devas, they do not punish their offenses nor correct them with the True Teaching; having abandoned and distanced themselves from wholesome dharmas, they increase the accumulation of evil.
Consequently, within the kingdom, there will be much treachery and strife.
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three each gave rise to resentment.
Because their king indulged evil without restraint, corrupt laws ruined the kingdom and deceit flourished;
consequently, enemies from other regions vied with one another to invade and plunder.
One's own wealth, money, and precious treasures may be plundered together by various evil thieves;
yet when the world is ruled according to the Dharma, such things do not occur.
If such things do occur, that nation will perish.
Violent winds suddenly arise, and evil rains fall repeatedly;
malevolent stars appear frequently, and the sun and moon lose their luster; the five grains and all fruits fail to flourish.
Because the king has abandoned his governance, the land suffers from famine; thus, the devas in their palaces all harbor grief and distress.
Because the king is afflicted by violent fever and fails to cultivate wholesome deeds, the celestial kings at that time say to one another:
"This king has practiced evil and associated with the wicked; because he has committed such evil, he quickly incurs the wrath of the devas.
Because of the devas' wrath, before long his kingdom will fall.
Unrighteous weapons, deceitful strife and litigation, pestilence, and malignant diseases will gather within his land."
The devas will immediately abandon this king, causing his kingdom to fall into ruin and giving rise to great sorrow and affliction;
his brothers, sisters, kinsmen, wives, and children will be scattered and driven into exile, and his own life shall likewise perish.
Meteors fall in great numbers and two suns appear simultaneously;
evil bandits from other regions invade and plunder the land;
the people suffer from famine and many diseases and epidemics break out.
The esteemed ministers abandon him and pass away;
elephants, horses, and chariots perish in a single thought;
the wealth and property of all households and everything within the realm are plundered by one another.
They die by the sword;
the five planets and various lunar mansions deviate from their regular courses;
all manner of evil pestilences spread throughout the land.
Those who receive favors and emoluments—the ministers appointed to office and the various officials—exclusively practice what is contrary to the Dharma.
While they thus commit evil deeds, they alone receive imperial favor;
those who cultivate wholesome dharmas decline day by day.
One shows reverence toward those who commit evil,
yet feels no regard for those who cultivate goodness.
When these three anomalies arise together, the stars lose their courses and violent winds and rains descend.
They destroy the nectar of immortality, the unsurpassed True Dharma,
and the very essence of the earth. By honoring the wicked and reviling the virtuous,
hail falls from heaven, and there is famine and death by pestilence.
The flavor of grains, rice, and fruits will diminish; beings afflicted by many diseases will fill the land.
Sweet and abundant fruits will decrease day by day, while bitter, astringent, and foul flavors will increase with the passing seasons.
The gardens where we used to play, those places so full of charm, have all withered away; there is nothing left to delight us.
The exquisite and superior flavors that sentient beings consume are gradually diminishing, until the food lacks any nutritional essence.
His countenance was ugly and his physical strength had declined;
whatever he consumed, he knew no satiety.
His vigor, diligence, and courage were all extinguished and gone.
Laziness and indolence fill the land;
many sufferings and ailments press upon their bodies. Malevolent stars shift and change, and rākṣasas roam in disorder.
If there is a king who acts contrary to the Dharma, increases his evil associates,
and harms the paths of humans and devas, he will undergo much suffering within the three realms of existence.
Such immeasurable evil deeds as these arise entirely because the king,
out of attachment to his retinue, permits them to commit wickedness and neglects to discipline them.
If one is born as a result of being protected by the various devas,
such a king of men would never act in this way;
those who practice goodness attain birth among the heavens.
Those who practice unwholesome deeds fall into the three miserable realms.
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three all experience burning heat because the king indulges in evil and neglects to rectify it.
Those who defy the various devas and the commands of their parents, and who fail to govern with rectitude, are not filial sons.
Those who incite all manner of villainy and evil, and who destroy the land, should not be left unchecked; they must be punished with justice.
Protecting this king, by extinguishing unwholesome dharmas and cultivating roots of goodness,
he shall govern righteously in the present life and increase his royal station.
One should explain for each person the deeds that are wholesome and unwholesome, being able to demonstrate cause and effect; thus one attains the status of a king.
Protected by the devas and assisted by neighboring kings, one governs the state with righteous conduct for the sake of both oneself and others.
If there is one who would destroy the kingdom, he should be properly instructed: "For the sake of your life and the kingdom, practice the True Dharma.
You should not commit evil, nor should you permit evil; regarding all other matters, you must not bring ruin to the kingdom."
When many forms of deceit arise, only then does ruin and collapse follow; if much deceit is provoked, the land will be destroyed.
It is like a great elephant that destroys a lotus pond.
The various devas harbor resentment; therefore, they cause affliction to arise among humans.
They incite all manner of evil deeds, which fill the land.
For this reason, one should follow the True Dharma to punish the wicked and transform the state with goodness, rather than complying with what is contrary to the Dharma.
One would rather sacrifice body and life than cherish one's kin; toward both relatives and non-relatives, the mind is always equal;
regarding relatives and non-relatives alike, one views them as a single harmonious whole.
His righteous reputation spreads throughout the three realms; he governs the country by the True Dharma, and many people practice goodness.
With constant virtuous hearts, they look up to the king; he is able to cause the hosts of devas to be fully satisfied.
Therefore, one who governs with righteousness is called a King of Men.
All the devas love and protect the king of men, just as parents cherish and guard their own child.
Therefore, they cause the sun, the moon, the five planets, and all the lunar mansions to follow their respective orbits, never failing in their regular courses.
Free from all calamities and misfortunes, may the land be abundant and prosperous;
may there be peace, happiness, and flourishing growth, increasing the welfare of the people and the hosts of devas.
For this reason, O kings and others, you should rather sacrifice your own bodies and lives than commit evil;
you must never abandon the precious treasure of the True Dharma.
Through the jewel of the True Dharma, people of the world find joy;
one should always draw near to those who practice the True Dharma, for they accumulate merit and adorn their bodies.
Regarding their own kin and retinue, they always know contentment.
One should keep far from evil people and cultivate the True Dharma.
One should establish sentient beings in all wholesome dharmas, instructing and protecting them so that they may leave unwholesomeness behind.
Therefore, the land shall be peaceful, secure, and prosperous;
this king, too, shall attain the fullness of majestic virtue.
According to the evil ways practiced by the people, he should subdue them and instruct them in accordance with the Dharma.
"This king shall obtain a fine name and good reputation; he will be well able to protect and sustain, bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
