Chapter Seventeen: On Skillful Accumulation (VII) In this, the seventeenth chapter, "On Skillful Accumulation," the Tathāgata further spoke to the earth goddess regarding past causes and conditions, uttering these verses:
"In the past, I was once a Wheel-Turning Sage King; I relinquished the four great continents, as well as the great oceans."
Furthermore, at that time, he filled the four continents with precious jewels and offered them to all the Buddhas.
In all his acts of giving, he relinquished whatever was most cherished; there was nothing he found desirable that he did not give away.
In past ages, throughout incalculable kalpas, for the sake of seeking the True Dharma,
he constantly sacrificed his body and life.
Furthermore, in a past age, an inconceivable kalpa ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Ratnashrī.
After his parinirvāṇa, there was a holy king named Saṃcaya,
who attained sovereign power over the four continents; his righteous governance extended as far as the limits of the great ocean.
That king had a city named Water-Sound Honored; within that city, he resided and governed.
Having heard of the Buddha’s merits and having seen a bhikṣu named Ratnāloka, who was well able to proclaim and expound the Tathāgata’s true Dharma—namely, the Golden Light—
This subtle and wondrous sutra is as bright as the midday sun, capable of illuminating everything everywhere.
Having dreamed of this matter, the Wheel-Turning King immediately awoke;
joy filled his heart and pervaded his entire body.
He immediately departed from the palace and went to the monastery, where he made offerings and paid homage to the assembly of great sages.
He asked the venerable ones:
"Within this great assembly, is there perhaps a bhikṣu named Ratnāloka?"
Having accomplished all virtues,
he sat peacefully and immovably within a single cave, contemplating with right mindfulness and reciting this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took the king to his dwelling and arrived at the place where Ratnākara resided.
At that moment, Ratnākara was still within the cave; his appearance was extraordinary, and his majestic virtue blazed forth.
He then pointed to the king, saying:
"The one within this cave is the very person you asked about—the Bhikṣu Ratnākara.
He is able to uphold the profound practice of all Buddhas, known as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras."
At that time, King Sañcaya immediately paid homage and said to the bhikṣu Ratnāloka:
"Your face is like the full moon; your majestic virtue shines brightly."
"I only pray that you will, for my sake, expound and proclaim this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*,
the king of all sutras.
Then the Honored One Ratnāloka immediately accepted the King's request and granted his permission to proclaim this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
The devas throughout the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, knowing that he was about to preach the Dharma, all gave rise to joy.
In a pure, subtle, and pristine place, the ground was inlaid with various kinds of precious jewels.
With exquisite, sublime perfumed water, he sprinkles it;
he scatters various beautiful flowers until they fill the entire place.
He personally prepares the Dharma seat, hanging silk streamers, banners, and canopies, and adorning it with precious ornaments and interlaced decorations.
Various kinds of subtle and exquisite, extraordinary incense powders were all offered and scattered.
Upon the high seat of the Great Dharma, all the devas, nāgas, spirits,
mahoragas, kinnaras, and others immediately rained down from the heavens.
Mandārava flowers were scattered everywhere upon the Dharma-seat, filling the entire place.
Inconceivable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of immeasurable devas all came at once, gathering at the site where the Dharma was being preached.
At that time, Ratnākara emerged from his cave;
immediately, the devas offered salākā flowers, scattering them as an offering to the bhikṣu Ratnākara.
At that time, Ratnāloka, having washed his body clean and donned pure, exquisite robes, went to the place of the Dharma seat;
there, with palms joined in reverence, he paid homage to this high seat of the Dharma.
All the celestial kings and the various devas rained down *māndārava* and great *māndārava* flowers.
Countless hundreds of thousands of various kinds of musical instruments resounded spontaneously in the void without being struck.
The bhikṣu Ratnāloka, a master of preaching the Dharma, immediately ascended the high seat and sat cross-legged.
He then brought to mind the inconceivable and immeasurable thousands of billions of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions.
And for King Susaṃmata, over the entire extent of his royal domain—
wherever the sun and moon shine—
the Dharma-preacher immediately proceeded to expound and proclaim this sublime sūtra for the king.
"At that time, the great king, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, stood before the bhikṣu with palms joined.
His heart was filled with sorrowful lamentation as tears flowed freely; yet immediately thereafter, he was filled with leaping joy."
With a joyful and serene mind,
he then grasped a wish-fulfilling jewel and made a great vow for the sake of all sentient beings:
A rain of immeasurable, various, and wondrous treasures, of exquisite seven-jeweled ornaments,
and of sublime necklaces fell everywhere.
By these causes and conditions, all immeasurable sentient beings were made to experience every form of happiness.
Then it rained down the seven treasures, as well as various jeweled ornaments, celestial crowns, ear-rings,
and all kinds of necklaces; sweet delicacies and precious thrones were all provided in abundance,
filling the entirety of the four continents.
Filling the four continents with immeasurable seven treasures,
one offers them as alms within the bequeathed Dharma of the Buddha Ratnottama, making offerings to the Triple Gem.
The bhikṣu who, at that time, preached the Dharma for the king,
is now the present Buddha Akṣobhya;
the King Susaṃcaya, who at that time listened to and received the Dharma, is now my very self, Śākyamuni.
Having relinquished this great earth, filling the four continents with precious jewels as an offering,
one may obtain the hearing of such a sutra as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Once he uttered "Excellent! and by virtue of these roots of goodness and the causal conditions of that karma, his body attained a golden hue, adorned with a hundred blessings.
To hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of beings of various kinds, he is a joy to behold;
once they have seen him, they never tire of looking upon him.
In the past, throughout ninety-nine billion and ten million kalpas, he constantly became a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
furthermore, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he constantly reigned as a sovereign over various minor kings.
Inconceivable, throughout kalpas he constantly acted as Śakra Devānām Indra and as the Pure Brahmā King;
furthermore, he encountered the World-Honored Ones of Ten Powers in numbers so immeasurable that they cannot be calculated.
The merit thus obtained is immeasurable and boundless; it all arises from hearing this sutra and exclaiming "Excellent!
Just as I have vowed, I have now attained the realization of Bodhi and the body of the True Dharma.

Chapter 18: On Ghosts and Spirits (7) The Golden Light Sūtra, Chapter Eighteen: On Ghosts and Spirits. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty. The Buddha addressed Bhadraśrī:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to make inconceivable and wondrous offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present; and if they wish to know the profound sphere of practice of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, these persons should, with resolute and utmost sincerity, wherever this sūtra is circulated—whether in cities, towns, villages, houses, or open spaces—listen to this subtle and wonderful scripture with right mindfulness and undistracted hearts."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one wishes to make offerings to all Buddhas, and wishes to know the sphere of activity of the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
one should go to those cities and villages."
Wherever this sutra exists, listen to and receive it with a sincere mind. This wondrous scripture is inconceivable;
it is an ocean of merit, immeasurable and boundless, capable of bringing all sentient beings to liberation and delivering them from immeasurable suffering.
All the great oceans of existence are surpassed by this sutra, which is profoundly deep;
being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, it cannot be described through words, nor can it be compared by means of metaphors.
The dust motes of the great earth, the waters of the great oceans, and all the mountains—
such things as these cannot serve as metaphors [for it].
If one enters this sutra, one enters the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); as in the profound nature of phenomena, one dwells securely therein.
Within this very scripture, within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, one shall behold me, Śākyamuni.
For inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they will be born among gods and humans, constantly experiencing happiness.
Because they have heard this sutra, they have already attained such immeasurable, inconceivable, and vast accumulations of merit and virtue.
Wherever one goes, even if for a hundred yojanas, one should pass through it even if it is filled with blazing fires.
Whether arriving at a village, a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), or a place where a Dharma assembly is held, one should listen and receive [the teaching] with a sincere heart;
because of listening to this sutra, evil dreams and malevolent sorcery—
The five planets and all the lunar mansions, their transformations, anomalies, calamities, misfortunes, and all evil matters,
shall be extinguished without remainder.
For those who speak this sutra, transcribe it, read it, or recite it— this speaker of the Dharma, [shall be protected].
When he descended from his seat, at that time the great assembly still saw the place where he had sat;
thus there were those who spoke of the physical forms of the Bodhisattvas, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and Mañjuśrī.
The Great Being Maitreya, as well as all other forms and colors—
having seen such various things as these— they immediately vanish and cease, no different from before.
Having accomplished such meritorious virtues, they are praised by all Buddhas;
their majestic power and physical marks are immeasurable and boundless.
Possessing great renown, he is able to repel enemies;
he can cause thieves and bandits from other regions to retreat and disperse;
courageous and possessing great strength, he is able to defeat powerful adversaries.
Evil dreams that afflict the mind and immeasurable evil karmas—
all such misfortunes shall be entirely stilled;
should one enter into battle, one will always be victorious over others.
His fame shall spread far and wide throughout Jambudvīpa;
he shall also be able to subdue all enemies,
remain far removed from all evils, cultivate and accumulate all virtues, achieve victory when entering battle, and his mind shall always be filled with joy.
The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, the Four World-Protecting Kings, Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada,
the kings of ghosts and spirits, the Great General Saṃjñeya,
the heroic ghosts of dhyāna, as well as the kiṃnaras, the dragon of Anavatapta, and King Sāgara.
The Asura King, the Garuḍa King, the Great Eloquence Deva, and the One of Great Merit—
these and other such chief deities shall always make offerings to those who listen to the Dharma, giving rise to inconceivable [virtues].
The perception of it as a Dharma-stūpa;
those sentient beings who see it will revere it with joy.
The various heavenly kings and others likewise each reflect upon it and say to one another:
"These sentient beings now possess immeasurable majesty and virtue; they have all achieved perfection.
If they can come to this place of the Dharma assembly, such persons shall fulfill the highest roots of goodness."
Therefore, he solemnly set out for the place of the Dharma assembly;
with a mind of inconceivable, right faith, he made offerings and paid homage to the unsurpassed Dharma-stūpa.
Such great compassion, which benefits sentient beings, is itself an immeasurable vessel for the profound treasure of the Dharma.
One is able to enter the most profound, unsurpassed nature of phenomena by listening to this sutra with a pure mind.
Such a person has made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas of the past.
By virtue of these roots of goodness and through immeasurable causes and conditions, they should listen to and receive this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Such sentient beings are always protected by immeasurable devas and heavenly kings;
the Four World-Protecting Kings, immeasurable spirits, and the various Māhasattvas diligently and tirelessly guard the four directions day and night.
As well as the gods of the sun and moon, King Yama, the various deities of wind and water,
the god Viṣṇu, the god Mahābhadra, the god Maheśvara, the god Agni, and other deities of great power and valor.
They constantly protect the world, never departing by day or night;
Nārāyaṇa and others, Maheśvara, and the twenty-eight classes of spirits and deities,
with Vajrapāṇi at their head— these hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities.
With the great power of the divine feet, they shall protect these [beings], causing them to have no fear;
Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, the Great Ghost King, and his retinue of five hundred followers—
all of whom are indeed great bodhisattvas— [shall likewise protect them].
They shall all provide protection for those who listen to this Dharma:
the great ghost-king Śūrapāla, Pūrṇabhadra, as well as Kiṃpila, Āḷavaka,
Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, and the great deity Pītaśiras.
Each of these deities has five hundred retinues of spirits and ghosts who also constantly provide protection for those who hear this sutra;
as well as the Asura Kings, the Gandharvas, and the Nārāyaṇas.
Kinnaraśva, Maṇicandra, and the Nigaṇṭha;
the Great Deity who Controls Rain, the Great Food-and-Drink Deity,
Mahākāla, the Golden-Haired Deity, the Bhūta Pañcika, and the Piṅgala.
Cāpala; Dharmabala, Makarabala, the Sūcīloma yakṣa, Śūramdhara, Renukeśa, and Mahāpana.
As well as Gundācā, Kambhasati, Śarameṭi, Hemavata, and Satākī— gods such as these,
all possessing immeasurable supernormal powers and great strength.
They shall always diligently protect those who hear and receive such a subtle and wondrous scripture:
the King of Anavatapta, the King Sāgara, the King Makara,
the King Elāpattra, the Naga King Nanda, and the Naga King Upananda.
There are such as these, hundreds of thousands of dragon kings,
who with great supernormal power constantly come to protect those who listen to this sutra, never departing by day or night;
[and] Pāli-rāhu, the asura king Vemacitra, and...
As well as Maucilinda, Śamāliputra, Pāhāliputra, Khara-karṇa, and Gandha—
all these are asura kings who possess great supernormal powers and constantly come to provide protection.
Those who listen to this sutra will not be parted from it day or night;
the Mother of Demons and her five hundred spirits will constantly come to protect those who listen to this sutra, whether they are asleep or awake.
The great female spirits and others— Kūṣmāṇḍī, Rākṣasī, and those who devour the vital essence of humans—
such deities as these all possess great power; they constantly and diligently protect those in the worlds of the ten directions who receive and uphold this sutra.
Mahāprajñāpāramitā-devī and countless other celestial maidens, as well as Śrī-devī and her like, each accompanied by their retinues; the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā,
the deities of planted groves and orchards, and the great spirits of fruits and grains—
may all such deities give rise to joy in their hearts and come to provide protection.

Those who love, delight in, and draw near to this sutra will have their lifespan, physical form, and strength increased for all sentient beings; their merit, majesty, and appearance will be adorned twice as much as usual;
and the portents of change and calamitous anomalies caused by the five planets and various lunar mansions shall all be entirely extinguished.
There shall be nothing left remaining;
as for evil dreams encountered while sleeping at night, upon waking one may be distressed and withered, but such evil matters will all be completely extinguished.
The earth deity possesses great power and profound majesty; by the power of this sutra, it is able to transform its flavor.
Thus, this great earth extends down to the adamantine base, with a thickness of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas.
Within it, there is no flavor that is not present; it causes all to emerge with vigor and brings moisture and benefit to sentient beings.
By the power of this sutra, it can cause the essence of the earth to emerge entirely above the ground to a thickness of one hundred *yojanas*;
it also enables the various devas to obtain great refined flavors, thereby filling and augmenting their physical strength.
They were filled with joy and happiness;
all the deities within Jambudvīpa felt gladness in their hearts and experienced immeasurable bliss.
By the power of this sutra, all the devas rejoice; the hundred grains and fruits all flourish and grow;
the gardens and groves have their flowers in full bloom, their fragrant scents overflowing and pervading everywhere.
The hundred grasses and trees grow upright; their substance is supple and they are free from crookedness.
All the dragon maidens, numbering in immeasurable and inconceivable quantities, give rise to joy and leap for boundless delight.
The lotus pond was adorned; within that pond grew various kinds of flowers:
blue utpala lotuses, red padma lotuses, yellow kumuda lotuses, and white puṇḍarīka lotuses.
Causing the void to be free from dust and obscuration, all directions become clear, pure, and luminous.
The Sun-King blazes fiercely, emitting a thousand rays of light; with joyful exultation, he illuminates all darkness and concealment.
With Jambūnada gold they have fashioned palaces, wherein they dwell, possessing immeasurable majesty and virtue.
Because the Son of Heaven, the Sun, and the Deity of the Moon hear this sutra,
their vital essence becomes fully replenished.
With a heart full of joy, he emitted immeasurable, brilliant nets of light that shone everywhere in all directions.
At the moment of his emergence, he radiated great nets of light, causing the various lotuses in all the ponds to bloom.
Within Jambudvīpa, immeasurable fruits ripen in their proper seasons, satisfying all sentient beings.
At that time, the illumination of the sun and moon is exceptionally sublime;
the constellations move in their correct courses, never failing their appointed measures.
Wind and rain come in their proper seasons; harvests are abundant and flourishing;
there is an abundance of wealth and treasures, with nothing lacking.
Wherever these subtle and wondrous scriptures circulate, and wherever they are expounded and recited—
"The realm of that land shall immediately attain increase and augmentation, possessing the immeasurable merits as described above. **Chapter 19:

Bestowal of Prophecy** *The Sutra of Golden Light*, Chapter Nineteen: Bestowal of Prophecy, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang. At that time, the Tathāgata was about to bestow the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon this Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa and his two sons, Rajalakṣaṇa and Rajaprabha.

At that time, there were ten thousand devaputras, with King Blazing Majesty as their leader, who together came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa:

"In a future age, after immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of incalculable nayutas of kalpas have passed, you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the world-system named Suvarṇāvabhāsa. You shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Suvarṇaratnacchatraśikhara-rāja."

Furthermore, after this Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have completely vanished, the eldest son, Rajata (Silver-Worthy), shall succeed him as the next Buddha in that realm. At that time, the world shall be renamed Viśuddhadhvaja (Pure Banner), and the Buddha shall be named Jambūnadasuvarṇadhvajaprabhāsasamantāvabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Even until after this Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, and when both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have completely vanished, his younger son, Silver Light (Rūpyaprabha), shall succeed him as the next Buddha. The name of the world shall remain the same as before, without change; the Buddha shall be named Golden Radiance Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

When these ten thousand devaputras heard that the three great beings had received their predictions of enlightenment, and further heard this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, they were filled with joy. They gave rise to a mind of profound reverence; their minds were free from defilement and impurity like pure lapis lazuli, and they were clear, pure, and unimpeded like space.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the roots of goodness of these ten thousand devaputras had matured, immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of the path to Bodhi:

"O devaputras, in a future age, after incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas have passed, you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this world. You shall all belong to the same family, the same clan, and the same name, being called the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyak-saṃbuddhas, Vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpannas, Sugatas, Lokavidas, Anuttaras, Puruṣa-damya-sārathis, Śāstṛs of gods and men, Buddhas, and Bhagavats named Nīlanetra-utpala-gandha-kūṭa. In this manner, they shall appear in the world in succession, totaling ten thousand Buddhas."
At that time, the tree deity of the site of enlightenment named Samudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

These ten thousand devaputras have come to this assembly from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for the sake of hearing the Dharma; why has the Tathāgata immediately bestowed upon them the prediction of enlightenment?"
“World-Honored One!

I have never before heard that these sons of the gods practice and fulfill the six *pāramitās*, nor have I ever heard that they give away their hands, feet, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, beloved wives and children, wealth and treasures, grain and silk, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, pearls, coral, conch shells, jade disks, delicious food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine for the sick, elephants, horses, carriages, palaces, houses, gardens, springs and ponds, or male and female servants.”

Just as other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas have reverently made offerings to the past immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddha-Bhagavāns with various requisites for life and sustenance, so too shall this bodhisattva in future ages renounce immeasurable things held dear—head, eyes, marrow, brain, beloved wife and children, wealth, treasures, grain, silk, and even servants—practicing the stages of cultivation in succession to fully accomplish the six pāramitās. Having accomplished these, he will undergo the practice of ascetic deeds for immeasurable and boundless kalpas, and only then shall he receive the prediction of enlightenment (bodhi-vyākaraṇa).
“World-Honored One!

By what cause and by what condition have these sons of heaven cultivated such supreme and wondrous roots of goodness that, having come from that celestial realm, they were able to hear the Dharma for a brief moment and immediately receive their prediction of enlightenment?”
"I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will explain this for me and sever the net of my doubts.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the tree spirit:
“O Good Goddess!
All possess causes and conditions, and possess wondrous roots of goodness that have already been cultivated according to their characteristics. Why is this?

Because these devaputras have renounced the pleasures of the five desires in their respective abodes, they have come to listen to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. Having heard the Dharma, they have cultivated a pure and reverent mind toward this sūtra and practice according to its teachings; furthermore, they have heard these three great bodhisattvas receive their predictions of enlightenment, as well as the causes and conditions of the vows they originally made in the past.
"Therefore, I now bestow upon all of you the prediction that in a future age you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Chapter 20: Eliminating Disease (7) The Sutra of Golden Light, Chapter Twenty: Eliminating Disease, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty. The Buddha addressed the Bodhi-tree goddess of the site of enlightenment:
"O Good Goddess!..."
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and retain this well in your memory; I shall expound for you the causes and conditions of my past vows.

In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Ratnashrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
“Good Goddess!

At that time, after that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma had been extinguished, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a king named Devendraprabha. He practiced the True Dharma and governed the world according to the law; the people were harmonious and submissive, and they filially supported their parents.”

In that king’s realm there was an elder named Jālinīprabha, who was well-versed in medical arts to alleviate the suffering of illness and skillfully understood through expedient means the increase and decrease of the four great elements.
“O Good Goddess!

At that time, a son was born later into the household of the great elder Jālinīprabha, named Jalavāhana. His physical appearance was exceptionally superior, his countenance was foremost in its beauty, his form and color were subtle and wondrous, and he was fully endowed with majestic virtue. He was naturally intelligent and quick-witted, well-versed in all treatises, and there was no skill, art, writing, calculation, or accounting to which he did not attain mastery.”

At that time, a pestilence descended upon the kingdom, and among the countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, there was none who could escape; they were all tormented by various sufferings and afflictions.
“Good Woman Devī!

At that time, the Elder’s son, Flowing Water, seeing these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, gave rise to great compassion for them and reflected thus: ‘These immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings are undergoing various sufferings and afflictions.

Although my father, the Elder, well understands medical prescriptions and is able to save others from suffering, being skillful in means regarding the increase and decrease of the four elements, he is already advanced in years; he is decrepit and withered, his skin is slack and his face is wrinkled, he is emaciated and trembling, and in coming and going he must rely on a staff. Being exhausted and fatigued, he cannot reach those cities and villages, yet these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings have encountered serious illnesses for which there is no one to provide relief.’”

"I shall now go to my father, the Great Physician, to inquire about the secret methods of medical prescriptions for treating diseases. Having received his instruction and gained this knowledge, I shall travel to cities, towns, villages, and hamlets to treat the various grave illnesses of sentient beings, causing them all to be liberated from immeasurable sufferings."

At that time, having reflected thus, the son of the elder went immediately to his father’s place, prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to his father, and standing back with palms joined, he questioned his father regarding the increase and decrease of the four great elements.
Then he spoke in verse:
"How should one know that the four great elements and the various sense faculties undergo decay and transformation,
thereby giving rise to all manner of illnesses?"
How should one know the proper timing for food and drink, so that after eating, the bodily fire does not diminish?
How should one know the treatment for wind, heat, water-disorders, diseases of the lungs, and those of equal proportions?
"When does the wind element become disturbed? When does the heat element become disturbed? When does the water element become disturbed, so as to harm sentient beings?
Then the father, the elder, immediately answered his son with verses, explaining the medical prescriptions:
"Three months are summer, three months are autumn, three months are winter, and three months are spring.
These twelve months are explained in groups of three."
From such reckonings, there are four seasons in a year; if expressed in pairs, they comprise six periods.
When three are subsumed as the fundamental [seasons] and two appear as the manifest [periods], one should adjust one's food and drink according to these seasonal changes;
this is what benefits the body, as taught in the medical treatises.
Throughout the course of the year, the various faculties and the four great elements undergo alternation, increase, and decrease,
causing the body to fall ill. For three months,
one should provide care to harmonize the six elements, adjusting food and drink according to the illness.
As for medicinal decoctions and drugs:
those with wind disorders are aggravated in summer;
those with heat disorders are aggravated in autumn.
For those with diseases of balanced temperament (*sāṃnipātika*), the condition is aggravated in winter.
For those with lung disease (*paittika*), it increases in severity in spring;
for those with wind disease (*vātika*), one should consume fatty, salty, and sour foods during the summer.
And warm food;
for those with feverish illnesses, one should take cold and sweet [medicines] in autumn;
in winter, those with balanced [humors] should take sweet, sour, and fatty [medicines].
In spring, one should consume fatty, pungent, and hot foods for lung ailments.
If one eats to satiety and then [indulges in these], lung disease will manifest;
when the food is being digested, feverish illness will manifest.
After food has been digested, wind disorders arise;
thus these four great elements manifest according to the three periods of time.
When wind disorders cause emaciation and depletion, one should supplement with ghee and fatty substances.
For febrile diseases, one should take *harītakī* as a purgative;
for balanced [humoral] disorders, one should take the three kinds of excellent medicines, namely those that are sweet, pungent, and oily (*sneha*).
For diseases of the lungs, one should take emetic medicines according to the season.
"If one administers [medicine] at an improper time, one should defer to the teacher, who shall deliberate upon and provide food, drink, and medicinal decoctions according to the illness.
"O Goddess of Goodness!"

At that time, the elder’s son, Jalavāhana, questioned his father, the physician, regarding the increase and decrease of the four great elements; by means of this, he mastered all medical prescriptions.

Having mastered the medical arts, the elder’s son traveled throughout the cities, towns, and villages within the kingdom, and wherever there were those suffering from the ailments of sentient beings, he would comfort them with gentle words, saying:
"I am a physician."
"I am a physician well-versed in prescriptions and medicines; I shall now treat and rescue you, ensuring that you are all completely healed. "O Good Goddess!

At that time, when the sentient beings heard the elder’s son speak with gentle words of consolation and promise to cure their illnesses, their hearts were filled with joy, and they leaped for immeasurable delight."

At that time, there were hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings who had contracted extremely grave illnesses; upon hearing these words, because their hearts were filled with joy, their various ailments were immediately cured and restored to their original state, their physical strength becoming fully restored.
“Good Goddess!

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings suffering from illnesses that were deep, heavy, and difficult to cure; they all came together to the place where the son of the elder was. At that time, the son of the elder immediately gave them excellent medicine to take, and once they had taken it, they were cured and restored to health.”
“O Good Goddess!
This son of a merchant, while governing all sentient beings within this kingdom, has caused every illness and suffering to be completely cured.

Chapter 21: The Son of a Merchant, Shrotapāla (7) The Sūtra of the Golden Light, Chapter Twenty-one: The Son of a Merchant, Shrotapāla. Translated by Dharmakṣema during the Northern Liang Dynasty. The Buddha addressed the tree deity:

"At that time, after the Elder’s Son Flowing Water had treated all sentient beings within the realm of King Devendra-prabhāsa from their immeasurable sufferings and ailments, he restored their bodies to their original state, so that they might experience various forms of happiness."
Because his illness had been cured, he performed many meritorious deeds, practiced giving, and showed honor and respect to this son of a householder, saying:
"Excellent, O Householder!"

"You are truly a great king of physicians, capable of greatly increasing the accumulation of merit and extending the immeasurable lifespans of sentient beings. You skillfully treat the immeasurable grave illnesses of sentient beings; you must surely be a bodhisattva well-versed in medical prescriptions and remedies."
"Good Woman Devī!

At that time, the elder’s son had a wife named Water-Empty Dragon-Treasury (Śūnyatā-jala-nāga-kośa), who gave birth to two sons: the first was named Water-Empty (Jala-śūnya), and the second was named Water-Treasury (Jala-kośa)."

At that time, the son of the elder took these two children and traveled in succession through cities and villages until he finally reached a vast, desolate marsh. There were many tigers, wolves, dogs, birds, and beasts, all of whom fed upon flesh and blood; they were all fleeing away in one direction.
At that time, the son of the elder had this thought:
"For what reason and by what cause are these birds and beasts all running away in one direction?
I shall follow after them and observe."
Then the son of the elder followed after him and saw a pond whose water had dried up, yet within that pond there were many fish.
Upon seeing these fish, the son of the elder gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
At that time, a tree spirit manifested half of its body and spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
O great son of good family!"
"These fish are pitiable; you should give them water, and for this reason you shall be named 'Flowing Water' (Śrotasvāhin).
Furthermore, there are two reasons for the name 'Flowing Water':
first, the ability to cause water to flow, and second, the ability to bestow water."
"You should now determine the reality according to the names.
Then the son of the elder asked the tree spirit,
"How many fish heads are there in total?"
The tree deity replied, "Their number is exactly ten thousand, fully complete.
"O Virtuous Goddess! [the Buddha continued.]
At that time, having heard these numbers, the Flowing Water (Jalavāhana) felt his great compassion increase all the more.
"O Good Goddess!

At that time, this empty pond was scorched by the sun until only a small amount of water remained; these ten thousand fish were about to enter the gates of death. They writhed in all four directions, and seeing this elder, they conceived a sense of reliance upon him. Following the direction in which the elder went, they gazed after him, their eyes never once leaving him."

At that time, the elder ran in all four directions, searching everywhere for water but was unable to find any. He then looked around and saw a large tree; he immediately took its branches and leaves and returned to the pond to provide shade and coolness.
Having created the shade, he again sought further:
"From where did this water in the pond originally come?
He then went out in the four directions, searching everywhere, but could not find the source of the water. Running even faster to other distant places, he saw a great river named Jalamudbhava.
At that time, there were yet other wicked men who, in order to capture these fish, dammed up the water at a steep and precipitous point upstream so that it could not flow downstream.
However, the breach is situated on a precipitous and dangerous cliff, making it difficult to repair:
"It is calculated that even with the labor of hundreds or thousands of people over ninety days, it could not be completed—how much less by my single self?"

Then the son of the elder quickly returned to the place where the great king was, prostrated himself with his head at the king’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and with palms joined toward the king, explained the circumstances, saying:

“I have been treating various ailments among the people of Your Majesty’s realm; traveling gradually, I arrived at that desolate marsh and saw a pond whose waters had dried up. Ten thousand fish were being scorched by the sun; today they are in dire distress and will soon die.”
"I only pray that Your Majesty will lend me twenty great elephants so that I may carry water to save the lives of those fish, just as I have preserved the lives of these sick people.
At that time, the Great King immediately commanded his ministers to provide them with the greatest haste.
At that time, the minister, having received the king’s command, spoke to the elder:
"Excellent, Great Being!
You may now go yourself to the elephant stable and select as you please, so as to benefit sentient beings and bring them happiness."

At that time, Flowing Water and his two sons took twenty large elephants and borrowed leather bags from the city builders. They quickly went to the breach in the upper reaches of the river, filled them with water, and had the elephants carry it back at full speed to the pond in the empty marsh. They lowered the bags from the elephants' backs and poured the water into the pond; the water then completely filled it, restoring it to its former state.
At that time, the son of the elder paced back and forth along the four sides of the pond, and the fish likewise followed him, moving along the bank.
Then the son of the elder thought to himself:
"For what reason does this fish follow me?"
"These fish must be tormented by the fire of hunger and wish to seek food and drink from me; I shall now give it to them.
"Good Woman Devī!
At that time, the Elder’s son, Flowing Water, said to his sons:"
"Take one of the elephants of greatest strength and go quickly to your home to inform your father, the elder:
'Gather all the edible things in the house—down to the portions for your parents' consumption and those for your wife, children, and servants—and load them all onto the elephant.'"
"Return with all haste.
At that time, the two sons followed their father's instructions; mounting the largest elephant, they went to the house and informed their grandfather of the aforementioned matters.
At that time, the two sons gathered whatever edible items were in the house, loaded them onto the elephant’s back, and quickly returned to their father’s location at the empty marsh and pond.

When the elder son saw his sons returning, his heart was filled with joy and he leaped for immeasurable delight. Taking the food and drink from his sons, he scattered it into the pond to feed the fish. Having done so, he reflected to himself:
"I have now been able to provide these fish with food until they are full; in future ages, I shall bestow upon them the food of the Dharma."
He further reflected:
"I have heard that in the past, in a secluded place, there was a bhikṣu who recited the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. In those sūtras it is said:
'If there are sentient beings who, at the time of their death, hear the name of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava, they will immediately be reborn in the heavens.'"
"I shall now explain the profound twelve links of dependent origination for these ten thousand fish, and I shall also proclaim the name of the Buddha Ratnashrī.
At that time, there were two kinds of people in Jambudvīpa:
first, those who deeply believed in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; second, those who disparaged them and did not give rise to faith or joy.
Then the son of the elder thought to himself:
"I shall now enter the waters of this pond and preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for these fish.
Having thought this, he immediately entered the water and spoke these words:
“Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, Ratnaśrī of the past.”
When the Tathāgata Ratnavijaya was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he made this vow:
"If there are sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who hear my name at the time of their death, may they, immediately upon passing away, attain rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."

At that time, Flowing Water further expounded this profound and wondrous Dharma for those fish, namely: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and the mass of suffering.
“Good Goddess!
At that time, after the Elder’s son Flowing Water and his two sons had preached this Dharma, they returned home together.
Later, on another occasion, the Elder’s son was reclining, having become intoxicated at a gathering of guests.”
At that time, the earth suddenly shook violently; ten thousand fish died on the same day, and immediately upon their death, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having been born there, they reflected:
"By what causes and conditions of wholesome karma have we been reborn here in this Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?"
They further said to one another:

"Previously, within Jambudvīpa, we fell among the animals and received the bodies of fish. The son of the Elder Śrotodāra gave us water and food, and further expounded for us the profound Twelve Links of Dependent Origination while reciting the name of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava. By these causes and conditions, we have been enabled to be born in this heaven."
"Therefore, we shall now go to the son of the elder to repay his kindness and make offerings.
At that time, ten thousand devaputras descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa and arrived at the house of the great physician, the son of the elder, Śrotas.

At that time, the son of the elder was sleeping while lying on his back upon the open roof of the upper story. These ten thousand devaputras placed ten thousand pearls and celestial, exquisite necklaces at the head of his bed; they further placed ten thousand at his feet, ten thousand at his right side, and ten thousand at his left side. They rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers until they reached his knees, and various celestial musical instruments produced wondrous sounds.
All those in Jambudvīpa who were asleep were awakened, and the elder’s son, Jalavāhana, also awoke from his sleep.
Those ten thousand devaputras soared and traveled through the air above, raining down exquisite celestial lotuses everywhere throughout the kingdom of King Divaukaspati;

these devaputras then returned to their original location at the pond in the wilderness and rained down celestial flowers once more, before vanishing from there to return to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, where they enjoyed the five celestial desires according to their will.
When that night in Jambudvīpa had passed, King Divyaprabhāsa asked his ministers:
"For what reason did such a pure and wondrous auspicious sign appear last night, accompanied by a great radiance?"
The minister replied,
"Your Majesty should know that the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have rained down forty thousand pearls, necklaces, and incalculable māndārava flowers upon the house of the Elder’s Son, Sudhana."
The king immediately commanded his ministers and officials:
"Go to that householder's home, entice him with kind words, and summon him here.
Having received the decree, the great minister went to the house, proclaimed the king's command, and called for the householder.
At that time, the elder went to the place where the king was.
The king asked the elder,
"For what reason have you manifested such an auspicious omen?"
The son of the elder said,
"I know for certain that these ten thousand fish have already passed away.
Then the great king said:
"Now you must send someone to verify this matter.
Thereupon, Shrotas immediately dispatched his son to the site of that pond to observe whether those fish were dead or alive, in order to ascertain the truth.

At that time, having heard these words, the son went toward that pond; once he arrived at the pond, he saw that within it there were many *mahāmandārava* flowers piled up in heaps, and all the fish therein had lost their lives.
Having seen this, he immediately returned and said to his father,
"Those fish have all already passed away. At that time,
having learned of these matters, Flowing Water went again to the king's presence and spoke these words:
"The ten thousand fish have all reached the end of their lives.
Upon hearing this, the king felt great joy in his heart.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhi-tree goddess of the site of enlightenment:
“Good Goddess!
If you wish to know who that merchant’s son, Flowing Water, was at that time, it is my own self here now;
and his eldest son, Water-Space, is Rāhula here now.”
The second son, Jala-nidhi, is now Ānanda;
those ten thousand fish of that time are now these ten thousand devaputras. For this reason, I now bestow upon them the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"The tree spirit who manifested half her body at that time is your very self now.
*The Combined Edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven;
*The Combined Edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Fascicle Eight.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Baogui of Da Xingshan Monastery during the Sui Dynasty, based on the translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India from the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter 22: The Relinquishing of the Body (8). Chapter Twenty-Two: The Relinquishing of the Body. At that time, the tree-spirit of the Bodhi-maṇḍala again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have heard that when the World-Honored One was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, you fully underwent immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices, relinquishing body, life, flesh, blood, bones, and marrow. I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly explain the causes and conditions of those former ascetic practices, so that sentient beings may receive all manner of happiness.”
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately manifested his supernormal powers.

By the power of these supernormal feats, he caused this great earth to tremble in six ways. In the midst of the assembly within the Great Lecture Hall, a stupa made of the seven treasures emerged from the ground, with nets of various jewels completely covering its summit.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the great assembly gave rise to a sense of wonder.
Then the World-Honored One rose from his seat, paid homage to this stūpa, circumambulated it with reverence, and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the tree deity of the bodhimaṇḍa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, the Hero of the World, has appeared in the world; he is constantly revered by all and is the most supreme and most honored among all sentient beings."
"For what reason and by what causes do you pay homage to this stūpa?
The Buddha said,
"O Goddess of Goodness!"
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, my own bodily relics were enshrined in this stūpa; by virtue of this body, I was enabled to quickly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“You may open the stūpa, take the śarīra from within, and show it to this great assembly.
These śarīras have been perfumed by the merit of immeasurable *ṣaṭ-pāramitā*s.”

At that time, Ānanda, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, went at once to the stūpa, prostrated and made offerings, and opened its door. Within the stūpa he saw a casket of the seven precious gems; opening it with his hand, he beheld the śarīra, wondrously red and white in color. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The śarīra within it is red and white.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You may bring it here; this is the śarīra of the true body of the Great Being."
At that time, Ānanda immediately took up the precious casket and returned to where the Buddha was;
he presented it to the Buddha. Then, the Buddha addressed the entire assembly:
"You all should now pay homage to these relics."
"These relics have been perfumed and cultivated by precept, concentration, and wisdom; they are most difficult to obtain and constitute the supreme field of merit.

At that time, having heard these words, the great assembly felt joy in their hearts; they immediately rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and prostrated themselves before the relics of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to sever the net of doubt for the great assembly, spoke of this past causal connection regarding the śarīra:
"Ānanda! In a past age there was a king named Mahāratha, who practiced wholesome dharmas, governed his realm well, and had no enemies."
At that time, he had three sons who were handsome and exquisite, with extraordinary physical features and preeminent majesty:
the eldest son was named Mahāpuraṇa, the middle son was named Mahādeva, and the youngest son was named Mahāsattva.
"These three princes, while wandering and sightseeing among the gardens and groves, gradually arrived at a large bamboo forest where they halted their carriage to rest.
The eldest prince spoke thus:
'Today my heart is filled with great dread; I fear we shall suffer some misfortune within this forest.'"
The second prince spoke again, saying:
"Today I do not begrudge my own body; I merely grieve because I am separated from that which I love.
The third prince spoke again, saying:
"Today I alone am without fear or anxiety, nor do I have any sorrow or distress.
This mountain is empty and tranquil, praised by the immortals:
'This place is secluded and quiet; it can cause a practitioner to receive peace and joy.'"

When the princes had spoken these words, they proceeded further and saw a tigress that had recently given birth seven days prior; she was surrounded on all sides by her seven cubs, emaciated and distressed by hunger, her body so wasted that her life was on the verge of ending.
When the first prince saw this tiger, he spoke these words:
"How strange! This tiger has been with her cubs for seven days; surrounded by her seven offspring, she is unable to seek food."
"If pressed by hunger, she will surely turn back to devour her own cubs.
The third prince said,
"What is it that this tigress usually eats?"
The first prince said,
"This tiger eats only fresh, warm flesh and blood.
The third prince said:
"Who among you is able to provide food for this tiger?
The second prince said, "This tiger is famished;

its body is emaciated and it is exhausted by its dire distress. Its remaining life is but a short time, and there is no time to seek food for it elsewhere. Even if one were to seek it elsewhere, its life would surely not be saved."
"Who is able to do this without sparing their own body or life?
The first prince said,
"There is nothing more difficult to relinquish than one's own body."
The third prince said:
"Because of our greed and attachment, we are unable to relinquish this body and life;
because our wisdom is meager, we give rise to fear and alarm regarding this matter."
"If great beings wish to benefit others and give rise to great compassion for the sake of sentient beings, it would not be difficult for them to sacrifice this body and life.
At that time, the princes were filled with great sorrow; they remained gazing at him for a long while, their eyes never once leaving him. Having made this observation, they then departed.
"At that time, the third prince thought to himself:
'The time for me to sacrifice my body has now arrived. Why is this?'"

Since time immemorial, I have cast away this body many times for no purpose at all; yet I have always cherished and protected it, dwelling it within houses, and further provided it with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, elephants, horses, and carriages, nourishing it according to the season so that it lacked nothing. Yet it was unaware of my kindness and instead gave rise to resentment and harm; moreover, it could not escape impermanence and decay.

Furthermore, this body is unsubstantial and offers no benefit; it is as loathsome as a thief and like a walking latrine. Today, I shall cause this body to perform the unsurpassed task, acting as a great bridge over the ocean of birth and death.
Furthermore, if one abandons this body, one abandons immeasurable abscesses, ulcers, and diseases, as well as hundreds of thousands of fears; this body consists of nothing but excrement and urine.
This body is not solid, like foam upon the water;
this body is impure, teeming with various openings for parasites;
this body is impure, bound together by sinews, smeared with blood, and held in place by skin, bone, marrow, and brain.

Observing in this way, [this world] is truly to be regarded with weariness and revulsion. Therefore, I should now renounce it in order to seek the quiescent, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, forever free from sorrow and affliction, and beyond impermanence and change. With the cessation of birth and death, free from all worldly burdens, and fully endowed with immeasurable meditative concentrations, wisdom, and merit; possessing a subtle and wondrous *dharmakāya* adorned with a hundred blessings and praised by all Buddhas—I shall realize such an unsurpassed *dharmakāya* and bestow immeasurable Dharma-joy upon all sentient beings.

At that time, the prince, being courageous and capable, made this great vow; having perfumed and cultivated his mind with supreme great compassion, he considered that his two elder brothers might harbor fear and anxiety, or perhaps obstruct him and create difficulties, so he spoke to them:
"Brothers, you should now return to your respective dwellings together with your retinues."
"At that time, Prince Mahāsattva returned to where the tigress was, took off his clothes, placed them upon a bamboo branch, and made this vow:

'I now do so for the benefit of all sentient beings; to realize the most supreme and unsurpassed path; out of great compassion, remaining unshakable in my renunciation of what is difficult to renounce; seeking the wisdom praised by the Buddhas; desiring to deliver all sentient beings from the three realms of existence; and to extinguish the fears of birth and death and the fever of all afflictions.'"
At that time, having made this vow, the prince immediately cast himself down and lay before the starving tigress.
Then, by the power of his great compassion, the tiger was unable to do him any harm.
The prince further thought to himself:
"The tigress is now emaciated and lacks physical strength; she will not be able to eat the flesh and blood of my body.

He immediately rose to seek a knife, but though he searched everywhere, he could find none. He then pierced his own neck with dry bamboo to draw blood and threw himself down from a high mountain before the tigress.

"At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, and the sun lost its brilliance—as if Rāhu, the asura king, had seized and obscured it—and various flowers and diverse wonderful fragrances rained down."
At that time, other devas in the void of space, having seen this event, felt joy in their hearts and, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O Great Being!

You are now truly one who practices great compassion; for the sake of sentient beings, you are able to relinquish what is difficult to give, and among all those in training, you are foremost in valor."
"You have already attained that dwelling place praised by all Buddhas, where one dwells eternally in joy; before long, you shall realize the pure Nirvana that is free from affliction and heat.
At that time, seeing the blood flowing and staining the prince's body, the tigress immediately licked the blood and devoured his flesh, leaving behind only the bones.
At that time, the first prince, seeing the earth shaking violently, spoke these verses for the second prince:
“The great earth and the vast oceans tremble; The sun’s brilliance has lost its luster, as if obscured by a veil.
From the sky above, A rain of various flowers and fragrances falls.”
"It must be my younger brother, who has sacrificed his beloved body.
The second prince then spoke another verse:
"That tigress has been giving birth for seven days already; her seven cubs surround her."
Exhausted and lacking food and drink, his strength was utterly depleted and his life was not far from its end.
My younger brother, moved by great compassion, perceived his wretched state;
fearing he could not endure it, he thought that the man might return to eat his own son, or perhaps resolve to sacrifice his own body to save the other’s life.

At that time, the two princes were filled with great sorrow and fear; weeping and lamenting in grief, their countenances grew haggard. Having seen this, he fainted and could not support himself; he threw his body onto the bones and only after a long while regained consciousness. He immediately rose, raised his hands, and cried out to heaven:
"My younger brother was young and his talents surpassed those of others; he was especially beloved by our parents. How could he have suddenly cast off his life to feed a starving tiger?"
"If I now return to the palace, how shall I answer when my parents question me?

I would rather remain here and perish together with this place than bear to see these bones, hair, and nails. With what heart could I abandon them to return and see my parents, wife, children, kinsmen, friends, and acquaintances?"
At that time, the two princes wailed in grief and distress, gradually departing.
Meanwhile, the attendants who had accompanied the younger prince dispersed in all directions, saying to one another:
"Where now has our lord gone?"
At that time, while the queen was sleeping, she had a dream in which her breasts were cut off, her teeth fell out, and she obtained three young pigeons, one of which was eaten by a hawk.
At that time, when the great earth shook, the queen immediately woke up in alarm; her heart was filled with great sorrow and fear, and she spoke these verses:
"For what reason today do the great earth and the vast waters all tremble?
All things find no rest, and the sun lacks its brilliant radiance, as if it were shrouded by a veil?"
My heart is filled with grief and suffering; my eyelids and muscles twitch.
Given the auspicious signs I have seen this day, there will surely be calamities and portents, as well as misfortune and distress.

Then, after the queen had spoken this verse, a maidservant who was outside and had already heard news of the prince became alarmed and terrified; she immediately entered the inner quarters and addressed the queen, saying:

Upon hearing this, the queen was overcome with great distress; her eyes filled with tears, she went to the Great King and said:

Upon hearing this, the Great King again fainted; choked with grief and tormented by suffering, he wiped away his tears and said:

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "In the past,
throughout immeasurable kalpas, I sacrificed my most cherished body in order to seek bodhi."
Whether as a king or as a prince, I always renounced what is difficult to renounce in order to seek bodhi.
I recall my past lives: there was a great king whose name was Mahāratha.
This king had a son who was able to practice great generosity;
his name was Mahāsattva.
He also had two elder brothers: the eldest was named Mahāpāṇḍara, and the next was named Mahādeva.
The three men were traveling together when they reached an empty mountain, where they saw a newly born tigress who was starving and destitute of food.
At that time, the Great Being Śibi gave rise to a heart of great compassion and thought:
"I shall now sacrifice this body, which I hold so dear."
"This tiger, perhaps driven by hunger, might even turn back to devour its own offspring.
Thinking thus, he immediately climbed a high mountain and threw himself before the tiger, so that the tiger’s cubs might preserve their lives.
At that time, the great earth and all the massive mountains quaked violently,
startling the insects and beasts; tigers, wolves, and lions fled in all directions,
and the world was plunged into darkness, devoid of light.
At that time, the two elder brothers were still at the Bamboo Grove; their hearts were filled with grief and distress, and they wept in sorrowful anguish.
Searching for him gradually, they eventually reached the place where the tiger was, and saw both the tiger and its cubs, their mouths stained with blood.
Furthermore, they saw skeletons, hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, with blood spurting everywhere and strewn in disarray upon the ground.
When the two princes witnessed these things, their hearts were once again overwhelmed with distress, and they collapsed to the earth.
With ashes, dust, and soil, he smeared his own body; having lost right mindfulness, he gave rise to a mind of madness and delusion.
His attendants, witnessing this sight, were likewise moved by grief and lamentation, wailing aloud with cries of sorrow.
They sprinkled each other with cold water, and only then did he revive and rise again. At that time,
when the prince was about to cast off his body, it happened that five hundred members of the inner palace—
consorts, queens, court ladies, and attendants— were together enjoying themselves.
At that time, the queen’s two breasts flowed with milk;

Thereupon the queen hastened to the king’s presence; her voice was faint and low as she wept and said:
"Great King, you must now listen, listen attentively:”
The fierce fire of sorrow now comes to burn me;
from both my breasts, milk flows forth at once, and my body is tormented as if pierced by needles.
I have seen such an inauspicious omen; I fear I shall never again see my beloved son.
Now, I offer my own body and life to Your Majesty; I pray you will quickly dispatch people to search for my son.
I dreamed of three young doves in my embrace; of these, the smallest was most pleasing to my heart.
A hawk flew down, snatched it away from me, and carried it off.
Having dreamed this, I immediately felt grief and distress.
"I am now filled with grief and fear; I dread that my life will not be sustained. I pray you, dispatch someone at once to search for my son.
When the queen had spoken these words, she immediately fainted and fell to the ground.
When the king heard these words, he was again overcome with grief and distress because he could not see his beloved son.
All those gathered there, standing by the king's side, wept and wailed piteously.
The sound shook heaven and earth.
At that time, all the people within the city, having heard this sound, came out in astonishment and said to one another:
"Is this prince now alive and here?"
"Has he already passed away?
Such a Great Being, who always spoke gentle words and was beloved by all,
is now difficult to behold."
"There are already many people who have entered the forest to search; before long, they shall surely obtain certain news.
At that time, the people were thus terrified and distressed, wailing in grief so as to move the gods and spirits with their lamentation.
At that time, the Great King rose from his seat and sprinkled water upon the queen;
after a long while she revived, regained her right mindfulness, and asked the King in a low voice:
"Is my son now alive or dead?"
At that time, because the queen longed for her son, her grief redoubled; her mind could not rest even for a moment as she thought:
"How regrettable it is that my son—so handsome in form and appearance—should suddenly abandon me and pass away!"
Why is it that my body has not yet perished, yet I must witness such matters of suffering and affliction?
My virtuous son, with a wondrous complexion like a pure lotus—whom has he harmed that his body is now torn from me?
Could it not be that I, your former enemy, have come here driven by the karmic conditions of our past deeds to kill you?
My child’s face was as pure as the full moon; I never imagined that in a single day, you would encounter such a calamity.
"May my own body be shattered like dust, rather than let my son lose his life.
The dream I saw has already brought its retribution; meeting me in such a state of mindlessness enables me to endure this suffering."
Both breasts simultaneously, Spontaneously flow with milk;
It must be that I have lost my beloved son.
In a dream, three young pigeons— A hawk snatched one away; Among my three children, I must have lost one.
At that time, the Great King immediately told his consort:

"You should now, for the time being, not grieve so greatly.
Having thus comforted the queen, the Great King immediately prepared his carriage and departed from the palace.
His heart was filled with grief and distress, pierced by the pain of sorrow;
though amidst the great multitude, his countenance was haggard and withered. He immediately left the city to search for his beloved son.
At that time, there were also immeasurable people who wailed with such grief that the earth shook,
following closely behind the king.

At that time, King Mahāratha, having seen this messenger, felt redoubled anguish.
Raising his hands, he wailed and cried out, weeping as he looked up toward heaven; the minister he had previously dispatched soon returned once more.
Having arrived at the king's location, he spoke these words:
"May the King not grieve; your sons are still alive and shall arrive before long, so that the King may behold them."
Again, another minister came and saw that the king was sorrowful and distressed, his countenance haggard and his body clad in garments soiled with grime and dust. He said:
"Great King, you should know: [the situation is as follows...]"
One son has already perished; though two sons remain, they are emaciated with grief and have no recourse.

Having seen this tiger, he gave rise to deep compassion and made a great vow:

He immediately climbed to a high place and threw himself to a starving tiger; driven by hunger, the tiger rose up and devoured him.

At that time, having heard the words of his ministers, the great king fell into a further state of fainting;
losing consciousness, he collapsed to the ground. The fierce fire of his grief and sorrow blazed intensely through his body;

He sprinkled water upon the king, who regained consciousness after a long while; rising again, he raised his hands and wailed to heaven.
Another minister came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"I have seen the two princes, overwhelmed by grief and bitter anguish, wailing and weeping."
Bewildered and distressed, he lost consciousness and threw himself to the ground.
His servant immediately sought water and sprinkled it over his body; after a long while, he finally regained his breath and revived.
Looking out in the four directions, he saw a great fire blazing fiercely;

Because he was separated from his beloved son, his mind was bewildered and overwhelmed;
his strength failed him, and he wept in grief and distress, further reflecting:
"This youngest son was my most cherished love, yet the great ghost of impermanence has suddenly devoured him."
As for my other two sons, though they currently still exist, they are being consumed by the fire of sorrow;
it is possible that because of this, they may lose their very life-force.
I ought to go quickly to that forest, To welcome my sons back and return in haste to the palace.

"If you see my two children, comfort their hearts so that they may preserve their remaining years of life.
At that time, the Great King mounted his famous elephant and, accompanied by his attendants,
set out for that forest.

Taking the two children in his arms, he wept and wailed with grief as he followed the path back to the palace,
where he quickly had the two sons brought to have an audience with their mother.
The Buddha told the tree deity:
"You should now know that the prince Mahāsattva, who at that time gave up his body to feed the tigress, was none other than my own self."
At that time, the great king Mahāratha was none other than our father, King Śuddhodana;
the queen at that time was none other than Māyā;
and the eldest prince was none other than Maitreya.
The second prince is now Devadatta;
the tigress of that time is now Gopī;
and the seven cubs of the tiger are now the five bhikṣus, as well as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.

"At that time, the Great King Mahāratha and his queen, wailing and weeping with grief, all removed their royal robes and jeweled ornaments and went with the great assembly to the Bamboo Grove to collect the relics; they then erected a stupa made of the seven precious substances at this very spot."
"At that time, when Prince Mahāsattva was about to give up his life, he made this vow:

When this sutra was being spoken, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya devas and humans resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“O Tree Spirit!

At that time, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the seven-jeweled stūpa immediately vanished and was no longer seen. Chapter 23:

Praising the Buddha (8) The Sutra of the Golden Light, Chapter Twenty-Three: Praising the Buddha Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang Dynasty At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas traveled from this world to the land of the Tathāgata King of the Mountain of the Golden Jewel Canopy.

Having reached that land, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to the Buddha. Stepping back to stand to one side, they joined their palms toward the Buddha and praised him with one voice:
"The body of the Tathāgata is golden and subtle; its brilliance shines forth like the king of golden mountains."
His body is pure and supple, like a golden lotus; adorned with immeasurable wondrous marks, it is graced by the secondary signs that beautify his form.
Immaculate and beyond compare, it is like a mountain of purple gold;
perfectly complete and stainless, it is like the pure, full moon.
Exquisite like the voice of Brahmā, the roar of a lion, and the thundering of a great storm;
pure in six ways, it is a subtle and wondrous sound, like the voices of the kalaviṅka,
the peacock, and the pheasant.
Pure and stainless, fully endowed with majestic power, adorned with the physical marks and signs of a hundred merits, his body is thus embellished.
His radiance shines afar without limit; his wisdom is tranquil and extinguished, free from all habitual tendencies of craving.
The World-Honored One has accomplished immeasurable merit, like the great ocean or Mount Sumeru,
the mountain of jewels.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, he is able to bestow happiness upon them in future ages.
The foremost, profound meaning spoken by the Tathāgata can cause sentient beings to attain tranquil extinction and peace;
it can bestow immeasurable happiness upon sentient beings;
and it can expound the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma of ambrosia.
Able to open the unsurpassed gateway to the nectar of Dharma;
Able to enter the cave-dwelling of all things, free from affliction;
Attaining complete liberation and crossing over the immeasurable ocean of suffering within the three realms of existence.
Abiding securely in the Right Path, free from all sorrow and suffering;
with merit, wisdom, the power of great compassion, diligence, and skillful means— such as these,
immeasurable and beyond calculation— we now, [take refuge].
One cannot provide a simile;
even by exhausting one's thoughts and measurements, one cannot know the merit and wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata.
I now briefly praise the merits of the Tathāgata; even with hundreds of thousands of millions of parts, I could not proclaim but one.
If my own merit could be gathered together, I would dedicate it to sentient beings so that they may realize the Unsurpassed Way.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa rose from his seat within this assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words of praise:
“World-Honored One of a hundred blessings, Your marks and signs are subtle and wondrous;
A thousandfold merits adorn your body. Your complexion is pure and shines afar; Beholding you, one never tires.”
Like the thousand rays of the sun, filling the void of space, its radiance blazing and intense, immeasurable and boundless.
Its light is of five colors: blue, crimson, red, white, and the hues of lapis lazuli and crystal.
Like refined pure gold, its radiance is brilliant and majestic;
it penetrates through all mountains and is able to shine afar across immeasurable buddha-fields.
They are able to extinguish the immeasurable suffering and affliction of sentient beings, and further bestow upon them supreme and wondrous happiness.
Their faculties are pure and sublime beyond compare; those who behold them can never be satiated.
His hair is deep blue and soft, like the neck of a peacock;
it gathers like the king of bees upon a lotus flower.
Adorned with merit, with immeasurable samādhis, and with great compassion—
All such merits are gathered together.
With the marks and signs of excellence and wondrous beauty, his body is adorned; through these various merits, he brings enlightenment to fulfillment.
The Tathāgata is fully able to subdue sentient beings, causing their minds to become supple and allowing them to experience all manner of happiness.
Adorned with various profound and wondrous merits, he is likewise praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions.

his merit is fully accomplished, like Mount Sumeru, manifesting everywhere throughout all worlds.

they curl to the right in graceful spirals, radiating light like lapis lazuli beads.

Awakening in accordance with their vows,
they emerge alone and preeminent; attaining the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha, they know both existence and non-existence,
for their fundamental nature is pure.
“Rare, rare indeed are the merits of the Tathāgata;
rare, rare indeed is the great ocean of the Tathāgata;
rare, rare indeed is he, like Mount Sumeru.”

rare, rare indeed, is the appearance of a Buddha in the world, like the udumbara flower, appearing but once in an age.

As the sun among men,
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he proclaims such a sublime and precious sūtra.
Excellent, O Tathāgata!
With all faculties stilled, you nevertheless enter and traverse the great city of sublime tranquility;
stainless and pure, through profound samādhi, you enter into the state of all Buddhas.
In all places where they travel,
the bodies of all śrāvakas are entirely empty and quiescent;
even the path traveled by the World-Honored One, the Two-Legged One, is likewise empty.
Thus, all these immeasurable dharmas, when one investigates their fundamental nature and characteristics, are likewise empty and quiescent.
The nature and characteristics of all sentient beings are also empty; yet because of their deluded and ignorant minds, they are unable to realize this.
I constantly mind the Buddha, Delighting in seeing the World-Honored One; I always make this vow: Never to be separated from the Buddha-sun.
Constantly upon the ground, I kneel long with palms joined, My heart full of longing and devotion, desiring to see the Buddha;
I constantly practice the supreme great compassion, Weeping and shedding tears like rain.
I wish to see the Buddha;
I am constantly thirsty and yearning to see the Buddha, and for this reason, the fire of my grief blazes intensely.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me His compassion and the cool water of the Dharma to extinguish this fire.
Out of Your loving-kindness and immeasurable mercy, O World-Honored One,
may I always have the fortune to behold the Buddha.
The World-Honored One constantly protects all humans and devas; therefore, I now thirst for and long to see him.
The bodies of the śrāvakas are like empty space, like a flame, a phantom, an echo, or a transformation; they are like the moon reflected in water.
The nature of sentient beings is like that which is seen in a dream.
Pure as lapis lazuli, he enters the unsurpassed state of the nectar-like Dharma;
he is able to bestow immeasurable happiness upon all sentient beings.
The sphere of the Tathāgata’s activity is subtle and profoundly deep; no sentient beings are able to know it,
nor can the immortals with the five supernatural powers, the śrāvakas, or any pratyekabuddhas know it.
"I now have no doubt regarding the sphere of the Buddha’s activity; I only pray that, out of compassion, you will manifest yourself before me.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and, with a subtle and wondrous voice, praised her, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, O tree-spirit, virtuous daughter!"
"Today you have spoken these words most excellently. **Chapter 24:

Who is able to protect this root of Dharma, which has been accumulated toward enlightenment by these Tathāgatas over incalculable eons, and who, after my parinirvāṇa, shall extensively manifest it so that the True Dharma may long endure?
At that time, among that assembly of bodhisattvas, there were sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas and sixty koṭis of goddesses who, with one voice and in unison, spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
